papers.conclusion: Class selectivity in individual units is neither necessary nor sufficient for CNN performance, and can be detrimental. This encourages caution when focusing on single-unit properties and emphasizes distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
Reducing class selectivity can improve test accuracy, e.g., by over 2% for ResNet18 on Tiny ImageNet.
Class selectivity can be reduced by a factor of 2.5 in ResNet20 on CIFAR10 with no impact on test accuracy, and nearly to zero with only a small drop.
Increasing class selectivity significantly decreases test accuracy across all models and datasets.
The regularizer suppresses selectivity generally, not just by rotating it off-axis, indicating viability of low-selectivity distributed representations.
Networks are at a performance cliff with regard to class selectivity; naturally learned levels are at the limit of what impairs performance.
papers.abstract: The properties of individual neurons are often analyzed in order to understand the biological and artificial neural networks in which they're embedded. Class selectivity-typically defined as how different a neuron's responses are across different classes of stimuli or data samples-is commonly used for this purpose. However, it remains an open question whether it is necessary and/or sufficient for deep neural networks (DNNs) to learn class selectivity in individual units. We investigated the causal impact of class selectivity on network function by directly regularizing for or against class selectivity. Using this regularizer to reduce class selectivity across units in convolutional neural networks increased test accuracy by over 2% for ResNet18 trained on Tiny ImageNet. For ResNet20 trained on CIFAR10 we could reduce class selectivity by a factor of 2.5 with no impact on test accuracy, and reduce it nearly to zero with only a small ($\sim$2%) drop in test accuracy. In contrast, regularizing to increase class selectivity significantly decreased test accuracy across all models and datasets. These results indicate that class selectivity in individual units is neither sufficient nor strictly necessary, and can even impair DNN performance. They also encourage caution when focusing on the properties of single units as representative of the mechanisms by which DNNs function.

papers.title: Properties from Mechanisms: An Equivariance Perspective on Identifiable\n Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can we identify latent properties by leveraging knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?
papers.core_contribution: If we know the exact mechanisms under which latent properties evolve, then identification can be achieved up to any equivariances that are shared by the underlying mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: By exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of new identifiable representation learning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
When the true mechanism is known, the system is identified up to any equivariances of the mechanism.
With multiple known mechanisms, identification is up to equivariances shared by all mechanisms.
When only a hypothesis class of possible mechanisms is known, additional non-identifiability arises via imitation among mechanisms.
For affine mechanisms with distinct eigenvalues and certain conditions, identification is up to an offset.
The framework generalizes to stochastic mechanisms and can recover existing identifiability results, such as those in Klindt et al. (2020).
papers.limitation: The analysis assumes the encoder/decoder functions are bijective and that reconstruction is perfectly solved, which is a strong assumption and not easy in practice.
papers.abstract:
A key goal of unsupervised representation learning is "inverting" a data
generating process to recover its latent properties. Existing work that
provably achieves this goal relies on strong assumptions on relationships
between the latent variables (e.g., independence conditional on auxiliary
information). In this paper, we take a very different perspective on the
problem and ask, "Can we instead identify latent properties by leveraging
knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?" We provide a complete
characterization of the sources of non-identifiability as we vary knowledge
about a set of possible mechanisms. In particular, we prove that if we know the
exact mechanisms under which the latent properties evolve, then identification
can be achieved up to any equivariances that are shared by the underlying
mechanisms. We generalize this characterization to settings where we only know
some hypothesis class over possible mechanisms, as well as settings where the
mechanisms are stochastic. We demonstrate the power of this mechanism-based
perspective by showing that we can leverage our results to generalize existing
identifiable representation learning results. These results suggest that by
exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of
new identifiable representation learning approaches.

papers.title: Critical Learning Periods in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do deep artificial neural networks exhibit critical periods during training similar to biological systems, and how does the early training phase affect the final performance and network connectivity?
papers.core_contribution: Deep neural networks exhibit critical periods during training where early sensory deficits cause permanent performance impairment, and this phenomenon is linked to a loss of 'Information Plasticity' measurable via the Fisher Information of the weights.
papers.conclusion: Critical periods are not restricted to biological systems but emerge naturally in learning systems due to fundamental constraints arising from learning dynamics and information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks exhibit critical periods: early sensory deficits (e.g., image blur) can cause permanent impairment in final performance.
Sensitivity to deficits peaks during the early rapid learning phase and decreases afterward.
High-level deficits (e.g., vertical flip, label permutation) do not induce critical periods.
The Fisher Information of the weights shows two phases: an initial increase (memorization) followed by a decrease (consolidation), and deficit sensitivity correlates with Fisher Information.
The loss of 'Information Plasticity' (inability to redistribute information across layers) underlies the critical period phenomenon.
future_direction: Exploring whether biological networks prune connections as a consequence of a loss of Information Plasticity, rather than as a cause.
papers.abstract: Similar to humans and animals, deep artificial neural networks exhibit critical periods during which a temporary stimulus deficit can impair the development of a skill. The extent of the impairment depends on the onset and length of the deficit window, as in animal models, and on the size of the neural network. Deficits that do not affect low-level statistics, such as vertical flipping of the images, have no lasting effect on performance and can be overcome with further training. To better understand this phenomenon, we use the Fisher Information of the weights to measure the effective connectivity between layers of a network during training. Counterintuitively, information rises rapidly in the early phases of training, and then decreases, preventing redistribution of information resources in a phenomenon we refer to as a loss of "Information Plasticity". Our analysis suggests that the first few epochs are critical for the creation of strong connections that are optimal relative to the input data distribution. Once such strong connections are created, they do not appear to change during additional training. These findings suggest that the initial learning transient, under-scrutinized compared to asymptotic behavior, plays a key role in determining the outcome of the training process. Our findings, combined with recent theoretical results in the literature, also suggest that forgetting (decrease of information in the weights) is critical to achieving invariance and disentanglement in representation learning. Finally, critical periods are not restricted to biological systems, but can emerge naturally in learning systems, whether biological or artificial, due to fundamental constrains arising from learning dynamics and information processing.

papers.title: Interpretation of Deep CNN Based on Learning Feature Reconstruction With Feedback Weights
papers.research_question: How can we interpret a deep CNN by learning feature reconstruction with feedback weights to understand which features contribute to recognition and evaluate recognition success?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes attaching a feedback CNN to a pretrained feedforward CNN to interpret the deep CNN by reconstructing features and analyzing clusters in feature spaces, enabling accurate recovery of ground truth, generation of novel inputs, and identification of recognition errors.
papers.conclusion: The feedback weights provide a means to interpret the deep CNN, and the clustering-based interpretation and feature interpolation algorithm offer meaningful insights into neuron collaboration and recognition.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed approach accurately recovers ground truth input under data corruption.
It generates novel input data corresponding to an untrained feature vector without input data iterations.
It identifies incorrectly recognized input data by pinpointing the source of error in feature spaces.
The experiments on ModelNet datasets show higher accuracy than conventional approaches.
future_direction: Extend interpretation to connect semantic knowledge while extracting meaningful features using a deep neural network.
papers.abstract: Interpreting a deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) involves identifying the features in a hierarchy of layers that contribute to recognition. Although the current approaches serve as methods to interpret a deep CNN, further advancement is required for a more accurate and efficient way of understanding how a hierarchy of features formed by a deep CNN contributes to recognition. In this paper, we propose attaching a feedback CNN to a pretrained feedforward CNN as a means of learning how recognition is performed by the feedforward CNN. In other words, the features reconstructed in a hierarchy of the feedback CNN represent those learned by the feedforward CNN. By analyzing how clusters are formed in the layers of feature spaces in the feedback CNN, we can interpret which features critically contribute to recognition. It also helps to evaluate whether or not recognition is done successfully. In order to show this, we experimentally verify the capabilities of the proposed approach in terms of 1) accurately recovering the ground truth input under data corruption; 2) generating novel input data corresponding to an untrained feature vector without input data iterations; and 3) identifying incorrectly recognized input data by pinpointing the source of the error in feature spaces. The experiments conducted on the ModelNet datasets indicate that the proposed approach offers an extended capability of interpreting a deep CNN as described above with higher accuracy than the conventional approaches.

papers.title: Learning from Emergence: A Study on Proactively Inhibiting the Monosemantic Neurons of Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether reducing monosemantic neurons in neural networks can improve performance, and proposes a method to proactively inhibit them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes that reducing monosemantic neurons improves model performance and introduces a metric (Monosemantic Scale) and a method (Reverse Deactivation) to inhibit monosemantic neurons during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that proactively inhibiting monosemantic neurons via the proposed MEmeL method can improve model performance across various tasks and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
MEmeL improves performance on language (GLUE), image (ImageNet), and precipitation forecasting (HKO-7) tasks.
Monosemanticity decreases with model scale, and inhibiting it can lead to better performance.
Naive deactivation methods can intensify monosemanticity, while the proposed Reverse Deactivation method effectively reduces it.
The proposed Monosemantic Scale metric enables efficient online detection of monosemantic neurons.
Pretraining with MEmeL shows greater improvement than finetuning with it, supporting the hypothesis that reducing monosemanticity enhances general ability.
papers.limitation: Extending the research to very large models (e.g., large language models) is appealing yet impossible for research departments due to limited computational resources.
future_direction: Extending the method to extremely large models trained on large datasets.
Studying the dynamics of MEmeL in more depth.
papers.abstract: Recently, emergence has received widespread attention from the research community along with the success of large-scale models. Different from the literature, we hypothesize a key factor that promotes the performance during the increase of scale: the reduction of monosemantic neurons that can only form one-to-one correlations with specific features. Monosemantic neurons tend to be sparser and have negative impacts on the performance in large models. Inspired by this insight, we propose an intuitive idea to identify monosemantic neurons and inhibit them. However, achieving this goal is a non-trivial task as there is no unified quantitative evaluation metric and simply banning monosemantic neurons does not promote polysemanticity in neural networks. Therefore, we first propose a new metric to measure the monosemanticity of neurons with the guarantee of efficiency for online computation, then introduce a theoretically supported method to suppress monosemantic neurons and proactively promote the ratios of polysemantic neurons in training neural networks. We validate our conjecture that monosemanticity brings about performance change at different model scales on a variety of neural networks and benchmark datasets in different areas, including language, image, and physics simulation tasks. Further experiments validate our analysis and theory regarding the inhibition of monosemanticity.

papers.title: Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity
papers.research_question: Is there a general mechanism behind a broad suite of subliminal effects in language model training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Logit-Linear Selection (LLS), a method to select subsets of preference data that subliminally transfer behaviors, and provides a theoretical framework based on log-linearity to explain the phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: LLS provides a general mechanism for subliminal effects in language models, grounded in the log-linear structure of language models, with implications for data selection and safety.
papers.key_findings:
LLS can select subsets of real-world datasets to elicit hidden effects such as specific preferences, responding in a different language, and adopting a persona.
The subliminal effect persists across models with varying architectures, demonstrating universality.
The mechanism is explained by the log-linear abstraction and linear representations of language models.
Subliminal learning can occur even when the dataset contains no obvious instances of the target behavior.
The method works with preference data and can transfer behaviors across teacher-student model pairs, though more effectively when models are the same.
papers.limitation: The subliminal effect is weaker when the teacher and student models are different, and the reasons for this variation are not fully understood.
future_direction: Understanding the factors that account for variations in subliminal learning across different student models.
Developing defenses against subliminal learning in datasets.
Applying LLS for jailbreaking closed models and watermarking datasets.
papers.abstract: Training modern large language models (LLMs) has become a veritable smorgasbord of algorithms and datasets designed to elicit particular behaviors, making it critical to develop techniques to understand the effects of datasets on the model's properties. This is exacerbated by recent experiments that show datasets can transmit signals that are not directly observable from individual datapoints, posing a conceptual challenge for dataset-centric understandings of LLM training and suggesting a missing fundamental account of such phenomena. Towards understanding such effects, inspired by recent work on the linear structure of LLMs, we uncover a general mechanism through which hidden subtexts can arise in generic datasets. We introduce Logit-Linear-Selection (LLS), a method that prescribes how to select subsets of a generic preference dataset to elicit a wide range of hidden effects. We apply LLS to discover subsets of real-world datasets so that models trained on them exhibit behaviors ranging from having specific preferences, to responding to prompts in a different language not present in the dataset, to taking on a different persona. Crucially, the effect persists for the selected subset, across models with varying architectures, supporting its generality and universality.

papers.title: Complexity for deep neural networks and other characteristics of deep feature representations
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the nonlinearity and effective dimensionality of feature representations in deep neural networks, and how do these measures vary with depth, dataset, and during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces two observables—complexity and effective dimension—to quantify the nonlinearity and dimensionality of feature representations in deep neural networks, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing depth-wise hierarchy, dataset difficulty, and training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The introduced observables provide quantitative insight into the information processing and feature representations in neural networks, and can be applied to both artificial and biological neural systems, opening up new research directions.
papers.key_findings:
Complexity and effective dimension increase with the difficulty of the dataset.
During training, complexity increases first, followed by a rise in effective dimension.
Total correlation between neurons decreases during training, following a power law.
The observables can be applied to biological neural data (mouse visual cortex) and show similar trends.
The observables reveal a depth-wise hierarchy in feature representations, with higher layers having higher complexity and effective dimension for more difficult datasets.
papers.limitation: The method is defined for ReLU activations and may not generalize to other activation functions.
future_direction: Investigate interrelations with the Information Bottleneck principle.
Use methods from statistical physics (e.g., Ising models) for analysis.
Apply the observables to more complex networks and tasks.
papers.abstract: We define a notion of complexity, which quantifies the nonlinearity of the computation of a neural network, as well as a complementary measure of the effective dimension of feature representations. We investigate these observables both for trained networks for various datasets as well as explore their dynamics during training, uncovering in particular power law scaling. These observables can be understood in a dual way as uncovering hidden internal structure of the datasets themselves as a function of scale or depth. The entropic character of the proposed notion of complexity should allow to transfer modes of analysis from neuroscience and statistical physics to the domain of artificial neural networks. The introduced observables can be applied without any change to the analysis of biological neuronal systems.

papers.title: Learning-induced reorganization of number neurons and emergence of numerical representations in a biologically inspired neural network
papers.research_question: How does numerosity training reorganize neuronal tuning properties and population-level representations in a biologically inspired neural network?
papers.core_contribution: Numerosity training reorganizes neuronal tuning and population representations, leading to the emergence of sharp numerosity tuning and latent magnitude representations in a biologically inspired neural network.
papers.conclusion: Our findings elucidate mechanisms by which learning builds novel representations supporting number sense.
papers.key_findings:
Numerosity training reorganizes spontaneous number neurons (SPONs), with most SPONs dropping or switching their preferred numerosity.
Training increases tuning precision, stability, and selectivity of number-sensitive neurons, especially in the IPS layer.
Ablation shows that persistent SPONs are not critical for numerosity classification; newly trained and switched neurons are more important.
Representational similarity analysis reveals increased differentiation between numerosities after training.
Multidimensional scaling reveals latent representations of absolute magnitude and relative magnitude (midpoint anchoring) post-training.
papers.abstract: Number sense, the ability to decipher quantity, forms the foundation for mathematical cognition. How number sense emerges with learning is, however, not known. Here we use a biologically-inspired neural architecture comprising cortical layers V1, V2, V3, and intraparietal sulcus (IPS) to investigate how neural representations change with numerosity training. Learning dramatically reorganized neuronal tuning properties at both the single unit and population levels, resulting in the emergence of sharply-tuned representations of numerosity in the IPS layer. Ablation analysis revealed that spontaneous number neurons observed prior to learning were not critical to formation of number representations post-learning. Crucially, multidimensional scaling of population responses revealed the emergence of absolute and relative magnitude representations of quantity, including mid-point anchoring. These learnt representations may underlie changes from logarithmic to cyclic and linear mental number lines that are characteristic of number sense development in humans. Our findings elucidate mechanisms by which learning builds novel representations supporting number sense.

papers.title: The Lazy Neuron Phenomenon: On Emergence of Activation Sparsity in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the prevalence, causes, and benefits of activation sparsity in Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that activation sparsity is a prevalent phenomenon in Transformers, arising from training dynamics, and that enforcing sparsity via Top-k Transformers improves efficiency, robustness, and calibration.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that activation sparsity is a fundamental property of trained Transformers with benefits for efficiency and reliability, and it may stem from training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Activation sparsity is prevalent in Transformers for both NLP and vision tasks, across all layers.
Larger Transformers (deeper and wider) are sparser in terms of percentage of nonzero activations.
Sparsity emerges even with random labels, random images, or infinite data, suggesting it is due to training dynamics rather than dataset properties.
Sparsity reduces FLOPs and can improve computational efficiency during inference.
Enforcing sparser activation via Top-k Transformers improves robustness to noisy training data, input corruptions, and calibration of prediction confidence.
papers.limitation: The benefit of sparse activation is not fully realized due to lack of hardware support for sparse computation.
papers.abstract: This paper studies the curious phenomenon for machine learning models with Transformer architectures that their activation maps are sparse. By activation map we refer to the intermediate output of the multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) after a ReLU activation function, and by sparse we mean that on average very few entries (e.g., 3.0% for T5-Base and 6.3% for ViT-B16) are nonzero for each input to MLP. Moreover, larger Transformers with more layers and wider MLP hidden dimensions are sparser as measured by the percentage of nonzero entries. Through extensive experiments we demonstrate that the emergence of sparsity is a prevalent phenomenon that occurs for both natural language processing and vision tasks, on both training and evaluation data, for Transformers of various configurations, at layers of all depth levels, as well as for other architectures including MLP-mixers and 2-layer MLPs. We show that sparsity also emerges using training datasets with random labels, or with random inputs, or with infinite amount of data, demonstrating that sparsity is not a result of a specific family of datasets. We discuss how sparsity immediately implies a way to significantly reduce the FLOP count and improve efficiency for Transformers. Moreover, we demonstrate perhaps surprisingly that enforcing an even sparser activation via Top-k thresholding with a small value of k brings a collection of desired but missing properties for Transformers, namely less sensitivity to noisy training data, more robustness to input corruptions, and better calibration for their prediction confidence.

papers.title: Half-Space Feature Learning in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks learn features? The paper investigates whether neural networks learn simple half-space features and how gradient descent allocates resources (paths) to different regions of the input space.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Deep Linearly Gated Network (DLGN), a model that learns simple half-space features, and shows that feature learning in neural networks involves gradient descent allocating more paths to easier regions of the input space.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn simple half-space features, and that gradient descent allocates more resources to easier regions, which can be visualized in DLGNs, providing enhanced interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DLGNs can perform comparably to ReLU networks on datasets like CIFAR-10 while being more interpretable.
Feature learning in neural networks involves changes in the active path regions, which can be tracked via the overlap kernel.
Gradient descent tends to allocate more paths (resources) to regions of the input space where the target function is simpler (lower frequency).
The empirical NTK changes during training to become better suited to the task, and this change is driven by the evolution of active path regions.
In DLGNs, neurons in later layers tend to specialize to simpler regions (e.g., half-spaces) that cover low-frequency parts of the target function.
papers.limitation: Analysis of ReLU networks is complicated due to their complex path active regions, so the study uses DLGNs as a surrogate.
future_direction: Investigating defects of gradient descent in resource allocation and developing architecture-aware optimization algorithms.
Further study of the phenomenon of neurons focusing on easy regions.
papers.abstract: There currently exist two extreme viewpoints for neural network feature learning -- (i) Neural networks simply implement a kernel method (a la NTK) and hence no features are learned (ii) Neural networks can represent (and hence learn) intricate hierarchical features suitable for the data. We argue in this paper neither interpretation is likely to be correct based on a novel viewpoint. Neural networks can be viewed as a mixture of experts, where each expert corresponds to a (number of layers length) path through a sequence of hidden units. We use this alternate interpretation to motivate a model, called the Deep Linearly Gated Network (DLGN), which sits midway between deep linear networks and ReLU networks. Unlike deep linear networks, the DLGN is capable of learning non-linear features (which are then linearly combined), and unlike ReLU networks these features are ultimately simple -- each feature is effectively an indicator function for a region compactly described as an intersection of (number of layers) half-spaces in the input space. This viewpoint allows for a comprehensive global visualization of features, unlike the local visualizations for neurons based on saliency/activation/gradient maps. Feature learning in DLGNs is shown to happen and the mechanism with which this happens is through learning half-spaces in the input space that contain smooth regions of the target function. Due to the structure of DLGNs, the neurons in later layers are fundamentally the same as those in earlier layers -- they all represent a half-space -- however, the dynamics of gradient descent impart a distinct clustering to the later layer neurons. We hypothesize that ReLU networks also have similar feature learning behaviour.

papers.title: Usable Information and Evolution of Optimal Representations During Training
papers.research_question: How do optimal (minimal and sufficient) representations emerge during training in deep networks, and what is the role of implicit regularization from SGD?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a notion of 'usable information' to study training dynamics, showing that SGD with high learning rate and small batch size leads to minimal sufficient representations through a dynamic process of acquiring and later discarding irrelevant information.
papers.conclusion: Usable information is a useful tool for studying training dynamics, revealing that SGD with specific hyperparameters leads to minimal representations through a dynamic process of acquiring and then discarding irrelevant information.
papers.key_findings:
SGD with random initialization leads to minimal sufficient representations in the checkerboard task and image classification.
Networks acquire semantically meaningful but irrelevant information early in training and later discard it to achieve minimality.
The learning dynamics (acquisition and forgetting) depend on hyperparameters like learning rate and batch size.
Pretraining on irrelevant information can prevent the formation of minimal representations and hurt generalization.
The phenomenon is observed in both simple perceptual tasks and standard image classification tasks with modern architectures.
papers.limitation: The usable information is estimated with a decoder network, which may not capture all information present in the representation.
future_direction: Investigate the tightness of the bound between usable information and mutual information.
Extend the approach to other tasks and architectures.
papers.abstract: We introduce a notion of usable information contained in the representation learned by a deep network, and use it to study how optimal representations for the task emerge during training. We show that the implicit regularization coming from training with Stochastic Gradient Descent with a high learning-rate and small batch size plays an important role in learning minimal sufficient representations for the task. In the process of arriving at a minimal sufficient representation, we find that the content of the representation changes dynamically during training. In particular, we find that semantically meaningful but ultimately irrelevant information is encoded in the early transient dynamics of training, before being later discarded. In addition, we evaluate how perturbing the initial part of training impacts the learning dynamics and the resulting representations. We show these effects on both perceptual decision-making tasks inspired by neuroscience literature, as well as on standard image classification tasks.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks to Improve Politeness Comprehension
papers.research_question: What do neural networks learn about politeness in natural language requests, and can we interpret their success?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents an interpretable CNN approach for politeness prediction and uses visualization techniques to understand what the network learns, discovering novel politeness strategies that improve feature-based models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretable neural network approach improves politeness prediction and provides insights into learned politeness strategies, which in turn help improve feature-based models.
papers.key_findings:
The CNN model outperforms previous feature-based methods on politeness prediction.
Visualization techniques (activation clustering, saliency, embedding transformations) rediscover, extend, and discover novel politeness strategies.
Two novel strategies, indefinite pronouns and punctuation, are identified as high-scoring negative politeness markers.
Adding the discovered strategies as features to the baseline featurized system improves its accuracy, reducing the performance gap with the neural model.
The analysis provides a quantitative interpretation of the neural network's success by linking discovered features to performance gains.
papers.abstract: We present an interpretable neural network approach to predicting and understanding politeness in natural language requests. Our models are based on simple convolutional neural networks directly on raw text, avoiding any manual identification of complex sentiment or syntactic features, while performing better than such feature-based models from previous work. More importantly, we use the challenging task of politeness prediction as a testbed to next present a much-needed understanding of what these successful networks are actually learning. For this, we present several network visualizations based on activation clusters, first derivative saliency, and embedding space transformations, helping us automatically identify several subtle linguistics markers of politeness theories. Further, this analysis reveals multiple novel, high-scoring politeness strategies which, when added back as new features, reduce the accuracy gap between the original featurized system and the neural model, thus providing a clear quantitative interpretation of the success of these neural networks.

papers.title: Representation biases: will we achieve complete understanding by analyzing representations?
papers.research_question: Will we achieve complete understanding by analyzing representations, given biases in learned feature representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that representation biases in learned models can lead to biased inferences from common representational analyses, challenging the assumption that variance in representations reflects computational importance.
papers.conclusion: While representational analysis remains useful, representation biases can limit our ability to achieve complete understanding; a focus on behavior and causal interventions is needed.
papers.key_findings:
Learned feature representations are biased towards simpler (linear) features over complex (nonlinear) ones, even when both are computed reliably.
These representation biases cause common analytic methods like PCA, regression, and RSA to be biased towards certain features.
Representation biases can lead to misleading conclusions when comparing models via representational similarity, e.g., models computing different functions can appear more similar than models computing the same function.
The biases are driven by factors like learning order and the multiplicity of representational solutions for nonlinear features.
Homomorphic encryption provides an extreme case where computation and representation are strongly dissociated.
future_direction: Exploring whether modified metrics can help ameliorate representation biases
Focusing on completely characterizing behavior and the causal role of representations
papers.abstract: A common approach in neuroscience is to study neural representations as a means to understand a system -- increasingly, by relating the neural representations to the internal representations learned by computational models. However, a recent work in machine learning (Lampinen, 2024) shows that learned feature representations may be biased to over-represent certain features, and represent others more weakly and less-consistently. For example, simple (linear) features may be more strongly and more consistently represented than complex (highly nonlinear) features. These biases could pose challenges for achieving full understanding of a system through representational analysis. In this perspective, we illustrate these challenges -- showing how feature representation biases can lead to strongly biased inferences from common analyses like PCA, regression, and RSA. We also present homomorphic encryption as a simple case study of the potential for strong dissociation between patterns of representation and computation. We discuss the implications of these results for representational comparisons between systems, and for neuroscience more generally.

papers.title: Microscopic and collective signatures of feature learning in neural networks
papers.research_question: What are the collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks in the proportional regime?
papers.core_contribution: In the proportional regime, feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks is characterized by a nonmonotonic distance between class manifolds and finite, data-dependent weight correlations.
papers.conclusion: The squared distance between class manifolds and the finite weight correlations are collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow networks in the proportional regime.
papers.key_findings:
The posterior distance between class manifolds remains unaltered in the infinite-width limit but departs from its prior value at proportional width.
The average squared distance is a nonmonotonic function of temperature, and this nonmonotonicity disappears in the infinite-width limit or when labels are randomized.
The hidden-layer weights become correlated in the proportional regime, undergoing a finite displacement.
The nonmonotonicity of the distance aligns with inversion dynamics observed during gradient descent training, serving as an equilibrium counterpart.
The second-order statistics of the weights depends on input patterns in a way not traceable to the infinite-width limit.
papers.limitation:
The results are limited to standard-scaled neural networks and do not apply to mean-field scaling.
The theory does not characterize feature learning closer to the interpolation threshold.
papers.abstract: Feature extraction - the ability to identify relevant properties of data - is a key factor underlying the success of deep learning. Yet, it has proved difficult to elucidate its nature within existing predictive theories, to the extent that there is no consensus on the very definition of feature learning. A promising hint in this direction comes from previous phenomenological observations of quasi-universal aspects in the training dynamics of neural networks, displayed by simple properties of feature geometry. We address this problem within a statistical-mechanics framework for Bayesian learning in one hidden layer neural networks with standard parameterization. Analytical computations in the proportional limit (when both the network width and the size of the training set are large) can quantify fingerprints of feature learning, both collective ones (related to manifold geometry) and microscopic ones (related to the weights). In particular, (i) the distance between different class manifolds in feature space is a nonmonotonic function of the temperature, which we interpret as the equilibrium counterpart of a phenomenon observed under gradient descent (GD) dynamics, and (ii) the microscopic learnable parameters in the network undergo a finite data-dependent displacement with respect to the infinite-width limit, and develop correlations. These results indicate that nontrivial feature learning is at play in a regime where the posterior predictive distribution is that of Gaussian process regression with a trivially rescaled prior.

papers.title: The Low-Dimensional Linear Geometry of Contextualized Word Representations
papers.research_question: How are linguistic features encoded in the linear geometry of contextualized word representations, and what are the geometric properties of these encodings?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that linguistic features are encoded in low-dimensional linear subspaces of contextualized word representations, that these subspaces have hierarchical structure and are distributed across neurons, and that they are causally relevant to model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a probing procedure that reveals low-dimensional linear subspaces encoding linguistic features in word representations, with hierarchical and distributed structure, and shows these subspaces are causally relevant to model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic features are encoded in low-dimensional subspaces of contextualized word representations.
These subspaces exhibit hierarchical structure (e.g., noun and verb subspaces nested within part-of-speech subspaces).
The subspaces are distributed across neurons rather than aligned with individual axes.
Ablating specific subspaces (e.g., nounspace or verbspace) impairs BERT's performance on subject-verb agreement, indicating causal relevance.
Contextual representations encode linguistic variables better but not more compactly than non-contextual word embeddings.
future_direction: Explore richer geometric structure in word representations and its effect on model behavior.
papers.abstract: Black-box probing models can reliably extract linguistic features like tense, number, and syntactic role from pretrained word representations. However, the manner in which these features are encoded in representations remains poorly understood. We present a systematic study of the linear geometry of contextualized word representations in ELMO and BERT. We show that a variety of linguistic features (including structured dependency relationships) are encoded in low-dimensional subspaces. We then refine this geometric picture, showing that there are hierarchical relations between the subspaces encoding general linguistic categories and more specific ones, and that lowdimensional feature encodings are distributed rather than aligned to individual neurons. Finally, we demonstrate that these linear subspaces are causally related to model behavior, and can be used to perform fine-grained manipulation of BERT's output distribution.

papers.title: Layer-Wise Interpretation of Deep Neural Networks Using Identity Initialization
papers.research_question: How can deep multilayer perceptrons be interpreted using identity initialization to analyze the contribution of each neuron to classification and class likelihood in each hidden layer?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an interpretation method for deep MLPs using identity initialization, enabling layer-wise analysis of neuron contributions to classification and class likelihoods, with theoretical demonstration of gradient propagation and experimental validation of weight proximity to identity.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents an interpretation method for MLPs based on identity initialization, demonstrating its effectiveness through theoretical analysis and experiments, and suggests future work on learning dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Identity-initialized MLPs can be trained without vanishing or exploding gradients due to dynamical isometry.
Learned weight matrices remain close to identity matrices after training.
Internal features can be separated into contribution maps and class likelihoods, allowing visualization of discriminative regions.
The contribution map becomes more discriminative in layers closer to the output.
The network uses early layers for feature extraction and later layers for classification.
papers.limitation: Test accuracy is lower than training accuracy because the theoretical result guarantees learnability, not generalization capability.
future_direction: Investigate changes in contribution maps and the starting layer of classification during learning.
papers.abstract: The interpretability of neural networks (NNs) is a challenging but essential topic for transparency in the decision-making process using machine learning. One of the reasons for the lack of interpretability is random weight initialization, where the input is randomly embedded into a different feature space in each layer. In this paper, we propose an interpretation method for a deep multilayer perceptron, which is the most general architecture of NNs, based on identity initialization (namely, initialization using identity matrices). The proposed method allows us to analyze the contribution of each neuron to classification and class likelihood in each hidden layer. As a property of the identity-initialized perceptron, the weight matrices remain near the identity matrices even after learning. This property enables us to treat the change of features from the input to each hidden layer as the contribution to classification. Furthermore, we can separate the output of each hidden layer into a contribution map that depicts the contribution to classification and class likelihood, by adding extra dimensions to each layer according to the number of classes, thereby allowing the calculation of the recognition accuracy in each layer and thus revealing the roles of independent layers, such as feature extraction and classification.

papers.title: Identifying and Disentangling Spurious Features in Pretrained Image Representations
papers.research_question: How are spurious features represented in pretrained image representations, and how can we remove or disentangle them to improve worst-group accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a linear autoencoder method to disentangle core and spurious features in pretrained image representations, leading to improved worst-group accuracy in classification.
papers.conclusion: Spurious features in pretrained representations can be identified and removed, and disentangling them via a linear autoencoder improves worst-group accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Pretrained representations contain spurious features that can be identified and removed to improve worst-group accuracy.
For some representations (ResNet-50 and RegNetY), spurious features are axis-aligned, allowing removal by dropping specific neurons.
For DINOv2, individual neurons are not pure spurious or non-spurious, so simple removal does not work.
The proposed linear autoencoder (GwAE) can disentangle core and spurious features, and training a classifier on the core part improves worst-group accuracy.
Applying PCA on the core features from the autoencoder further improves performance.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to the Waterbirds dataset and three backbones (ResNet-50, RegNetY, DINOv2).
The method requires group information (spurious feature labels) for training the autoencoder.
The use of L-BFGS for linear models may not capture the full potential of SGD with early stopping, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Experiments with more backbones and datasets to see how well the findings generalize.
Analysis of SGD-based optimization with early stopping for linear models.
papers.abstract: Neural networks employ spurious correlations in their predictions, resulting in decreased performance when these correlations do not hold. Recent works suggest fixing pretrained representations and training a classification head that does not use spurious features. We investigate how spurious features are represented in pretrained representations and explore strategies for removing information about spurious features. Considering the Waterbirds dataset and a few pretrained representations, we find that even with full knowledge of spurious features, their removal is not straightforward due to entangled representation. To address this, we propose a linear autoencoder training method to separate the representation into core, spurious, and other features. We propose two effective spurious feature removal approaches that are applied to the encoding and significantly improve classification performance measured by worst group accuracy.

papers.title: What Causes Polysemanticity? An Alternative Origin Story of Mixed Selectivity from Incidental Causes
papers.research_question: What causes polysemanticity? Can it arise incidentally from non-task factors like regularization and noise, even when there are enough neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Polysemanticity can arise incidentally from non-task factors like regularization and noise, even when there are enough neurons to represent all features, due to random initialization and training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Incidental polysemanticity poses a challenge for interpretability and may require new methods to mitigate, as simply increasing neurons is insufficient; future work could explore ways to nudge learning trajectories to avoid it.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemanticity can arise from l1 regularization due to winner-take-all dynamics.
Polysemanticity can also arise from noise in the hidden layer when the noise has negative excess kurtosis.
The number of polysemantic neurons scales as Θ(n^2/m) in the regularization case.
Incidental polysemanticity can occur even when the number of neurons m is greater than or equal to the number of features n.
Different types of polysemantic configurations can arise depending on the incidental factor (e.g., regularization vs. noise).
future_direction: Developing methods to eliminate incidental polysemanticity by nudging learning trajectories
Distinguishing incidental from necessary polysemanticity in practice
Investigating dependence on architecture and data
papers.abstract: Polysemantic neurons -- neurons that activate for a set of unrelated features -- have been seen as a significant obstacle towards interpretability of task-optimized deep networks, with implications for AI safety. The classic origin story of polysemanticity is that the data contains more ``features" than neurons, such that learning to perform a task forces the network to co-allocate multiple unrelated features to the same neuron, endangering our ability to understand networks' internal processing. In this work, we present a second and non-mutually exclusive origin story of polysemanticity. We show that polysemanticity can arise incidentally, even when there are ample neurons to represent all features in the data, a phenomenon we term \textit{incidental polysemanticity}. Using a combination of theory and experiments, we show that incidental polysemanticity can arise due to multiple reasons including regularization and neural noise; this incidental polysemanticity occurs because random initialization can, by chance alone, initially assign multiple features to the same neuron, and the training dynamics then strengthen such overlap. Our paper concludes by calling for further research quantifying the performance-polysemanticity tradeoff in task-optimized deep neural networks to better understand to what extent polysemanticity is avoidable.

papers.title: What Do Neural Networks Learn When Trained With Random Labels?
papers.research_question: What do deep neural networks learn when trained on natural image data with entirely random labels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that training neural networks with random labels leads to an alignment between the principal components of the network parameters and the data, which explains positive transfer in downstream tasks, while specialization in later layers can cause negative transfer.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks trained on random labels learn an alignment between weight covariance and data covariance, which can benefit downstream tasks, but specialization in later layers may sometimes hide this benefit.
papers.key_findings:
An alignment between the principal components of the first layer weights and the data covariance occurs when training with random labels.
This alignment leads to positive transfer: pre-training on random labels accelerates downstream training even after accounting for weight scaling.
Specialization in later layers can lead to negative transfer by causing inactive ReLUs, which masks the positive alignment effect.
The alignment effect is also observed when training on real labels.
The transfer function f(σ) mapping data eigenvalues to weight eigenvalues has a regular shape (increasing then decreasing).
papers.limitation:
Theoretical alignment result is proven for centered Gaussian inputs.
Data augmentation is not used, which could provide additional supervisory signal.
Specialization in later layers can lead to negative transfer.
future_direction: Understanding the shape of the transfer function f(σ) is an interesting area of research.
papers.abstract: We study deep neural networks (DNNs) trained on natural image data with entirely random labels. Despite its popularity in the literature, where it is often used to study memorization, generalization, and other phenomena, little is known about what DNNs learn in this setting. In this paper, we show analytically for convolutional and fully connected networks that an alignment between the principal components of network parameters and data takes place when training with random labels. We study this alignment effect by investigating neural networks pre-trained on randomly labelled image data and subsequently fine-tuned on disjoint datasets with random or real labels. We show how this alignment produces a positive transfer: networks pre-trained with random labels train faster downstream compared to training from scratch even after accounting for simple effects, such as weight scaling. We analyze how competing effects, such as specialization at later layers, may hide the positive transfer. These effects are studied in several network architectures, including VGG16 and ResNet18, on CIFAR10 and ImageNet.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Simplicity Bias in 1-Hidden Layer Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can we rigorously define and establish simplicity bias (as low-dimensional input dependence) for one-hidden-layer neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper rigorously defines low-dimensional simplicity bias (LD-SB) for one-hidden-layer neural networks and proposes OrthoP, an ensemble method that trains diverse models by projecting out features used by previous models, leading to improved robustness.
papers.conclusion: Simplicity bias in one-hidden-layer neural networks can be characterized as low-dimensional input dependence, and the OrthoP ensemble method can mitigate this bias to produce more robust models.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretically, for linearly separable data in the Independent Features Model, gradient descent on 1-hidden layer networks converges to a model that relies exclusively on the linearly separable feature, even in the presence of more complex features.
Empirically, trained models on real datasets (Imagenette, Waterbirds-Landbirds, MNIST-CIFAR) exhibit LD-SB, depending on a low-dimensional projection of the input.
The proposed OrthoP method trains successive models on features orthogonal to those used by previous models, resulting in ensembles with significantly better robustness to Gaussian noise.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical and empirical results are restricted to one-hidden-layer neural networks; extending to deeper networks is an open problem.
Theoretical results for the lazy regime require specific conditions on the dataset and parameters.
future_direction: Extending the characterization of simplicity bias to deeper networks and other architectures.
papers.abstract: Recent works have demonstrated that neural networks exhibit extreme simplicity bias(SB). That is, they learn only the simplest features to solve a task at hand, even in the presence of other, more robust but more complex features. Due to the lack of a general and rigorous definition of features, these works showcase SB on semi-synthetic datasets such as Color-MNIST, MNIST-CIFAR where defining features is relatively easier. In this work, we rigorously define as well as thoroughly establish SB for one hidden layer neural networks. More concretely, (i) we define SB as the network essentially being a function of a low dimensional projection of the inputs (ii) theoretically, we show that when the data is linearly separable, the network primarily depends on only the linearly separable ($1$-dimensional) subspace even in the presence of an arbitrarily large number of other, more complex features which could have led to a significantly more robust classifier, (iii) empirically, we show that models trained on real datasets such as Imagenette and Waterbirds-Landbirds indeed depend on a low dimensional projection of the inputs, thereby demonstrating SB on these datasets, iv) finally, we present a natural ensemble approach that encourages diversity in models by training successive models on features not used by earlier models, and demonstrate that it yields models that are significantly more robust to Gaussian noise.

papers.title: The Early Phase of Neural Network Training
papers.research_question: What changes do deep neural networks undergo during the early phase of training, and how do these changes depend on data and labels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the early phase of training involves structured changes in weight distributions that are not captured by signs alone, and that these changes can be approximated by self-supervised pre-training without labels, though labels accelerate the process.
papers.conclusion: The early phase of training is crucial for subsequent learning, and the changes are not simply due to noise but involve structured learning that can be achieved via self-supervised pre-training.
papers.key_findings:
The early phase of training consists of three sub-phases: initial large gradients and rapid motion, followed by gradient stabilization and rapid performance increase, and then deceleration.
Deeper networks are not robust to reinitialization with random weights while maintaining signs, contrary to findings in smaller networks.
Weight distributions after early training are highly non-i.i.d., as permuting them within layers or globally harms performance.
Pre-training with self-supervised tasks (e.g., rotation prediction) can approximate the changes from supervised training, but requires many more epochs (32x longer).
Labels are not necessary for the early phase changes, but they significantly accelerate the process; however, misleading labels (random labels) prevent these changes.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that many important aspects of neural network learning take place within the very earliest iterations or epochs of training. For example, sparse, trainable sub-networks emerge (Frankle et al., 2019), gradient descent moves into a small subspace (Gur-Ari et al., 2018), and the network undergoes a critical period (Achille et al., 2019). Here, we examine the changes that deep neural networks undergo during this early phase of training. We perform extensive measurements of the network state during these early iterations of training and leverage the framework of Frankle et al. (2019) to quantitatively probe the weight distribution and its reliance on various aspects of the dataset. We find that, within this framework, deep networks are not robust to reinitializing with random weights while maintaining signs, and that weight distributions are highly non-independent even after only a few hundred iterations. Despite this behavior, pre-training with blurred inputs or an auxiliary self-supervised task can approximate the changes in supervised networks, suggesting that these changes are not inherently label-dependent, though labels significantly accelerate this process. Together, these results help to elucidate the network changes occurring during this pivotal initial period of learning.

papers.title: Mechanism of feature learning in deep fully connected networks and kernel machines that recursively learn features
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism through which deep fully connected neural networks learn features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper posits the Deep Neural Feature Ansatz, which states that neural feature learning occurs by implementing the average gradient outer product to up-weight features strongly related to model output. This leads to a backpropagation-free method for feature learning, applied to kernel machines as Recursive Feature Machines, achieving state-of-the-art performance on tabular data.
papers.conclusion: The average gradient outer product is the mechanism for feature learning in deep fully connected networks, and this mechanism can be applied to other models like kernel machines to achieve strong performance.
papers.key_findings:
The Deep Neural Feature Ansatz is empirically validated across 121 tabular datasets and image tasks.
The ansatz explains deep learning phenomena such as spurious features, simplicity biases, grokking, and lottery tickets.
Recursive Feature Machines (RFMs) enable feature learning in kernel machines and achieve state-of-the-art performance on tabular data benchmarks.
RFMs exhibit similar feature learning phenomena as deep networks (grokking, lottery tickets, simplicity biases).
The feature matrices learned by RFMs are highly correlated with the first layer neural feature matrices of deep networks.
papers.abstract: In recent years neural networks have achieved impressive results on many technological and scientific tasks. Yet, the mechanism through which these models automatically select features, or patterns in data, for prediction remains unclear. Identifying such a mechanism is key to advancing performance and interpretability of neural networks and promoting reliable adoption of these models in scientific applications. In this paper, we identify and characterize the mechanism through which deep fully connected neural networks learn features. We posit the Deep Neural Feature Ansatz, which states that neural feature learning occurs by implementing the average gradient outer product to up-weight features strongly related to model output. Our ansatz sheds light on various deep learning phenomena including emergence of spurious features and simplicity biases and how pruning networks can increase performance, the "lottery ticket hypothesis." Moreover, the mechanism identified in our work leads to a backpropagation-free method for feature learning with any machine learning model. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this feature learning mechanism, we use it to enable feature learning in classical, non-feature learning models known as kernel machines and show that the resulting models, which we refer to as Recursive Feature Machines, achieve state-of-the-art performance on tabular data.

papers.title: Can RNNs learn Recursive Nested Subject-Verb Agreements?
papers.research_question: Can recurrent neural networks (RNNs) learn recursive nested subject-verb agreements, and how do they represent such structures internally?
papers.core_contribution: RNNs do not learn systematic recursive rules for nested subject-verb agreement but show bounded generalization with primacy and recency effects, and a single unit can encode multiple grammatical numbers.
papers.conclusion: RNNs do not learn systematic recursive rules but approximate nested structures with bounded mechanisms, showing similarities to human cognitive limitations in processing center-embedded sentences.
papers.key_findings:
RNNs generalize to longer subject-verb dependencies but not to deeper tree structures.
LSTM-based models exhibit primacy and recency effects, performing well on outer- and innermost verbs but poorly on middle verbs.
Ablation studies show that a single unit can encode grammatical number for multiple nouns and its ablation dramatically affects performance on outer dependencies.
All tested RNN types, including those with structural bias (ON-LSTM, stack-RNNs, stack-LSTMs), fail to generalize to deeper structures.
Internal dynamics of key units reveal a fractal-like encoding that may implement a memory stack.
future_direction: Explore the similarity between RNN generalization patterns and human cognitive patterns in processing nested structures.
papers.abstract: One of the fundamental principles of contemporary linguistics states that language processing requires the ability to extract recursively nested tree structures. However, it remains unclear whether and how this code could be implemented in neural circuits. Recent advances in Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which achieve near-human performance in some language tasks, provide a compelling model to address such questions. Here, we present a new framework to study recursive processing in RNNs, using subject-verb agreement as a probe into the representations of the neural network. We trained six distinct types of RNNs on a simplified probabilistic context-free grammar designed to independently manipulate the length of a sentence and the depth of its syntactic tree. All RNNs generalized to subject-verb dependencies longer than those seen during training. However, none systematically generalized to deeper tree structures, even those with a structural bias towards learning nested tree (i.e., stack-RNNs). In addition, our analyses revealed primacy and recency effects in the generalization patterns of LSTM-based models, showing that these models tend to perform well on the outer- and innermost parts of a center-embedded tree structure, but poorly on its middle levels. Finally, probing the internal states of the model during the processing of sentences with nested tree structures, we found a complex encoding of grammatical agreement information (e.g. grammatical number), in which all the information for multiple words nouns was carried by a single unit. Taken together, these results indicate how neural networks may extract bounded nested tree structures, without learning a systematic recursive rule.

papers.title: DoLFIn: Distributions over Latent Features for Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we achieve interpretability in neural models without sacrificing accuracy by using probability distributions over latent features?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes DoLFIn, a novel architecture for interpretability that uses probability distributions over latent features, and shows it achieves comparable or better accuracy than baselines while providing interpretability.
papers.conclusion: DoLFIn provides a new way to build explainable models without sacrificing accuracy, and it offers better interpretability than attention and saliency maps.
papers.key_findings:
DoLFIn achieves slightly higher accuracy than CNN and BiLSTM on SST2 and AG-news datasets.
DoLFIn provides interpretability by computing the probability that an input word supports a category, which is more informative than attention or saliency maps.
The latent features in DoLFIn can be analyzed to understand which categories they support, and some features are more specific to certain categories.
papers.limitation: The analysis of the meaning of latent features is only done on a cherry-picked example and deeper analysis is left for future work.
future_direction: Deeply analyzing the meaning of latent features.
papers.abstract: Interpreting the inner workings of neural models is a key step in ensuring the robustness and trustworthiness of the models, but work on neural network interpretability typically faces a trade-off: either the models are too constrained to be very useful, or the solutions found by the models are too complex to interpret. We propose a novel strategy for achieving interpretability that -- in our experiments -- avoids this trade-off. Our approach builds on the success of using probability as the central quantity, such as for instance within the attention mechanism. In our architecture, DoLFIn (Distributions over Latent Features for Interpretability), we do no determine beforehand what each feature represents, and features go altogether into an unordered set. Each feature has an associated probability ranging from 0 to 1, weighing its importance for further processing. We show that, unlike attention and saliency map approaches, this set-up makes it straight-forward to compute the probability with which an input component supports the decision the neural model makes. To demonstrate the usefulness of the approach, we apply DoLFIn to text classification, and show that DoLFIn not only provides interpretable solutions, but even slightly outperforms the classical CNN and BiLSTM text classifiers on the SST2 and AG-news datasets.

papers.title: Teasing Apart Architecture and Initial Weights as Sources of Inductive Bias in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can the inductive bias provided by a neural network's architecture be overridden by meta-learned initial weights, such that a given inductive bias can be realized equally well in different architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Meta-learning can substantially reduce or eliminate performance differences across neural network architectures by learning appropriate initial weights, suggesting initial weights are a significant source of inductive bias that can override architectural biases in some settings, though architectural biases remain important for out-of-distribution generalization.
papers.conclusion: While neural architectures impose constraints on what problems can be solved, these constraints are weak relative to the inductive biases afforded by initial weights; meta-learning can distill task-specific knowledge that reduces architectural differences, but architectural biases persist when generalization beyond the meta-training distribution is required.
papers.key_findings:
Meta-learning reduces or eliminates performance differences across architectures and data representations for in-distribution tasks.
Architectures that perform well without meta-learning also tend to meta-train more effectively.
All architectures generalize poorly on problems far from their meta-training experience, highlighting the need for stronger inductive biases for robust generalization.
In few-shot learning, CNNs are less sensitive to distribution shifts due to their spatial inductive biases.
LSTMs perform well on modular arithmetic tasks due to their sequential processing bias.
papers.limitation:
All architectures generalize poorly on problems that are far from their meta-training experience.
Meta-learning lacks the ability to distill stronger forms of generalization, such as extrapolation beyond the training task distribution.
future_direction: Exploring architectural constraints for stronger generalization
Using reinforcement learning to incentivize stronger generalization
Developing meta-learning variations that encourage finding structures beyond the data
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks can acquire many aspects of human knowledge from data, making them promising as models of human learning. But what those networks can learn depends upon their inductive biases -- the factors other than the data that influence the solutions they discover -- and the inductive biases of neural networks remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to draw conclusions about human learning from the performance of these systems. Cognitive scientists and machine learning researchers often focus on the architecture of a neural network as a source of inductive bias. In this paper we explore the impact of another source of inductive bias -- the initial weights of the network -- using meta-learning as a tool for finding initial weights that are adapted for specific problems. We evaluate four widely-used architectures -- MLPs, CNNs, LSTMs, and Transformers -- by meta-training 430 different models across three tasks requiring different biases and forms of generalization. We find that meta-learning can substantially reduce or entirely eliminate performance differences across architectures and data representations, suggesting that these factors may be less important as sources of inductive bias than is typically assumed. When differences are present, architectures and data representations that perform well without meta-learning tend to meta-train more effectively. Moreover, all architectures generalize poorly on problems that are far from their meta-training experience, underscoring the need for stronger inductive biases for robust generalization.

papers.title: Deep Neural Model Inspection and Comparison via Functional Neuron Pathways
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and compare neural models by identifying functional groups of co-firing neurons (neural pathways) and associating them with task and linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a general post-hoc method for interpreting and comparing neural models by factoring them into functional components (neural pathways) and associating these pathways with task-level and linguistic heuristics.
papers.conclusion: The neural pathways method provides a way to interpret and compare neural models by abstracting away from individual neurons, offering a simpler starting point for analysis that can draw conclusions similar to domain-specific analyses.
papers.key_findings:
The decomposable attention model has more internal coherence (fewer pathways explain variance) than the BiLSTM encoder for the entailment task.
For the NER task, both models have similar amounts of observable structure.
The method can identify pathways that correspond to specific linguistic features (e.g., a pathway activated by words with capital letters and memorized exceptions).
Linear probes show that models encode external task knowledge, but the pathways (functional groups) do not always strongly correlate with this knowledge, suggesting models may use heuristics not directly aligned with the intended task knowledge.
The method provides a quantitatively backed interpretation that can explain differences in model performance.
papers.limitation:
The method depends on external task knowledge; if the knowledge is partial, only partial understanding of network function is possible.
The choice of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction may not be optimal; other methods could be explored.
future_direction: Examining the effects of different dimensionality reduction methods on extracting the most informative pathways from the activations.
papers.abstract: We introduce a general method for the interpretation and comparison of neural models. The method is used to factor a complex neural model into its functional components, which are comprised of sets of co-firing neurons that cut across layers of the network architecture, and which we call neural pathways. The function of these pathways can be understood by identifying correlated task level and linguistic heuristics in such a way that this knowledge acts as a lens for approximating what the network has learned to apply to its intended task. As a case study for investigating the utility of these pathways, we present an examination of pathways identified in models trained for two standard tasks, namely Named Entity Recognition and Recognizing Textual Entailment.

papers.title: White Noise Analysis of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the inherent biases of deep neural networks and how can we understand and visualize them using methods from computational neuroscience (classification images and spike triggered analysis)?
papers.core_contribution: White noise analysis (using classification images and spike triggered averaging) can reveal inherent biases in neural networks, visualize filters, and be used for adversarial attack and defense.
papers.conclusion: White noise analysis is effective for understanding and interpreting neural networks, demonstrating successful cross-fertilization between neuroscience and machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
Classification images derived from white noise resemble target classes and can be used for classification above chance level.
Classification images can be used to attack black-box classifiers by adding bias maps to inputs.
Classification images can detect adversarial patch attacks by revealing perturbed regions.
Spike triggered averaging can visualize filters in CNNs, showing oriented edges similar to those learned from real data.
Micro-stimulation of neurons in different layers can bias network decisions, producing psychometric curves similar to biological systems.
papers.limitation:
Requires a large number of trials (sample complexity) to compute classification images.
Classification images over natural scene datasets may not resemble sharp object instances.
