papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods to compare neural network representations and shows that networks exhibit partial convergent learning, with some features learned reliably across networks and others not, and that representations are a mix of local and slightly distributed codes.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks exhibit convergent learning to some extent, and the introduced methods are effective for understanding and comparing the representations they learn.
papers.key_findings:
Some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned.
Units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not.
The representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local (single unit) code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.
The average activation values of neurons vary considerably within a network, yet the mean activation values across different networks converge to an almost identical distribution.
Features learned in different networks are most convergent on the first convolutional layer (conv1) and least convergent on the fourth (conv4).
papers.limitation: Mapping layers for higher layers (conv3-conv5) showed poor performance, and the reasons are not fully understood.
future_direction: Investigate different architectures, training algorithms, and hyperparameters.
Train more powerful predictive models for higher layers with different hyperparameters or architectures.
papers.abstract: Recent success in training deep neural networks have prompted active investigation into the features learned on their intermediate layers. Such research is difficult because it requires making sense of non-linear computations performed by millions of parameters, but valuable because it increases our ability to understand current models and create improved versions of them. In this paper we investigate the extent to which neural networks exhibit what we call convergent learning, which is when the representations learned by multiple nets converge to a set of features which are either individually similar between networks or where subsets of features span similar low-dimensional spaces. We propose a specific method of probing representations: training multiple networks and then comparing and contrasting their individual, learned representations at the level of neurons or groups of neurons. We begin research into this question using three techniques to approximately align different neural networks on a feature level: a bipartite matching approach that makes one-to-one assignments between neurons, a sparse prediction approach that finds one-to-many mappings, and a spectral clustering approach that finds many-to-many mappings. This initial investigation reveals a few previously unknown properties of neural networks, and we argue that future research into the question of convergent learning will yield many more. The insights described here include (1) that some features are learned reliably in multiple networks, yet other features are not consistently learned; (2) that units learn to span low-dimensional subspaces and, while these subspaces are common to multiple networks, the specific basis vectors learned are not; (3) that the representation codes show evidence of being a mix between a local code and slightly, but not fully, distributed codes across multiple units.

papers.title: Codebook Features: Sparse and Discrete Interpretability for Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can we train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into codebook features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces codebook features, a method to make neural network hidden states sparse and discrete via vector quantization bottlenecks, enabling improved interpretability and control.
papers.conclusion: Codebook features are a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks, providing a sparse, discrete interface for understanding and steering model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can operate with extreme sparse, discrete bottlenecks at each layer with only modest performance degradation.
In a finite state machine task, codebooks overcome superposition by assigning distinct states to discrete codes, and activating a state's code causes the network to behave as if in that state.
In language models, codebooks learn codes representing diverse, disentangled concepts (e.g., topics, emotions, syntax).
Activating topic-related codes during inference can steer language model generations towards those topics.
Codes are better classifiers of simple textual features than individual neurons in the network.
papers.limitation:
Codebook models exhibit modest degradation in performance compared to the original models.
In larger models, many codes do not have a comprehensible interpretation.
future_direction: Understanding circuits and weights by leveraging the sparse, discrete nature of codebooks.
Understanding adversarial examples by identifying which codes shift to cause misclassifications.
Improving interpretability in larger models by using larger codebooks or analyzing code co-occurrence.
Understanding shared representations across domains and modalities (e.g., text and image).
papers.abstract: Understanding neural networks is challenging in part because of the dense, continuous nature of their hidden states. We explore whether we can train neural networks to have hidden states that are sparse, discrete, and more interpretable by quantizing their continuous features into what we call codebook features. Codebook features are produced by finetuning neural networks with vector quantization bottlenecks at each layer, producing a network whose hidden features are the sum of a small number of discrete vector codes chosen from a larger codebook. Surprisingly, we find that neural networks can operate under this extreme bottleneck with only modest degradation in performance. This sparse, discrete bottleneck also provides an intuitive way of controlling neural network behavior: first, find codes that activate when the desired behavior is present, then activate those same codes during generation to elicit that behavior. We validate our approach by training codebook Transformers on several different datasets. First, we explore a finite state machine dataset with far more hidden states than neurons. In this setting, our approach overcomes the superposition problem by assigning states to distinct codes, and we find that we can make the neural network behave as if it is in a different state by activating the code for that state. Second, we train Transformer language models with up to 410M parameters on two natural language datasets. We identify codes in these models representing diverse, disentangled concepts (ranging from negative emotions to months of the year) and find that we can guide the model to generate different topics by activating the appropriate codes during inference. Overall, codebook features appear to be a promising unit of analysis and control for neural networks and interpretability. Our codebase and models are open-sourced at https://github.com/taufeeque9/codebook-features.

papers.title: Gaussian Pre-Activations in Neural Networks: Myth or Reality?
papers.research_question: Is the Gaussian hypothesis for pre-activations in neural networks valid, and how can we construct activation functions and initialization distributions to ensure Gaussian pre-activations even in narrow networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper constructs a family of activation functions and initialization distributions that ensure pre-activations remain Gaussian throughout the network depth, even in narrow neural networks, without relying on the infinite-width limit.
papers.conclusion: The proposed activation functions and initialization distributions successfully maintain Gaussian pre-activations in narrow and deep neural networks, leading to better training performance compared to standard setups.
papers.key_findings:
The Gaussian hypothesis for pre-activations is mostly invalid in multilayer perceptrons with finite width.
Contrary to a claim in the Edge of Chaos literature, the variance of pre-activations can have an infinite number of attraction points for certain activation functions.
A unified view on pre-activation propagation encompasses several well-known initialization procedures.
Constraints are derived for activation functions and initialization distributions to guarantee Gaussian pre-activations under an independence assumption.
New families of activation functions (φ_oθ and φ_pθ) and initialization distributions (symmetric Weibull) are proposed and shown to maintain Gaussian pre-activations and improve training in narrow networks.
papers.limitation:
The construction of the activation functions is approximate and may not exactly yield Gaussian pre-activations in practice.
The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test has limitations in confirming the Gaussian hypothesis, as it cannot prove the null hypothesis.
papers.abstract: The study of feature propagation at initialization in neural networks lies at the root of numerous initialization designs. An assumption very commonly made in the field states that the pre-activations are Gaussian. Although this convenient Gaussian hypothesis can be justified when the number of neurons per layer tends to infinity, it is challenged by both theoretical and experimental works for finite-width neural networks. Our major contribution is to construct a family of pairs of activation functions and initialization distributions that ensure that the pre-activations remain Gaussian throughout the network's depth, even in narrow neural networks. In the process, we discover a set of constraints that a neural network should fulfill to ensure Gaussian pre-activations. Additionally, we provide a critical review of the claims of the Edge of Chaos line of works and build an exact Edge of Chaos analysis. We also propose a unified view on pre-activations propagation, encompassing the framework of several well-known initialization procedures. Finally, our work provides a principled framework for answering the much-debated question: is it desirable to initialize the training of a neural network whose pre-activations are ensured to be Gaussian? Our code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/p-wol/gaussian-preact/ .

papers.title: Random Feature Amplification: Feature Learning and Generalization in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How does gradient descent in two-layer ReLU networks learn meaningful features from data with noisy labels, even when linear classifiers fail, by amplifying weak random features into strong useful features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical characterization of feature learning in two-layer ReLU networks trained by gradient descent on a noisy XOR-like distribution, showing that gradient descent amplifies weak random features into strong useful features, leading to generalization error close to the noise rate.
papers.conclusion: Gradient descent on two-layer ReLU networks can learn useful features from data with noisy labels by amplifying random features, achieving generalization error close to the noise rate.
papers.key_findings:
At initialization, most neurons are weakly correlated with useful features (cluster means).
A single step of gradient descent with a sufficiently large step-size amplifies these weak correlations to strong ones (order O(1/√d) to O(1)).
The trained network correctly classifies all clean training samples and misclassifies all noisy training samples.
The generalization error is bounded by the label noise rate η plus a term that decays with the sample size.
The feature maps change significantly during training, indicating feature learning beyond the neural tangent kernel (NTK) regime.
papers.limitation: The analysis is restricted to two-layer ReLU networks with a fixed second layer; extending it to training both layers is left for future work.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to the setting where both layers of the network are trained.
Generalizing the analysis to other data distributions beyond the specific XOR-like cluster distribution.
papers.abstract: In this work, we provide a characterization of the feature-learning process in two-layer ReLU networks trained by gradient descent on the logistic loss following random initialization. We consider data with binary labels that are generated by an XOR-like function of the input features. We permit a constant fraction of the training labels to be corrupted by an adversary. We show that, although linear classifiers are no better than random guessing for the distribution we consider, two-layer ReLU networks trained by gradient descent achieve generalization error close to the label noise rate. We develop a novel proof technique that shows that at initialization, the vast majority of neurons function as random features that are only weakly correlated with useful features, and the gradient descent dynamics 'amplify' these weak, random features to strong, useful features.

papers.title: On the Origins of the Block Structure Phenomenon in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: What is the origin of the block structure phenomenon in neural network representations? Does it arise from overfitting to spurious data features or does it capture meaningful dataset statistics?
papers.core_contribution: The block structure phenomenon arises from dominant datapoints that share simple image statistics (e.g., background color), which vary across random seeds. The block structure can be eliminated via principal component regularization without harming performance.
papers.conclusion: The block structure captures real but simple dataset statistics, and its inconsistency across seeds is due to variation in which statistics are captured. Training interventions like principal component regularization can reduce the block structure and improve representational consistency.
papers.key_findings:
The block structure is caused by a small set of dominant datapoints that share similar image statistics (e.g., background color).
The set of dominant datapoints and the specific image statistic they capture vary across random seeds.
Removing dominant datapoints from the analysis eliminates the block structure.
The block structure emerges early in training, but the dominant datapoints and representations continue to change substantially.
Principal component regularization can eliminate the block structure and improve model consistency across seeds without hurting accuracy.
papers.limitation:
Focus on image classification tasks and ResNet architectures; it remains to be seen how the block structure manifests in other domains and architectures.
Analysis is primarily empirical; a theoretical understanding is left for future work.
future_direction: Exploring how dominant datapoints manifest in other domains and applications.
Applying principal component regularization to distribution shift and self-supervision problems.
papers.abstract: Recent work has uncovered a striking phenomenon in large-capacity neural networks: they contain blocks of contiguous hidden layers with highly similar representations. This block structure has two seemingly contradictory properties: on the one hand, its constituent layers exhibit highly similar dominant first principal components (PCs), but on the other hand, their representations, and their common first PC, are highly dissimilar across different random seeds. Our work seeks to reconcile these discrepant properties by investigating the origin of the block structure in relation to the data and training methods. By analyzing properties of the dominant PCs, we find that the block structure arises from dominant datapoints - a small group of examples that share similar image statistics (e.g. background color). However, the set of dominant datapoints, and the precise shared image statistic, can vary across random seeds. Thus, the block structure reflects meaningful dataset statistics, but is simultaneously unique to each model. Through studying hidden layer activations and creating synthetic datapoints, we demonstrate that these simple image statistics dominate the representational geometry of the layers inside the block structure. We explore how the phenomenon evolves through training, finding that the block structure takes shape early in training, but the underlying representations and the corresponding dominant datapoints continue to change substantially. Finally, we study the interplay between the block structure and different training mechanisms, introducing a targeted intervention to eliminate the block structure, as well as examining the effects of pretraining and Shake-Shake regularization.

papers.title: Under the Hood of Neural Networks: Characterizing Learned Representations by Functional Neuron Populations and Network Ablations
papers.research_question: What are the roles of single neurons and groups of neurons within a neural network in fulfilling a learned task? How can learned representations be characterized by activation patterns and network ablations to reveal functional neuron populations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper characterizes learned representations in neural networks by identifying functional neuron populations through activation patterns and network ablations, showing that a neuron's activation magnitude, selectivity, and impact on performance are insufficient stand-alone indicators for its importance.
papers.conclusion: Understanding how knowledge is represented and localized in artificial networks is beneficial for advancing transfer learning and for providing measures for large-scale studies in neuroscience.
papers.key_findings:
Learned representations evolve to become more distinct along network layers, improving class separation in the activation-space.
Network ablations distort the activation-space, leading to misclassifications, but the relative positions of units are mostly preserved, suggesting a holistic effect.
Functional neuron populations exist: groups of neurons that jointly activate in response to specific stimuli or have a similar impact on network accuracy when ablated.
The size of functional neuron populations varies greatly across classes, indicating different network capacity usage per class.
No single metric (activation magnitude, selectivity, or ablation impact) sufficiently describes the role of a single unit within the whole network.
papers.limitation:
The number of samples (10 classes) is small, limiting the descriptive statistical power of the correlation tests.
Investigating the effect of single unit ablations does not allow determining whether the ablated unit is singly important or part of an important path through the network that has been altered.
future_direction: Determine how robustness of class-specific representations against network ablations can be characterized and achieved purposefully.
Identify important paths along the network, rather than just single units, to understand the flow of information.
Investigate how the localization of a class-specific representation is affected by class-specific properties and how the robustness of these representations depends on these properties.
papers.abstract: The need for more transparency of the decision-making processes in artificial neural networks steadily increases driven by their applications in safety critical and ethically challenging domains such as autonomous driving or medical diagnostics. We address today's lack of transparency of neural networks and shed light on the roles of single neurons and groups of neurons within the network fulfilling a learned task. Inspired by research in the field of neuroscience, we characterize the learned representations by activation patterns and network ablations, revealing functional neuron populations that a) act jointly in response to specific stimuli or b) have similar impact on the network's performance after being ablated. We find that neither a neuron's magnitude or selectivity of activation, nor its impact on network performance are sufficient stand-alone indicators for its importance for the overall task. We argue that such indicators are essential for future advances in transfer learning and modern neuroscience.

papers.title: On the Power and Limitations of Random Features for Understanding Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can the random features approach, which fixes some network components at random initialization, fully explain the empirical success of neural networks, particularly the learnability of simple functions like a single ReLU neuron?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that while over-parameterized neural networks can learn low-degree polynomials via random features, the random features approach is inherently limited and cannot efficiently approximate a single ReLU neuron unless the network size or weight magnitudes are exponential in the input dimension.
papers.conclusion: The random features approach captures important aspects of neural network training but is insufficient to provide a complete explanation for their empirical success, as it fails to account for the learnability of simple functions like a single neuron.
papers.key_findings:
Over-parameterized one-hidden-layer neural networks can provably learn low-degree polynomials using standard stochastic gradient descent and random features.
Random features cannot approximate a single ReLU neuron with standard Gaussian inputs unless the number of features or the magnitude of the weights is exponential in the input dimension.
Since single ReLU neurons are learnable with gradient-based methods, the random features approach cannot fully explain the empirical success of neural networks.
papers.limitation:
The positive result on learning polynomials requires the network size to be exponential in the degree of the polynomial.
The random features approach cannot fully explain polynomial-time learnability of neural networks, indicating that we are still far from a satisfying general explanation.
papers.abstract: Recently, a spate of papers have provided positive theoretical results for training over-parameterized neural networks (where the network size is larger than what is needed to achieve low error). The key insight is that with sufficient over-parameterization, gradient-based methods will implicitly leave some components of the network relatively unchanged, so the optimization dynamics will behave as if those components are essentially fixed at their initial random values. In fact, fixing these explicitly leads to the well-known approach of learning with random features. In other words, these techniques imply that we can successfully learn with neural networks, whenever we can successfully learn with random features. In this paper, we first review these techniques, providing a simple and self-contained analysis for one-hidden-layer networks. We then argue that despite the impressive positive results, random feature approaches are also inherently limited in what they can explain. In particular, we rigorously show that random features cannot be used to learn even a single ReLU neuron with standard Gaussian inputs, unless the network size (or magnitude of the weights) is exponentially large. Since a single neuron is learnable with gradient-based methods, we conclude that we are still far from a satisfying general explanation for the empirical success of neural networks.

papers.title: Towards Understanding the Condensation of Neural Networks at Initial Training
papers.research_question: How does small initialization lead to condensation of input weights in neural networks during initial training, and how is this condensation related to the multiplicity of the activation function?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the maximal number of condensed orientations in the initial training stage is twice the multiplicity of the activation function, and provides theoretical analysis for two specific cases.
papers.conclusion: The multiplicity of the activation function is a key factor in understanding the complexity of neural network output and the weight condensation at initial training, which restricts the network to effectively low capacity initially.
papers.key_findings:
Condensation of input weights onto isolated orientations occurs during initial training with small initialization.
The maximal number of condensed orientations is twice the multiplicity p of the activation function (e.g., one line for p=1, two lines for p=2).
For common activation functions with multiplicity one (tanh, sigmoid, softplus), condensation occurs on one line (two opposite directions).
Theoretical analysis confirms the condensation bound for activation functions of multiplicity one with arbitrary input dimension, and for layers with one-dimensional input and arbitrary multiplicity.
The condensation phenomenon is observed in both synthetic data experiments and image classification tasks (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, MNIST).
papers.limitation: Theoretical analysis is only provided for two specific cases: activation functions of multiplicity one with arbitrary dimension input, and layers with one-dimensional input and arbitrary multiplicity. The general case with high-dimensional input and arbitrary multiplicity remains an open problem.
future_direction: Studying condensation for multiple-layer neural networks throughout the entire training process.
Theoretical analysis for the general case of high-dimensional input data with arbitrary multiplicity.
Investigating how training data (e.g., frequency, complexity) affects the condensation phenomenon.
papers.abstract: Empirical works show that for ReLU neural networks (NNs) with small initialization, input weights of hidden neurons (the input weight of a hidden neuron consists of the weight from its input layer to the hidden neuron and its bias term) condense on isolated orientations. The condensation dynamics implies that the training implicitly regularizes a NN towards one with a much smaller effective size. In this work, we illustrate the formation of the condensation in multi-layer fully connected NNs and show that the maximal number of condensed orientations in the initial training stage is twice the multiplicity of the activation function, where "multiplicity" indicates the multiple roots of activation function at origin. Our theoretical analysis confirms experiments for two cases, one is for the activation function of multiplicity one with arbitrary dimension input, which contains many common activation functions, and the other is for the layer with one-dimensional input and arbitrary multiplicity. This work makes a step towards understanding how small initialization leads NNs to condensation at the initial training stage.

papers.title: What’s Hidden in a Randomly Weighted Neural Network?
papers.research_question: What lies hidden in an overparameterized neural network with random weights? The paper investigates whether there exist subnetworks within randomly weighted neural networks that achieve good performance without ever modifying the weight values.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that randomly weighted neural networks contain subnetworks which achieve impressive performance without training the weights, and introduces the edge-popup algorithm to effectively find such subnetworks.
papers.conclusion: Hidden within randomly weighted neural networks are subnetworks with compelling accuracy, and this work provides an avenue for further exploration in understanding neural network initialization and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Randomly weighted neural networks contain subnetworks that achieve impressive performance without modifying the weight values.
The edge-popup algorithm effectively finds subnetworks within randomly weighted neural networks.
As randomly weighted neural networks grow wider and deeper, the untrained subnetwork approaches a trained network in accuracy.
On ImageNet, a subnetwork of a randomly weighted Wide ResNet-50 matches the performance of a trained ResNet-34.
The performance of the subnetwork depends on the percentage of weights kept and the width of the network.
papers.abstract: Training a neural network is synonymous with learning the values of the weights. In contrast, we demonstrate that randomly weighted neural networks contain subnetworks which achieve impressive performance without ever modifying the weight values. Hidden in a randomly weighted Wide ResNet-50 [32] we find a subnetwork (with random weights) that is smaller than, but matches the performance of a ResNet-34 [9] trained on ImageNet [4]. Not only do these “untrained subnetworks” exist, but we provide an algorithm to effectively find them. We empirically show that as randomly weighted neural networks with fixed weights grow wider and deeper, an “untrained subnetwork” approaches a network with learned weights in accuracy. Our code and pretrained models are available at: https://github.com/allenai/hidden-networks.

papers.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we relate distributed neural representations back to human-interpretable concepts?
papers.core_contribution: This perspective paper presents a theoretical framework explaining how neural networks encode information in superposition and argues that sparse coding, supported by identifiability theory and compressed sensing, can extract interpretable, sparse features from these distributed representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that neural networks learn linear representations of latent variables and that sparse coding can recover interpretable features, providing a foundation for understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks encode information in superposition, meaning multiple concepts are linearly combined in a shared representational space.
Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation.
Sparse coding methods, such as sparse autoencoders, can extract disentangled, interpretable features from superposed neural representations.
Quantitative interpretability metrics, like psychophysics tasks, are needed to assess the success of feature extraction methods.
The framework bridges insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes sparse latent variables in Euclidean space, whereas some latent variables (e.g., object pose) may have non-Euclidean topology, and the linear representation hypothesis may only hold approximately in such cases.
Practical recovery of sparse codes in large-scale models remains challenging, requiring more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms.
Interpretability scores based on pairwise human similarity judgments are insufficient as they depend on context, motivating the need for contextualized similarity metrics.
future_direction: Extending the framework to incorporate latent variables with non-Euclidean geometry or discrete structure.
Developing more efficient and scalable sparse coding algorithms for large-scale models.
Addressing the binding problem—how multiple objects and attributes are encoded without losing relational information when representations are summed.
papers.abstract: Understanding how information is represented in neural networks is a fundamental challenge in both neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Despite their nonlinear architectures, recent evidence suggests that neural networks encode features in superposition, meaning that input concepts are linearly overlaid within the network's representations. We present a perspective that explains this phenomenon and provides a foundation for extracting interpretable representations from neural activations. Our theoretical framework consists of three steps: (1) Identifiability theory shows that neural networks trained for classification recover latent features up to a linear transformation. (2) Sparse coding methods can extract disentangled features from these representations by leveraging principles from compressed sensing. (3) Quantitative interpretability metrics provide a means to assess the success of these methods, ensuring that extracted features align with human-interpretable concepts. By bridging insights from theoretical neuroscience, representation learning, and interpretability research, we propose an emerging perspective on understanding neural representations in both artificial and biological systems. Our arguments have implications for neural coding theories, AI transparency, and the broader goal of making deep learning models more interpretable.

papers.title: On the Power and Limitations of Random Features for Understanding Neural\n Networks
papers.research_question: Can the random features approach fully explain the success of neural networks, particularly the learnability of simple functions like a single ReLU neuron?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that random features are insufficient to explain the learnability of neural networks because they cannot efficiently approximate a single ReLU neuron without exponential network size or weight magnitude, while gradient-based methods can learn such neurons.
papers.conclusion: While random features capture important aspects of neural network training, they are not the whole story, and a satisfying general explanation for the success of neural networks is still lacking.
papers.key_findings:
Over-parameterized one-hidden-layer neural networks can learn low-degree polynomials using random features and gradient descent.
Random features cannot approximate a single ReLU neuron with polynomial-sized networks or weights; exponential size is required.
Thus, the random features approach has inherent limitations in explaining the empirical success of neural networks.
future_direction: Removing the dependence on max_i |u_i| in the lower bound for approximating ReLU neurons with random features.
papers.abstract:
Recently, a spate of papers have provided positive theoretical results for
training over-parameterized neural networks (where the network size is larger
than what is needed to achieve low error). The key insight is that with
sufficient over-parameterization, gradient-based methods will implicitly leave
some components of the network relatively unchanged, so the optimization
dynamics will behave as if those components are essentially fixed at their
initial random values. In fact, fixing these explicitly leads to the well-known
approach of learning with random features. In other words, these techniques
imply that we can successfully learn with neural networks, whenever we can
successfully learn with random features. In this paper, we first review these
techniques, providing a simple and self-contained analysis for one-hidden-layer
networks. We then argue that despite the impressive positive results, random
feature approaches are also inherently limited in what they can explain. In
particular, we rigorously show that random features cannot be used to learn
even a single ReLU neuron with standard Gaussian inputs, unless the network
size (or magnitude of the weights) is exponentially large. Since a single
neuron is learnable with gradient-based methods, we conclude that we are still
far from a satisfying general explanation for the empirical success of neural
networks.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: Multifaceted Feature Visualization: Uncovering the Different Types of\n Features Learned By Each Neuron in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the multiple different types of features (facets) that each neuron in a deep neural network responds to?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple types of features (facets) each neuron responds to, and improves activation maximization visualizations with more natural colors and coherent structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization by producing higher quality images and shows the multiple feature facets each neuron detects, providing a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level ones.
Multifaceted feature visualization produces more realistic and interpretable visualizations than previous activation maximization methods.
The method reveals that DNNs learn not only discriminative features but also global structure and context, similar to generative models.
Hidden fully connected layer neurons sometimes represent amalgams of different concepts.
papers.limitation:
The number of facets visualized depends on the manually set parameter k in k-means; automatically determining the true number of facets remains an open problem.
The method does not always reconstruct a proper facet (e.g., for stuffed peppers), possibly because the neuron ignores certain features.
Center-biased regularization is not guaranteed to produce a single object; it only biases optimization toward the center.
future_direction: Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron.
Investigating the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves visualization quality.
Further research into understanding the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons.
papers.abstract:
We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features
each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have
created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which
synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each
neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron
detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted,
in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example,
a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a
storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images
without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating
inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc.
Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of
each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of
images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that
produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images
obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of
image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate
colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus
provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each
neuron.

papers.title: Multifaceted Feature Visualization: Uncovering the Different Types of Features Learned By Each Neuron in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we visualize the multiple different types of features (facets) that each neuron in a deep neural network responds to, given that neurons are multifaceted?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm that uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron and improves activation maximization image quality with more natural colors and coherent global structure.
papers.conclusion: The Multifaceted Feature Visualization algorithm improves the state of the art of activation maximization and provides a more comprehensive understanding of each neuron's function by revealing its multiple facets.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in deep neural networks are multifaceted, responding to multiple types of features.
Higher-level neurons are more multifaceted than lower-level neurons.
The MFV algorithm produces visualizations with more natural colors and coherent global structure by separately synthesizing each facet.
The algorithm reveals that DNNs learn global structure, details, and context of objects, acting more like generative models.
A center-biased regularization technique reduces the repetition of object fragments in activation maximization images.
papers.limitation:
The number of unique images MFV produces for a unit depends on the manually set k in k-means; automatically identifying the true number of facets remains an open question.
It is unclear whether hidden fully connected layer neurons are truly amalgams of different concepts or part of distributed representations; current visualization methods (Deconv, LRP) do not conclusively reveal this.
future_direction: Future research is needed to understand the precise dynamics of why initializing with a mean facet image improves activation maximization quality.
Automatically identifying the true number of facets per neuron is an important open scientific question.
Further investigation into the function of hidden fully connected layer neurons and whether they are amalgams or represent abstract concepts.
papers.abstract: We can better understand deep neural networks by identifying which features each of their neurons have learned to detect. To do so, researchers have created Deep Visualization techniques including activation maximization, which synthetically generates inputs (e.g. images) that maximally activate each neuron. A limitation of current techniques is that they assume each neuron detects only one type of feature, but we know that neurons can be multifaceted, in that they fire in response to many different types of features: for example, a grocery store class neuron must activate either for rows of produce or for a storefront. Previous activation maximization techniques constructed images without regard for the multiple different facets of a neuron, creating inappropriate mixes of colors, parts of objects, scales, orientations, etc. Here, we introduce an algorithm that explicitly uncovers the multiple facets of each neuron by producing a synthetic visualization of each of the types of images that activate a neuron. We also introduce regularization methods that produce state-of-the-art results in terms of the interpretability of images obtained by activation maximization. By separately synthesizing each type of image a neuron fires in response to, the visualizations have more appropriate colors and coherent global structure. Multifaceted feature visualization thus provides a clearer and more comprehensive description of the role of each neuron.

papers.title: Toward Deeper Understanding of Neural Networks: The Power of Initialization and a Dual View on Expressivity
papers.research_question: Why do neural network training algorithms succeed despite non-convex optimization, and what is the role of random initialization and network architecture in this success?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a duality between neural networks and compositional kernels, showing that random initialization yields representations that approximate the kernel space, thus providing a theoretical explanation for the effectiveness of training neural networks from random initialization.
papers.conclusion: The duality between neural networks and compositional kernels provides a theoretical framework for understanding the success of neural network training and offers insights into architectural design choices, highlighting the importance of initialization and network structure.
papers.key_findings:
Random initialization of neural networks approximates the corresponding compositional kernel, meaning the initial weights form a good starting point for optimization.
The dual view reveals design principles for neural networks, such as the suitability of convolutional kernels for vision and acoustic tasks compared to fully connected kernels.
The ReLU activation has favorable properties: its dual kernel is expressive and can be well approximated by random initialization even when the initialization scale is moderately changed.
As the number of layers in a fully connected network becomes very large, its dual kernel converges to a degenerate form for any non-linear activation.
Optimizing only the weights of the last layer can serve as a convex proxy for choosing among different architectures prior to training.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other architectural components like max-pooling and recursive neural networks.
Use the framework to understand procedures like dropout and batch-normalization.
Devise new architectural components inspired by the duality and improve quantitative bounds on the approximation.
papers.abstract: We develop a general duality between neural networks and compositional kernels, striving towards a better understanding of deep learning. We show that initial representations generated by common random initializations are sufficiently rich to express all functions in the dual kernel space. Hence, though the training objective is hard to optimize in the worst case, the initial weights form a good starting point for optimization. Our dual view also reveals a pragmatic and aesthetic perspective of neural networks and underscores their expressive power.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Learning Representations: To What Extent Do\n Different Neural Networks Learn the Same Representation
papers.research_question: How similar are the representations learned by two networks with identical architecture but trained from different initializations?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a theory and efficient algorithms based on neuron activation subspace matches to analyze representation similarity, and finds that representations learned by differently initialized convolutional networks are not as similar as expected.
papers.conclusion: Representations learned by convolutional layers are not as similar as prevalently expected, raising fundamental questions about whether networks learn different representations or if subspace match is an inadequate metric.
papers.key_findings:
For most convolutional layers, the maximum match similarity is very low, indicating low overall similarity of representations.
Layers close to the output sometimes exhibit high similarity, likely due to alignment with the output task.
Layers close to the input show relatively high similarity, likely due to alignment with input data and low-dimensional nature.
Simple matches reveal that very few single neurons or small neuron sets learn similar representations.
The distribution of simple match sizes shows that similarity is not local, even in layers with high overall similarity.
papers.limitation: The result may indicate either that networks learn completely different representations or that the subspace match metric is not suitable for measuring representation similarity.
future_direction: Investigating what is the right metric for similarity of representations.
Systematic and in-depth study of representation similarity in deep learning.
papers.abstract:
It is widely believed that learning good representations is one of the main
reasons for the success of deep neural networks. Although highly intuitive,
there is a lack of theory and systematic approach quantitatively characterizing
what representations do deep neural networks learn. In this work, we move a
tiny step towards a theory and better understanding of the representations.
Specifically, we study a simpler problem: How similar are the representations
learned by two networks with identical architecture but trained from different
initializations. We develop a rigorous theory based on the neuron activation
subspace match model. The theory gives a complete characterization of the
structure of neuron activation subspace matches, where the core concepts are
maximum match and simple match which describe the overall and the finest
similarity between sets of neurons in two networks respectively. We also
propose efficient algorithms to find the maximum match and simple matches.
Finally, we conduct extensive experiments using our algorithms. Experimental
results suggest that, surprisingly, representations learned by the same
convolutional layers of networks trained from different initializations are not
as similar as prevalently expected, at least in terms of subspace match.

papers.title: Transformers Are Born Biased: Structural Inductive Biases at Random Initialization and Their Practical Consequences
papers.research_question: Do randomly initialized transformers exhibit systematic structural biases, and what are their mechanisms and practical consequences?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers exhibit strong structural biases at random initialization due to representation contraction driven by MLP and attention, which persist through training and enable seed-specific fingerprinting (SeedPrint) and explain the attention-sink phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are not blank slates; they possess inherent structural biases at initialization that persist through training, with implications for model fingerprinting and architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
Randomly initialized transformers show extreme token preferences, with certain tokens predicted orders of magnitude more often than others.
This preference arises from inter-sequence representation contraction, where last-token representations from different sequences become highly similar.
The contraction is primarily driven by asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP layers, and amplified by self-attention through intra-sequence aggregation.
These initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable model identity that can be used for fingerprinting (SeedPrint).
The attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction leads to a positional discrepancy that causally explains the attention-sink phenomenon in trained LLMs.
future_direction: Design architectures that are more neutral or explicitly incorporate desired inductive biases.
Treat initialization choices as hyperparameters tuned for final model behavior, not just optimization stability.
Extend the fingerprinting method to more challenging scenarios, such as detecting obfuscated or distilled models.
papers.abstract: Transformers underpin modern large language models (LLMs) and are commonly assumed to be behaviorally unstructured at random initialization, with all meaningful preferences emerging only through large-scale training. We challenge this assumption by showing that randomly initialized transformers already exhibit strong and systematic structural biases. In particular, untrained models display extreme token preferences: across random input sequences, certain tokens are predicted with probabilities orders of magnitude larger. We provide a mechanistic explanation for this phenomenon by dissecting the transformer architecture at initialization. We show that extreme token preference arises from a contraction of token representations along a random seed-dependent direction. This contraction is driven by two interacting forces: (i) asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP sublayers induce global (inter-sequence) representation concentration, and (ii) self-attention further amplifies this effect through local (intra-sequence) aggregation. Together, these mechanisms align hidden representations along a direction determined solely by the random initialization, producing highly non-uniform next-token predictions. Beyond mechanistic insight, we demonstrate that these initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable and intrinsic model identity. Leveraging this property, we introduce SeedPrint, a fingerprinting method that can reliably distinguish models that differ only in their random initialization, even after extensive training and under substantial distribution shift. Finally, we identify a fundamental positional discrepancy inherent to the attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction that is causally linked to the attention-sink phenomenon. This discovery provides a principled explanation for the emergence of sinks and offers a pathway for their control.

papers.title: An Interpretability Illusion for BERT
papers.research_question: What gives rise to the illusion that individual neurons in BERT encode simple, consistent concepts when probed with a single dataset, and why does this interpretation fail to generalize across datasets?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an 'interpretability illusion' in BERT where neurons appear to encode simple concepts when probed with a single dataset, but these interpretations fail to generalize across datasets. It traces the illusion to dataset idiosyncrasy and local semantic coherence, and introduces a taxonomy of concept directions (global, dataset-level, local).
papers.conclusion: The work highlights the role of datasets in interpretability research and recommends testing interpretations across multiple datasets to avoid illusions. It also points to the need for further work in characterizing the geometry of concept representation.
papers.key_findings:
Many neurons in BERT's final layer show consistent, interpretable patterns when looking at top-activating sentences from a single dataset, but these patterns are not consistent across datasets.
The illusion arises because datasets occupy distinct regions of BERT's embedding space (dataset idiosyncrasy), as shown by UMAP visualization and linear SVM classification.
The patterns observed are largely due to local semantic coherence in the embedding space, not global concept directions, as evidenced by locality scores.
There exist both global and dataset-level concept directions in BERT's embedding space, as shown by monotonic token frequency changes along some neuron directions.
Annotator bias also contributes to the illusion, as people tend to see patterns even in random sentences.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to the final layer of BERT; earlier layers are not fully analyzed.
Annotator bias can lead to seeing patterns where none exist.
future_direction: Replicate the analysis in other settings, such as with other sentence models, token-level embeddings, and earlier layers of BERT.
Look for similar illusions in other types of input like images and graphs.
Characterize the geometry of concept representation in more depth.
papers.abstract: We describe an "interpretability illusion" that arises when analyzing the BERT model. Activations of individual neurons in the network may spuriously appear to encode a single, simple concept, when in fact they are encoding something far more complex. The same effect holds for linear combinations of activations. We trace the source of this illusion to geometric properties of BERT's embedding space as well as the fact that common text corpora represent only narrow slices of possible English sentences. We provide a taxonomy of model-learned concepts and discuss methodological implications for interpretability research, especially the importance of testing hypotheses on multiple data sets.

papers.title: Towards Interpretable Deep Neural Networks by Leveraging Adversarial Examples
papers.research_question: What do neurons in deep neural networks truly detect, and are deep visual representations robust distributed codes of visual concepts? The paper investigates these questions using adversarial examples.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that neurons in DNNs are not true object detectors but respond to discriminative patches, and deep visual representations are not robust. It then proposes an adversarial training scheme with a consistent loss to improve interpretability and consistency of representations.
papers.conclusion: Adversarial training with a consistent loss improves the interpretability and robustness of DNNs, allowing human users to understand model predictions and errors through interpretable representations.
papers.key_findings:
Neurons in DNNs do not truly detect semantic objects/parts but respond to objects/parts as recurrent discriminative patches.
Deep visual representations are not robust distributed codes of visual concepts because representations of adversarial images are inconsistent with those of real images.
Adversarial training with a consistent loss improves interpretability, making neurons detect true objects/parts and representations more consistent.
Interpretable representations enable tracing predictions back to influential neurons, explaining how models make predictions and errors.
Adversarial training also improves model robustness against adversarial attacks.
papers.limitation: Adversarial training causes a drop in accuracy on real images, representing a trade-off between performance and interpretability/robustness.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated impressive performance on a wide array of tasks, but they are usually considered opaque since internal structure and learned parameters are not interpretable. In this paper, we re-examine the internal representations of DNNs using adversarial images, which are generated by an ensemble-optimization algorithm. We find that: (1) the neurons in DNNs do not truly detect semantic objects/parts, but respond to objects/parts only as recurrent discriminative patches; (2) deep visual representations are not robust distributed codes of visual concepts because the representations of adversarial images are largely not consistent with those of real images, although they have similar visual appearance, both of which are different from previous findings. To further improve the interpretability of DNNs, we propose an adversarial training scheme with a consistent loss such that the neurons are endowed with human-interpretable concepts. The induced interpretable representations enable us to trace eventual outcomes back to influential neurons. Therefore, human users can know how the models make predictions, as well as when and why they make errors.

papers.title: Understanding polysemanticity in neural networks through coding theory
papers.research_question: How can coding theory and eigenspectrum analysis provide insights into polysemanticity and improve interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a coding theory perspective to neural network interpretability, using eigenspectrum analysis of activation covariance and random projections to understand polysemanticity, redundancy, and the trade-off between capacity and robustness in network codes.
papers.conclusion: The eigenspectrum analysis and random projections offer a top-down perspective on neural network interpretability, advancing understanding of code structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks learn codes that balance capacity and redundancy, with eigenspectrum decay indicating the level of redundancy.
Dropout during training leads to faster eigenspectrum decay, more robust codes, and smoother random projections.
Random projections of hidden activations reveal the smoothness of the code, which is linked to eigenspectrum decay and can complement single-neuron interpretability methods.
In large language models, random projections provide explanatory power in layers where single-neuron methods perform poorly, suggesting complementary approaches.
The framework explains polysemanticity as an efficient encoding strategy and provides theoretical insights into optimal coding and error correction.
papers.limitation: Identifying the exact error-correcting code is beyond the scope of this paper.
future_direction: A systematic study of how eigenspectrum decay changes with network size.
Investigating the role of nonlinearities in the network code.
Further research into the underlying structure and behavior of deep learning models from a coding perspective.
papers.abstract: Despite substantial efforts, neural network interpretability remains an elusive goal, with previous research failing to provide succinct explanations of most single neurons' impact on the network output. This limitation is due to the polysemantic nature of most neurons, whereby a given neuron is involved in multiple unrelated network states, complicating the interpretation of that neuron. In this paper, we apply tools developed in neuroscience and information theory to propose both a novel practical approach to network interpretability and theoretical insights into polysemanticity and the density of codes. We infer levels of redundancy in the network's code by inspecting the eigenspectrum of the activation's covariance matrix. Furthermore, we show how random projections can reveal whether a network exhibits a smooth or non-differentiable code and hence how interpretable the code is. This same framework explains the advantages of polysemantic neurons to learning performance and explains trends found in recent results by Elhage et al.~(2022). Our approach advances the pursuit of interpretability in neural networks, providing insights into their underlying structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of layers in neural networks and how do learning dynamics evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that layers are over-parameterized, learning converges from bottom up, and proposes Freeze Training to save computation and improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful tool for comparing learned representations across layers, architectures, and time, providing insights into learning dynamics and motivating new training and compression techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is often much smaller than the number of neurons, indicating over-parameterization.
Learning dynamics show that networks converge from the bottom up, with lower layers solidifying before higher ones.
SVCCA can capture semantic similarities between classes, with similar classes having similar sensitivity patterns in the network.
Freeze Training, which sequentially freezes lower layers during training, can save computation and sometimes improve generalization.
The important directions found by SVCCA are distributed across many neurons rather than being axis-aligned.
papers.abstract: We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization; to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code: https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: Beyond Signal Propagation: Is Feature Diversity Necessary in Deep Neural Network Initialization?
papers.research_question: Does deviating from the standard of independent, random initialization of weights have negative effects on training? Specifically, is feature diversity necessary in deep neural network initialization?
papers.core_contribution: Random, diverse initializations are not necessary for training neural networks; networks with identical features at initialization can be trained successfully if a mechanism for symmetry breaking (e.g., non-deterministic GPU operations) is present.
papers.conclusion: Feature diversity at initialization is not a necessary condition for training deep neural networks, as long as there is a mechanism to break symmetry during training.
papers.key_findings:
Networks with identical features at initialization (ConstNet) can achieve high accuracy on standard image classification benchmarks, matching the performance of randomly initialized networks.
Symmetry breaking is essential for training networks with identical initial features, and can be provided by non-deterministic GPU operations or dropout.
The forward and backward weight correlations in ConstNet converge to similar values as those in randomly initialized networks during training.
Training with zero initialization can be slower and less robust to learning rate changes compared to standard random initialization.
The study of LeakyNet shows that identity initialization facilitates symmetry breaking better than averaging initialization.
papers.limitation:
Training with zero initialization is typically slower and can be less robust to learning rate changes.
Reliance on hardware noise for symmetry breaking may lead to variability and failure on different hardware or with lower precision (e.g., FP16).
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are typically initialized with random weights, with variances chosen to facilitate signal propagation and stable gradients. It is also believed that diversity of features is an important property of these initializations. We construct a deep convolutional network with identical features by initializing almost all the weights to $0$. The architecture also enables perfect signal propagation and stable gradients, and achieves high accuracy on standard benchmarks. This indicates that random, diverse initializations are \textit{not} necessary for training neural networks. An essential element in training this network is a mechanism of symmetry breaking; we study this phenomenon and find that standard GPU operations, which are non-deterministic, can serve as a sufficient source of symmetry breaking to enable training.

papers.title: Shape or Texture: Understanding Discriminative Features in CNNs
papers.research_question: What type of shape information is discriminative in CNNs, where is shape information encoded, and when does the network learn about object shape during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that CNNs learn shape information early in training, encode it primarily in the last few layers, and that shape encoding does not guarantee per-pixel semantic understanding.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a systematic study of shape encoding in CNNs, revealing important mechanisms that characterize a network's ability to encode shape information, which can inform the design of more robust and trustworthy computer vision algorithms.
papers.key_findings:
CNNs learn the majority of shape information during the first few epochs of training.
Shape information is largely encoded in the last few layers of a CNN.
Biasing a CNN towards shape changes the number of shape encoding neurons in the last feature encoding stage.
Early layers also encode shape information, which can be combined with deeper layers for better shape extraction.
Encoding shape does not imply the encoding of localized per-pixel semantic information.
papers.abstract: Contrasting the previous evidence that neurons in the later layers of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) respond to complex object shapes, recent studies have shown that CNNs actually exhibit a `texture bias': given an image with both texture and shape cues (e.g., a stylized image), a CNN is biased towards predicting the category corresponding to the texture. However, these previous studies conduct experiments on the final classification output of the network, and fail to robustly evaluate the bias contained (i) in the latent representations, and (ii) on a per-pixel level. In this paper, we design a series of experiments that overcome these issues. We do this with the goal of better understanding what type of shape information contained in the network is discriminative, where shape information is encoded, as well as when the network learns about object shape during training. We show that a network learns the majority of overall shape information at the first few epochs of training and that this information is largely encoded in the last few layers of a CNN. Finally, we show that the encoding of shape does not imply the encoding of localized per-pixel semantic information. The experimental results and findings provide a more accurate understanding of the behaviour of current CNNs, thus helping to inform future design choices.

papers.title: Feature selection of neural networks is skewed towards the less abstract cue
papers.research_question: When artificial neural networks are trained on data containing both low-level (pattern) and high-level (symbolic) cues, which type of cue does the network learn to use for classification?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on data containing equally significant low-level (pattern) and high-level (symbolic) cues favor learning the low-level cue, but this bias can be shifted towards the high-level cue by reducing the reliability of the low-level cue.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks exhibit a bias towards learning less abstract (low-level) features when multiple cues are available, but this bias can be altered by manipulating the data statistics.
papers.key_findings:
When trained on data containing both cues, the network learns the low-level pattern cue and largely ignores the symbolic cue, achieving high accuracy on pattern-only test data but chance-level accuracy on symbol-only test data.
When trained only on symbols, the network learns the symbolic cue but cannot generalize to classify patterns.
When trained only on patterns, the network learns the pattern cue but cannot generalize to classify symbols.
When the low-level cue is made less reliable by introducing distorted pattern labels, the network learns to use both cues.
The number of hidden layers and neurons does not change the overall trend of favoring the less abstract cue when both are equally reliable.
future_direction: Developing strategies that allow shifting learning to specific, user-defined cues, potentially by including information about the desired cues into the training data.
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have become an important tool for image classification with many applications in research and industry. However, it remains largely unknown how relevant image features are selected and how data properties affect this process. In particular, we are interested whether the abstraction level of image cues correlating with class membership influences feature selection. We perform experiments with binary images that contain a combination of cues, representing two different levels of abstractions: one is a pattern drawn from a random distribution where class membership correlates with the statistics of the pattern, the other a combination of symbol-like entities, where the symbolic code correlates with class membership. When the network is trained with data in which both cues are equally significant, we observe that the cues at the lower abstraction level, i.e., the pattern, is learned, while the symbolic information is largely ignored, even in networks with many layers. Symbol-like entities are only learned if the importance of low-level cues is reduced compared to the high-level ones. These findings raise important questions about the relevance of features that are learned by deep ANNs and how learning could be shifted towards symbolic features.

papers.title: Complexity Matters: Dynamics of Feature Learning in the Presence of Spurious Correlations
papers.research_question: How do the relative complexity and correlation strength of spurious features affect the learning dynamics of core features in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a boolean framework to study feature learning dynamics under spurious correlations, revealing that simpler spurious features and higher correlation strength slow core feature learning, lead to separate subnetworks, and challenge existing debiasing algorithms.
papers.conclusion: The complexity and correlation strength of spurious features significantly impact feature learning dynamics, and existing debiasing algorithms that assume separable learning phases may fail when spurious features are complex.
papers.key_findings:
Stronger spurious correlations or simpler spurious features slow down the learning rate of core features.
Two distinct subnetworks are formed to learn core and spurious features separately.
Learning phases of spurious and core features are not always separable.
Spurious features are not forgotten even after core features are fully learned.
Last layer retraining works by decreasing reliance on the spurious subnetwork, and popular debiasing algorithms fail in more general settings.
papers.limitation: The theoretical understanding of end-to-end dynamics of feature learning in the boolean case is still very limited, and the analysis is restricted to simple networks and parity functions.
future_direction: Full end-to-end analysis of feature learning dynamics in the boolean case with spurious correlations.
papers.abstract: Existing research often posits spurious features as easier to learn than core features in neural network optimization, but the impact of their relative simplicity remains under-explored. Moreover, studies mainly focus on end performance rather than the learning dynamics of feature learning. In this paper, we propose a theoretical framework and an associated synthetic dataset grounded in boolean function analysis. This setup allows for fine-grained control over the relative complexity (compared to core features) and correlation strength (with respect to the label) of spurious features to study the dynamics of feature learning under spurious correlations. Our findings uncover several interesting phenomena: (1) stronger spurious correlations or simpler spurious features slow down the learning rate of the core features, (2) two distinct subnetworks are formed to learn core and spurious features separately, (3) learning phases of spurious and core features are not always separable, (4) spurious features are not forgotten even after core features are fully learned. We demonstrate that our findings justify the success of retraining the last layer to remove spurious correlation and also identifies limitations of popular debiasing algorithms that exploit early learning of spurious features. We support our empirical findings with theoretical analyses for the case of learning XOR features with a one-hidden-layer ReLU network.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning\n Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of neural network layers and how do learning dynamics progress during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations that is invariant to affine transforms, and uses it to show that layers have lower intrinsic dimensionality than the number of neurons, and that networks converge from the bottom up during training.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful method for comparing neural network representations, providing insights into learning dynamics, intrinsic dimensionality, and enabling applications like model compression and improved training regimes.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is less than the number of neurons, and projecting onto the top SVCCA directions preserves accuracy without retraining.
Networks converge from the bottom up during training, with lower layers solidifying their representations earlier than higher layers.
SVCCA captures semantic class information, with similar classes having similar sensitivities in the network.
Freeze Training, based on the bottom-up convergence, can save computation and improve generalization by sequentially freezing lower layers during training.
SVCCA can be used for model compression by projecting layer outputs onto top SVCCA directions, reducing parameter count and computational cost.
papers.abstract:
We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis
(SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both
invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and
networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than
with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic
dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization;
to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge
to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific
information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that
simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code:
https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: Local vs distributed representations: What is the right basis for interpretability?
papers.research_question: Are dictionary-based representations more interpretable than neuron-based representations for understanding convolutional neural networks, and how does the choice of representational basis affect model comparisons?
