papers.core_contribution: Dictionary-based representations are consistently more interpretable than neuron-based representations in CNNs, and model comparisons based solely on neuron-level analyses can be misleading due to differences in superposition.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary-based representations constitute a superior basis for interpretability, and comparing models using only neuron-based representations can lead to misleading conclusions about their relative interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Dictionary-based representations were consistently more interpretable than neuron-based representations across three psychophysics experiments, with the advantage increasing in deeper layers.
ResNet50 exhibits greater superposition (lower axis-alignment) than VGG16, which masks its higher interpretability in neuron-based comparisons.
ResNet50 is more interpretable than VGG16 when evaluated using dictionary-based representations, but this difference disappears when using neuron-based representations.
Dictionary elements are at least as decision-relevant as individual neurons, as measured by Gradient×Input importance.
papers.limitation:
The experimental protocol may be confounded by semantics, as participants could solve trials by simple semantic grouping rather than identifying visual patterns.
The study is limited to two CNN architectures (ResNet50 and VGG16).
future_direction: Further refinement of the experimental protocol to better mitigate semantic confounds.
Examination of the interpretability of dictionary elements recovered by applying dictionary learning to full layer activations.
Expanding the range of architectures to understand why certain models are inherently more interpretable than others.
papers.abstract: Much of the research on the interpretability of deep neural networks has focused on studying the visual features that maximally activate individual neurons. However, recent work has cast doubts on the usefulness of such local representations for understanding the behavior of deep neural networks because individual neurons tend to respond to multiple unrelated visual patterns, a phenomenon referred to as "superposition". A promising alternative to disentangle these complex patterns is learning sparsely distributed vector representations from entire network layers, as the resulting basis vectors seemingly encode single identifiable visual patterns consistently. Thus, one would expect the resulting code to align better with human perceivable visual patterns, but supporting evidence remains, at best, anecdotal. To fill this gap, we conducted three large-scale psychophysics experiments collected from a pool of 560 participants. Our findings provide (i) strong evidence that features obtained from sparse distributed representations are easier to interpret by human observers and (ii) that this effect is more pronounced in the deepest layers of a neural network. Complementary analyses also reveal that (iii) features derived from sparse distributed representations contribute more to the model's decision. Overall, our results highlight that distributed representations constitute a superior basis for interpretability, underscoring a need for the field to move beyond the interpretation of local neural codes in favor of sparsely distributed ones.

papers.title: Efficient neural codes naturally emerge through gradient descent learning
papers.research_question: Does gradient descent learning in neural networks naturally lead to efficient coding, where sensitivity to input features matches their frequency in the input statistics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows mathematically that gradient descent learning in neural networks leads to efficient coding, where sensitivity to input features matches their frequency, even without explicit coding constraints.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that gradient descent learning can explain the emergence of efficient coding in both artificial and biological neural systems, providing a mechanistic account for perceptual sensitivity patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Artificial neural networks trained on ImageNet show sensitivity patterns to orientation and hue that match human perceptual sensitivity and the statistics of natural images.
Linear networks trained with gradient descent on image reconstruction learn principal components in order of their variance, leading to higher sensitivity for more common features.
The learning dynamics of gradient descent cause features with higher variance to be learned earlier, resulting in sigmoidal learning curves similar to human perceptual learning.
In supervised learning, gradient descent also biases learning towards more frequent features, independent of their task relevance.
The framework reproduces human developmental trends in visual acuity, with sensitivity improving linearly with training experience.
papers.limitation: The pattern of orientation sensitivity is partially due to architectural factors like spatial pooling, not solely learning.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which batch size affects anisotropy of sensitivity.
Verify predictions in experiments that separably vary label noise and input statistics in supervised perceptual learning problems.
Unravel optimal learning algorithms and characterize their sensory consequences.
papers.abstract: Abstract Animal sensory systems are more sensitive to common features in the environment than uncommon features. For example, small deviations from the more frequently encountered horizontal orientations can be more easily detected than small deviations from the less frequent diagonal ones. Here we find that artificial neural networks trained to recognize objects also have patterns of sensitivity that match the statistics of features in images. To interpret these findings, we show mathematically that learning with gradient descent in deep neural networks preferentially creates representations that are more sensitive to common features, a hallmark of efficient coding. This result suggests that efficient coding naturally emerges from gradient-like learning on natural stimuli.

papers.title: Individual differences among deep neural network models
papers.research_question: How do random initializations affect the internal representations of neural networks, and how do these differences vary with network depth, regularization, and training?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that neural networks trained with different random seeds develop substantially different internal representations, with greater variability in deeper layers, and that regularization techniques like dropout can reduce this variability. The authors recommend using multiple network instances when comparing to brain data.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that neural networks exhibit substantial individual differences in internal representations due to random initialization, especially in deeper layers. This variability should be accounted for by using multiple network instances when comparing to brain data.
papers.key_findings:
Representational consistency decreases with network depth, indicating greater individual differences in deeper layers.
Regularization via dropout increases representational consistency across networks.
Representational consistency decreases during training, showing a strong negative correlation with task performance.
Category centroid arrangements are highly consistent across networks, but exemplar-level representations differ.
Results replicate across different network architectures (ConvNet8 and AlexNet) and datasets (CIFAR-10 and ILSVRC 2012).
papers.abstract: Abstract Deep neural networks (DNNs) excel at visual recognition tasks and are increasingly used as a modelling framework for neural computations in the primate brain. However, each DNN instance, just like each individual brain, has a unique connectivity and representational profile. Here, we investigate individual differences among DNN instances that arise from varying only the random initialization of the network weights. Using representational similarity analysis, we demonstrate that this minimal change in initial conditions prior to training leads to substantial differences in intermediate and higher-level network representations, despite achieving indistinguishable network-level classification performance. We locate the origins of the effects in an under-constrained alignment of category exemplars, rather than a misalignment of category centroids. Furthermore, while network regularization can increase the consistency of learned representations, considerable differences remain. These results suggest that computational neuroscientists working with DNNs should base their inferences on multiple networks instances instead of single off-the-shelf networks.

papers.title: From Lazy to Rich: Exact Learning Dynamics in Deep Linear Networks
papers.research_question: How does initialization, specifically λ-balanced initializations, influence learning dynamics and the transition between lazy and rich regimes in deep linear networks?
papers.core_contribution: Derives exact solutions for the learning dynamics (gradient flow, internal representations, NTK) in λ-balanced two-layer deep linear networks, capturing the full spectrum from lazy to rich learning regimes as a function of initialization relative scale λ.
papers.conclusion: The relative scale λ of weight initialization in deep linear networks fundamentally shapes the learning dynamics, governing the transition between rich, feature-learning regimes and lazy, kernel-like regimes, with implications for understanding and designing learning systems in both machine learning and neuroscience.
papers.key_findings:
Exact analytical solutions for the temporal evolution of the network function, internal representational similarity, and the finite-width Neural Tangent Kernel are provided for λ-balanced initializations.
The relative scale parameter λ controls the learning regime: as λ → 0, dynamics are sigmoidal (rich regime); as |λ| → ∞, dynamics become exponential (lazy regime).
In the rich regime (λ=0), networks develop task-specific internal representations; in the lazy regime (|λ| large), representations become task-agnostic (identity-like).
The Neural Tangent Kernel evolves during training in the rich regime but remains static in the lazy regime.
The solutions provide insights for applications like continual learning, reversal learning, and transfer learning, showing how λ affects catastrophic forgetting and generalization.
papers.limitation: The exact solutions require assumptions of whitened inputs, λ-balanced initialization, and no bottleneck in network dimensions.
future_direction: Connecting the analysis of λ-balanced linear networks to low-rank fine-tuning (LoRA) dynamics and understanding how initialization scales affect fine-tuning performance.
papers.abstract: Biological and artificial neural networks develop internal representations that enable them to perform complex tasks. In artificial networks, the effectiveness of these models relies on their ability to build task specific representation, a process influenced by interactions among datasets, architectures, initialization strategies, and optimization algorithms. Prior studies highlight that different initializations can place networks in either a lazy regime, where representations remain static, or a rich/feature learning regime, where representations evolve dynamically. Here, we examine how initialization influences learning dynamics in deep linear neural networks, deriving exact solutions for lambda-balanced initializations-defined by the relative scale of weights across layers. These solutions capture the evolution of representations and the Neural Tangent Kernel across the spectrum from the rich to the lazy regimes. Our findings deepen the theoretical understanding of the impact of weight initialization on learning regimes, with implications for continual learning, reversal learning, and transfer learning, relevant to both neuroscience and practical applications.

papers.title: Categorization in Unsupervised Generative Self-learning Systems
papers.research_question: What is the nature of the effect of unsupervised categorization in self-encoding generative models? Is it coincidental or caused by underlying principles?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves the Unsupervised Categorization Conjecture, showing that under conditions of Bayesian training, constant accuracy, generalization, and compression, unsupervised self-encoding generative models statistically prefer representations with better geometric categorization of hidden concepts.
papers.conclusion: The effect of unsupervised categorization is a general phenomenon in generative self-learning systems under the stated conditions, offering insights for developing flexible, minimally supervised learning methods and connecting to biological learning processes.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretical proof shows that configurations with better categorization minimize regeneration loss and free energy.
Experimental results demonstrate that classifiers trained on unsupervised representations achieve better accuracy than those trained on raw input data.
The representation space exhibits compact and well-separated concept distributions (manifolds).
The effect of unsupervised categorization is general and not coincidental, providing a link between artificial and biological learning systems.
papers.limitation:
Existence of categorized representations is assumed.
Observable parameters must be relevant and specific enough to differentiate between hidden concepts.
Hidden concepts must be sufficiently represented in the dataset (balanced and large enough).
Compression is essential to avoid identity transformation.
future_direction: Investigate structure and distributions of concepts in representations of regenerative self-learning models in more depth.
Develop new methods for self-learning and general learning systems that are flexible and require minimal supervision.
papers.abstract: In this study the authors investigated the connections between the training processes of unsupervised neural network models with self-encoding and regeneration and the information structure in the representations created by such models. We propose theoretical arguments leading to conclusions, confirmed by previously published experimental results that unsupervised representations obtained under certain constraints in training compliant with Bayesian inference principle, favor configurations with better categorization of hidden concepts in the observable data. The results provide an important connection between training of unsupervised machine learning models and the structure of representations created by them and can be used in developing new methods and approaches in self-learning as well as provide insights into common principles underlying the emergence of intelligence in machine and biologic systems.

papers.title: Modeling the Influence of Data Structure on Learning in Neural Networks: The Hidden Manifold Model
papers.research_question: How does the structure of data (specifically, data lying on a lower-dimensional manifold) affect the learning dynamics and generalization performance of two-layer neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Hidden Manifold Model (HMM), a generative model for structured data, and proves a Gaussian Equivalence Property (GEP) that enables analytical derivation of learning dynamics for two-layer neural networks trained with online stochastic gradient descent.
papers.conclusion: The Hidden Manifold Model provides a tractable framework for studying how data structure influences learning in neural networks, and the analytical results offer insights into the dynamics of specialization and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
The Gaussian Equivalence Property holds for the HMM, allowing the learning dynamics to be described by a set of integro-differential equations.
Neural networks learn functions of increasing complexity during training, with a specialization transition where hidden units gradually align with teacher nodes.
Generalization performance deteriorates as the manifold dimension increases and improves with network width, but saturates beyond a certain width.
The learning rate has a minor influence on asymptotic error, but affects the time to reach specialization.
The HMM captures key properties of real data sets (MNIST, CIFAR10) in terms of learning dynamics and memorization patterns.
papers.abstract: Understanding the reasons for the success of deep neural networks trained using stochastic gradientbased methods is a key open problem for the nascent theory of deep learning. The types of data where these networks are most successful, such as images or sequences of speech, are characterized by intricate correlations. Yet, most theoretical work on neural networks does not explicitly model training data or assumes that elements of each data sample are drawn independently from some factorized probability distribution. These approaches are, thus, by construction blind to the correlation structure of real-world datasets and their impact on learning in neural networks. Here, we introduce a generative model for structured datasets that we call the hidden manifold model. The idea is to construct high-dimensional inputs that lie on a lower-dimensional manifold, with labels that depend only on their position within this manifold, akin to a single-layer decoder or generator in a generative adversarial network. We demonstrate that learning of the hidden manifold model is amenable to an analytical treatment by proving a "Gaussian equivalence property" (GEP), and we use the GEP to show how the dynamics of two-layer neural networks trained using one-pass stochastic gradient descent is captured by a set of integro-differential equations that track the performance of the network at all times. This approach permits us to analyze in detail how a neural network learns functions of increasing complexity during training, how its performance depends on its size, and how it is impacted by parameters such as the learning rate or the dimension of the hidden manifold.

papers.title: Beyond Distribution Shift: Spurious Features Through the Lens of Training Dynamics
papers.research_question: How do spurious features affect model generalization, and can harmful spurious features be detected early during training by monitoring training dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Spurious features can be benign or harmful depending on whether they are harder or easier to learn than core features. Harmful spurious features can be detected early by monitoring training dynamics using instance difficulty metrics like Prediction Depth.
papers.conclusion: Monitoring early training dynamics using suitable instance difficulty metrics can help identify harmful spurious features, saving time and computational costs and aiding in developing reliable models.
papers.key_findings:
Not all spurious features are harmful; they are harmful only if they are easier to learn than core features.
Prediction Depth (PD) can quantify feature difficulty and identify harmful spurious features during training.
Harmful spurious features can be detected by observing the learning dynamics of a DNN's early layers.
Monitoring only accuracy during training is insufficient to detect spurious features; instance difficulty metrics are needed.
Theoretical connections exist between Prediction Depth and information-theoretic concepts like V-usable information.
future_direction: Develop intervention schemes to fix spurious feature problems early.
Unlearning spurious features from model representations.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are prone to learning spurious features that correlate with the label during training but are irrelevant to the learning problem. This hurts model generalization and poses problems when deploying them in safety-critical applications. This paper aims to better understand the effects of spurious features through the lens of the learning dynamics of the internal neurons during the training process. We make the following observations: (1) While previous works highlight the harmful effects of spurious features on the generalization ability of DNNs, we emphasize that not all spurious features are harmful. Spurious features can be "benign" or "harmful" depending on whether they are "harder" or "easier" to learn than the core features for a given model. This definition is model and dataset dependent. (2) We build upon this premise and use instance difficulty methods (like Prediction Depth (Baldock et al., 2021)) to quantify "easiness" for a given model and to identify this behavior during the training phase. (3) We empirically show that the harmful spurious features can be detected by observing the learning dynamics of the DNN's early layers. In other words, easy features learned by the initial layers of a DNN early during the training can (potentially) hurt model generalization. We verify our claims on medical and vision datasets, both simulated and real, and justify the empirical success of our hypothesis by showing the theoretical connections between Prediction Depth and information-theoretic concepts like 𝒱-usable information (Ethayarajh et al., 2021). Lastly, our experiments show that monitoring only accuracy during training (as is common in machine learning pipelines) is insufficient to detect spurious features. We, therefore, highlight the need for monitoring early training dynamics using suitable instance difficulty metrics.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine\n Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops unsupervised methods (based on correlations between models) for discovering important neurons in Neural Machine Translation models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates how to control translations by modifying their activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and that many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Moreover, modifying the activations of individual neurons allows controlling the translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Unsupervised correlation methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) can rank neurons by importance, with top-ranked neurons having a larger impact on translation quality when erased.
Many top-ranked neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as position in sentence, parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Modifying the activations of individual neurons (e.g., tense neurons) allows for controlling translation output (e.g., changing verb tense) with varying degrees of success.
Different ranking methods highlight different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find information distributed across tokens.
The work indicates that not all linguistic information in NMT models is fully distributed; some properties are captured by individual neurons.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional seq2seq).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Apply the methods to other tasks beyond machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing
substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such
information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to
individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important
neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models
learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision.
We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered
neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena.
Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by
modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Neural networks behave as hash encoders: An empirical study
papers.research_question: Do well-trained neural networks for classification behave as hash encoders, mapping inputs to unique binary codes (neural codes) that preserve categorical information?
papers.core_contribution: Well-trained neural networks for classification behave as hash encoders without extra effort, mapping inputs to unique binary neural codes that exhibit determinism and categorization properties, and these encoding properties are influenced by model size, training time, and sample size.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks with ReLU-like activations naturally perform hash encoding, where the neural code serves as a hash code that preserves categorical information, and this behavior is shaped by model size, training time, and sample size.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks with ReLU-like activations partition the input space into linear regions, each corresponding to a unique binary neural code.
The neural code exhibits determinism (almost every training example has a unique code) and categorization (codes of same-class examples are similar).
Encoding properties strengthen with larger model size, longer training time, and larger sample size, while regularization and label noise have smaller effects.
An activation hash phase chart is defined, partitioning the space into under-expressive, critically-expressive, and sufficiently-expressive regimes.
The encoding properties do not hold for random data, indicating that the hash-like behavior is driven by the structure of the training data.
papers.limitation: The thresholds between the three regimes (under-expressive, critically-expressive, sufficiently-expressive) in the activation hash phase chart are currently unknown.
future_direction: Exploring the thresholds between the three regimes in the activation hash phase chart.
papers.abstract: The input space of a neural network with ReLU-like activations is partitioned into multiple linear regions, each corresponding to a specific activation pattern of the included ReLU-like activations. We demonstrate that this partition exhibits the following encoding properties across a variety of deep learning models: (1) {\it determinism}: almost every linear region contains at most one training example. We can therefore represent almost every training example by a unique activation pattern, which is parameterized by a {\it neural code}; and (2) {\it categorization}: according to the neural code, simple algorithms, such as $K$-Means, $K$-NN, and logistic regression, can achieve fairly good performance on both training and test data. These encoding properties surprisingly suggest that {\it normal neural networks well-trained for classification behave as hash encoders without any extra efforts.} In addition, the encoding properties exhibit variability in different scenarios. {Further experiments demonstrate that {\it model size}, {\it training time}, {\it training sample size}, {\it regularization}, and {\it label noise} contribute in shaping the encoding properties, while the impacts of the first three are dominant.} We then define an {\it activation hash phase chart} to represent the space expanded by {model size}, training time, training sample size, and the encoding properties, which is divided into three canonical regions: {\it under-expressive regime}, {\it critically-expressive regime}, and {\it sufficiently-expressive regime}. The source code package is available at \url{https://github.com/LeavesLei/activation-code}.

papers.title: Uncovering Layer-Dependent Activation Sparsity Patterns in ReLU Transformers
papers.research_question: How does token-level sparsity evolve over training in ReLU Transformers, and how do sparsity patterns differ across layers and between token, sequence, and batch levels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that sparsity patterns in ReLU Transformers are layer-dependent, with the first and last layers exhibiting inverted sparsity behaviors, and that neuron death is driven by training dynamics rather than random outliers.
papers.conclusion: Sparsity in ReLU Transformers varies systematically across layers, with the first and last layers being inverses in sparsity behavior, and that one can prune a significant fraction of hidden units without affecting accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Different layers in a ReLU Transformer exhibit distinct sparsity patterns, with the first layer using few hidden units per batch but using them frequently, and the last layer using many hidden units per batch but infrequently per token.
Sparsity patterns at token, sequence, and batch levels often anticorrelate, with layers that use few hidden units per token using many over a batch.
Neuron death (hidden units that never activate) is driven by training dynamics and occurs in specific regimes, rather than randomly.
A significant fraction of hidden units (about 5%) are never used from initialization, suggesting potential for better initialization methods.
Pruning hidden units that are never used after a point in training does not harm model performance, indicating potential for compute savings.
papers.limitation: The study focuses exclusively on small models and ReLU activation functions, which limits immediate applicability to modern foundation models.
future_direction: Investigate changes to initialization functions or model structure to allow more effective use of capacity in both ReLU and more competitive activation functions.
Study the underlying similarities in features learned between ReLU and smoothly-activated networks.
papers.abstract: Previous work has demonstrated that MLPs within ReLU Transformers exhibit high levels of sparsity, with many of their activations equal to zero for any given token. We build on that work to more deeply explore how token-level sparsity evolves over the course of training, and how it connects to broader sparsity patterns over the course of a sequence or batch, demonstrating that the different layers within small transformers exhibit distinctly layer-specific patterns on both of these fronts. In particular, we demonstrate that the first and last layer of the network have distinctive and in many ways inverted relationships to sparsity, and explore implications for the structure of feature representations being learned at different depths of the model. We additionally explore the phenomenon of ReLU dimensions "turning off", and show evidence suggesting that "neuron death" is being primarily driven by the dynamics of training, rather than simply occurring randomly or accidentally as a result of outliers.

papers.title: Cellular automata as convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules, specifically in the context of cellular automata?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that convolutional neural networks can represent and learn arbitrary cellular automata rules, and that the internal representations of trained networks reflect the complexity (entropy) of the CA rules.
papers.conclusion: Convolutional neural networks can learn cellular automata rules, and the complexity of the rules affects the depth and specialization of the learned representations, suggesting that the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Any cellular automaton can be represented by a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture.
A general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture can learn arbitrary CA rules when given videos of the CA as training data.
In the limit of large network widths, training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates.
Cellular automata with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations.
The entropy of the CA rule table influences the specificity of the internal representations in the trained network.
future_direction: Determine whether neural networks can more broadly inform efforts to understand the dynamical space of CA, including relating a CA's a priori rules to its apparent dynamical complexity during simulation.
Relate observations to more general patterns in deep networks, such as the information bottleneck.
papers.abstract: Deep-learning techniques have recently demonstrated broad success in predicting complex dynamical systems ranging from turbulence to human speech, motivating broader questions about how neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules. We explore this problem in the context of cellular automata (CA), simple dynamical systems that are intrinsically discrete and thus difficult to analyze using standard tools from dynamical systems theory. We show that any CA may readily be represented using a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture. This motivates the development of a general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture, which we find can learn the dynamical rules for arbitrary CA when given videos of the CA as training data. In the limit of large network widths, we find that training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates, and that common patterns emerge in the structure of networks trained on different CA rulesets. We train ensembles of networks on randomly sampled CA, and we probe how the trained networks internally represent the CA rules using an information-theoretic technique based on distributions of layer activation patterns. We find that CA with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations-illustrating how the underlying complexity of the CA's rules influences the specificity of these internal representations. Our results suggest how the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.

papers.title: Get rich quick: exact solutions reveal how unbalanced initializations promote rapid feature learning
papers.research_question: How do layer-specific initialization variances and learning rates determine the transition between lazy and rich learning regimes in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Derives exact solutions for a minimal model showing how unbalanced initializations and learning rates determine the transition between lazy and rich learning via conserved quantities, and shows that upstream initializations accelerate feature learning in nonlinear networks.
papers.conclusion: The theory motivates further exploration of unbalanced initializations to enhance efficient feature learning.
papers.key_findings:
In linear networks, rapid feature learning only occurs from balanced initializations.
In nonlinear networks, unbalanced initializations that promote faster learning in earlier layers (upstream) can accelerate rich learning.
The conserved quantity δ constrains learning trajectories and determines the geometry of parameter dynamics.
Upstream initializations reduce sample complexity for hierarchical data and decrease grokking time in modular arithmetic.
Upstream initializations promote interpretable filters in CNNs.
papers.limitation: Extending the mirror flow analysis to non-trivial piecewise linear networks is very difficult or provably impossible.
future_direction: Further exploration of unbalanced initializations to enhance efficient feature learning.
papers.abstract: While the impressive performance of modern neural networks is often attributed to their capacity to efficiently extract task-relevant features from data, the mechanisms underlying this rich feature learning regime remain elusive, with much of our theoretical understanding stemming from the opposing lazy regime. In this work, we derive exact solutions to a minimal model that transitions between lazy and rich learning, precisely elucidating how unbalanced layer-specific initialization variances and learning rates determine the degree of feature learning. Our analysis reveals that they conspire to influence the learning regime through a set of conserved quantities that constrain and modify the geometry of learning trajectories in parameter and function space. We extend our analysis to more complex linear models with multiple neurons, outputs, and layers and to shallow nonlinear networks with piecewise linear activation functions. In linear networks, rapid feature learning only occurs from balanced initializations, where all layers learn at similar speeds. While in nonlinear networks, unbalanced initializations that promote faster learning in earlier layers can accelerate rich learning. Through a series of experiments, we provide evidence that this unbalanced rich regime drives feature learning in deep finite-width networks, promotes interpretability of early layers in CNNs, reduces the sample complexity of learning hierarchical data, and decreases the time to grokking in modular arithmetic. Our theory motivates further exploration of unbalanced initializations to enhance efficient feature learning.

papers.title: Wider Networks Learn Better Features
papers.research_question: How does network width affect the features learned by neural networks, and do wider networks learn more transferable features for novel tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Wider networks learn more informative and transferable features in their hidden states, as visualized by activation atlases, leading to better performance when fine-tuning on novel tasks, even when test accuracy on the original task is independent of width.
papers.conclusion: Wider networks learn more informative features that are beneficial for transfer learning, even when original task performance is unchanged.
papers.key_findings:
Individual neurons in wide networks do not learn interpretable features, but groups of neurons (via activation atlases) do.
Hidden states of wide networks contain more information about inputs than narrow networks, even when test accuracy on the original task is the same.
Fine-tuning a linear classifier on features from a wide network on a new task yields better performance than on narrow networks, even with the same original task accuracy.
The additional information in wide networks (e.g., translation information in translated MNIST) is preserved and useful for transfer.
The features learned by wide networks are distributed across neurons, not sparse.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters for wider networks (e.g., learning rate) might be tuned to improve performance on the original task, but this was not explored.
The experiments are conducted on relatively small datasets (MNIST, CIFAR) and network widths, not in the infinite width or lazy training regime.
future_direction: Explore the effect of network width on the performance of transfer learning algorithms like MAML.
Investigate feature learning in the infinite width limit and lazy training regime.
papers.abstract: Transferability of learned features between tasks can massively reduce the cost of training a neural network on a novel task. We investigate the effect of network width on learned features using activation atlases --- a visualization technique that captures features the entire hidden state responds to, as opposed to individual neurons alone. We find that, while individual neurons do not learn interpretable features in wide networks, groups of neurons do. In addition, the hidden state of a wide network contains more information about the inputs than that of a narrow network trained to the same test accuracy. Inspired by this observation, we show that when fine-tuning the last layer of a network on a new task, performance improves significantly as the width of the network is increased, even though test accuracy on the original task is independent of width.

papers.title: The Surprising Simplicity of the Early-Time Learning Dynamics of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What is the early-time learning dynamics of neural networks? The paper investigates whether the early-time learning dynamics can be approximated by a linear model.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that in the early phase of training, neural networks learn a linear function of the input, which can be mimicked by training a simple linear model.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks initially learn simple linear functions, and only later in training do they exercise their nonlinear capacity.
papers.key_findings:
For two-layer fully-connected networks, the early-time learning dynamics are close to a linear model, whether training the first layer, second layer, or both.
The linear model includes features such as the input and its norm, depending on which layer is trained.
The agreement holds until the linear model converges to its optimum.
Empirical results show the phenomenon persists for multi-layer and convolutional networks on synthetic data and CIFAR-10.
The analysis relies on bounding the spectral norm of the difference between the Neural Tangent Kernel and a linear kernel.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical result is limited to two-layer fully-connected networks with data satisfying certain concentration properties.
The analysis only applies to the early phase of training.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other architectures and training settings.
papers.abstract: Modern neural networks are often regarded as complex black-box functions whose behavior is difficult to understand owing to their nonlinear dependence on the data and the nonconvexity in their loss landscapes. In this work, we show that these common perceptions can be completely false in the early phase of learning. In particular, we formally prove that, for a class of well-behaved input distributions, the early-time learning dynamics of a two-layer fully-connected neural network can be mimicked by training a simple linear model on the inputs. We additionally argue that this surprising simplicity can persist in networks with more layers and with convolutional architecture, which we verify empirically. Key to our analysis is to bound the spectral norm of the difference between the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) at initialization and an affine transform of the data kernel; however, unlike many previous results utilizing the NTK, we do not require the network to have disproportionately large width, and the network is allowed to escape the kernel regime later in training.

papers.title: Structure and Representation in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we find modular structure in neural networks, and does this structure have functional relevance in terms of local specialization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that trained neural networks exhibit clusterability (modular structure) and that clustering can find locally specialized groups of neurons. It also shows that interpretability tools reveal shortcomings in reward models' feature representation and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation advances understanding of neural network structure and representation, and highlights the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Trained neural networks are more clusterable than randomly initialized networks.
Clustering finds groups of neurons that are important and coherent, indicating local specialization.
Interpretability tools applied to reward models show they do not adequately represent relevant features and mispredict reward out of distribution.
These tools do not reveal a clear picture of the computation the networks are performing.
There is a need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.limitation: Interpretability tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are performing.
future_direction: Applying the methods to larger networks.
Studying the dynamics of clusterability during training.
Developing better interpretability tools for understanding generalization.
papers.abstract: Since neural networks have become dominant within the field of artificial intelligence, a sub-field of research has emerged attempting to understand their inner workings. One standard method within this sub-field has been to primarily understand neural networks as representing human-comprehensible features. Another possibility that has been less explored is to understand them as multi-step computer programs. A seeming prerequisite for this is some form of modularity: for different parts of the network to operate independently enough to be understood in isolation, and to implement distinct interpretable sub-routines.To find modular structure inside neural networks, we initially use the tools of graphical clustering. A network is clusterable in this sense if it can be divided into groups of neurons with strong internal connectivity but weak external connectivity. We find that a trained neural network is typically more clusterable than randomly initialized networks, and often clusterable relative to random networks with the same distribution of weights as the trained network. We investigate factors that promote clusterability, and also develop novel methods targeted at that end.For modularity to be valuable for understanding neural networks, it needs to have some sort of functional relevance.The type of functional relevance we target is local specialization of functionality. A neural network is locally specialized to the extent that parts of its computational graph can be abstractly represented as performing some comprehensible sub-task relevant to the overall task. We propose two proxies for local specialization: importance, which reflects how valuable sets of neurons are to network performance; and coherence, which reflects how consistently their neurons associate with features of the inputs. We then operationalize these proxies using techniques conventionally used to interpret individual neurons, applying them instead to groups of neurons produced by graph clustering algorithms. Our results show that clustering succeeds at finding groups of neurons that are important and coherent, although not all groups of neurons found are so.We conclude with a case study of using more standard interpretability tools, designed to understand the features being represented by directions in activation space, applying them to the analysis of neural networks trained on the reward function of the game CoinRun. Despite our networks achieving a low test loss, the application of interpretability tools shows that networks do not adequately represent relevant features and badly mispredict reward out of distribution. That said, these tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are in fact performing. This not only illustrates the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behaviour, but motivates it: if we take these networks as models of 'motivation systems' of policies trained by reinforcement learning, the conclusion is that such networks may competently pursue the wrong objectives when deployed in richer environments, indicating a need for interpretability techniques to shed light on generalization behaviour.

papers.title: Understanding trained CNNs by indexing neuron selectivity
papers.research_question: How can we understand and visualize the internal representations of Convolutional Neural Networks by indexing neuron selectivity to specific properties like color and class?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework to understand CNN internal representations by visualizing Neuron Features and quantifying neuron selectivity indexes for color and class, enabling the analysis of how features and classes are represented across layers.
papers.conclusion: The framework successfully indexes neuron selectivity, showing how color and class representations are organized across CNN layers, with implications for understanding neural coding principles.
papers.key_findings:
Color selectivity is present in all convolutional layers, with 40% in conv1 and 30% in conv2, decreasing but still present in deeper layers.
Class selectivity increases with depth, with over 50% of neurons in conv5 having high class selectivity (index >0.6).
Neuron Feature visualization reveals clear shapes for some neurons and blurred features for others, suggesting different coding strategies.
The framework can identify specific neurons selective to colors or classes, such as a red-mushroom neuron in conv4 or dog-face neurons in conv5.
Color is important for object recognition, as grayscale images lead to higher classification errors.
future_direction: Apply indexes to different neural network architectures.
Define new selectivity indexes for shape, texture, or part detection.
Study relations between indexes.

papers.title: Coloring the Black Box: Visualizing neural network behavior with a self-introspective model
papers.research_question: How can autoencoding the hidden activations of a neural network provide insight into its structure, behavior, and vulnerabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method called self-introspection, which uses an autoencoder to create a low-dimensional visualization of a neural network's hidden activations, enabling model evaluation, error estimation, layer reordering, and analysis of noise and adversarial attacks.
papers.conclusion: Self-introspection via autoencoders provides a flexible, interactive way to visualize and understand neural network behavior, offering potential for model evaluation, reliability assessment, and further research into interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden activations of a trained model cluster by category in a low-dimensional embedding, with misclassifications occurring in fringe areas between clusters.
The method allows for real-time model evaluation and error estimation based on the activation patterns.
The hidden layers of a network can be reordered by their relevance to specific output categories, revealing a latent structure.
The activation space visualization can be used to study the network's response to input noise and adversarial attacks, showing trajectories from correct to incorrect classifications.
Error estimates from the self-introspective framework are higher for misclassified samples, suggesting its use as a confidence metric.
papers.limitation: The method is demonstrated on feedforward and convolutional networks with relatively simple datasets; its application to recurrent, convolutional, and attention-based models is noted as potential but not shown.
future_direction: Extending the method to recurrent, convolutional, and attention-based models.
Studying the reliability and structure of the low-dimensional representations for more complex problems.
Using the method for adversarial attack detection and as a human interface for model reliability in ensembles.
papers.abstract: The following work presents how autoencoding all the possible hidden activations of a network for a given problem can provide insight about its structure, behavior, and vulnerabilities. The method, termed self-introspection, can show that a trained model showcases similar activation patterns (albeit randomly distributed due to initialization) when shown data belonging to the same category, and classification errors occur in fringe areas where the activations are not as clearly defined, suggesting some form of random, slowly varying, implicit encoding occurring within deep networks, that can be observed with this representation. Additionally, obtaining a low-dimensional representation of all the activations allows for (1) real-time model evaluation in the context of a multiclass classification problem, (2) the rearrangement of all hidden layers by their relevance in obtaining a specific output, and (3) the obtainment of a framework where studying possible counter-measures to noise and adversarial attacks is possible. Self-introspection can show how damaged input data can modify the hidden activations, producing an erroneous response. A few illustrative are implemented for feedforward and convolutional models and the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, showcasing its capabilities as a model evaluation framework.

papers.title: A Theoretical Analysis on Feature Learning in Neural Networks: Emergence from Inputs and Advantage over Fixed Features
papers.research_question: How can effective features emerge from inputs in the training dynamics of gradient descent? Is learning features from inputs necessary for the superior performance of neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Theoretical analysis proves that feature learning in neural networks emerges from input structure via gradient descent, providing an advantage over fixed-feature models.
papers.conclusion: Feature learning in neural networks depends strongly on the input structure and leads to superior performance.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks trained by gradient descent can learn effective features from input data structure.
Feature learning involves emergence and improvement of features through gradient steps.
Linear models on data-independent fixed features require exponentially large models to achieve similar performance.
Without the input structure, no polynomial-time algorithm in the Statistical Query model can learn effectively.
Experiments on synthetic and real data support the theoretical findings.
papers.limitation: The problem setup does not include hierarchical representations, which are important in practical data.
future_direction: Extend analysis to hierarchical representations in data.
Further studies on modeling input structure and analyzing feature learning.
papers.abstract: An important characteristic of neural networks is their ability to learn representations of the input data with effective features for prediction, which is believed to be a key factor to their superior empirical performance. To better understand the source and benefit of feature learning in neural networks, we consider learning problems motivated by practical data, where the labels are determined by a set of class relevant patterns and the inputs are generated from these along with some background patterns. We prove that neural networks trained by gradient descent can succeed on these problems. The success relies on the emergence and improvement of effective features, which are learned among exponentially many candidates efficiently by exploiting the data (in particular, the structure of the input distribution). In contrast, no linear models on data-independent features of polynomial sizes can learn to as good errors. Furthermore, if the specific input structure is removed, then no polynomial algorithm in the Statistical Query model can learn even weakly. These results provide theoretical evidence showing that feature learning in neural networks depends strongly on the input structure and leads to the superior performance. Our preliminary experimental results on synthetic and real data also provide positive support.

papers.title: Image denoising with multi-layer perceptrons, part 2: training trade-offs and analysis of their mechanisms
papers.research_question: What trade-offs must be considered when training multi-layer perceptrons for image denoising, and how do these networks internally achieve denoising?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides detailed guidelines for training MLPs to achieve state-of-the-art image denoising and analyzes their inner workings, showing that denoising is achieved through saturation of the tanh activation function, leading to binary hidden representations.
papers.conclusion: MLPs can achieve excellent image denoising performance when trained with appropriate trade-offs, and their internal mechanisms can be understood through analysis of hidden unit activation patterns, revealing a denoising process based on saturation and binary codes.
papers.key_findings:
More training data and more hidden units per layer consistently improve performance.
There exists an ideal number of hidden layers; too many layers, especially in deep and narrow networks, can cause catastrophic performance degradation.
Fine-tuning with a lower learning rate after initial training reduces test error fluctuations and improves final performance.
Denoising in single-hidden-layer MLPs is achieved through saturation of the tanh layer, which attenuates noise while preserving features detected by highly active neurons.
The feature detectors (input weights) adapt to the noise type and strength; for example, larger input patches are learned for stronger noise.
papers.limitation:
Deep and narrow networks (with many hidden layers but few units per layer) are difficult to optimize and can suffer catastrophic degradation in performance.
Block-matching MLPs do not provide a clear advantage at very low or very high noise levels, and their performance can deteriorate compared to plain MLPs at high noise levels.
future_direction: Applying similar training guidelines and analysis to other image processing tasks like super-resolution, deconvolution, and demosaicking.
Exploring the benefits of binary representations compared to sparse representations in deep networks.
papers.abstract: Image denoising can be described as the problem of mapping from a noisy image to a noise-free image. In another paper, we show that multi-layer perceptrons can achieve outstanding image denoising performance for various types of noise (additive white Gaussian noise, mixed Poisson-Gaussian noise, JPEG artifacts, salt-and-pepper noise and noise resembling stripes). In this work we discuss in detail which trade-offs have to be considered during the training procedure. We will show how to achieve good results and which pitfalls to avoid. By analysing the activation patterns of the hidden units we are able to make observations regarding the functioning principle of multi-layer perceptrons trained for image denoising.

papers.title: MoEfication: Transformer Feed-forward Layers are Mixtures of Experts
papers.research_question: Do functional partitions emerge in feed-forward networks (FFNs) of pre-trained Transformers, similar to mixtures of experts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that feed-forward networks in Transformers are naturally mixtures of experts and introduces MoEfication, a method to convert standard models into MoE versions, enabling efficient inference with minimal performance loss.
papers.conclusion: The work verifies that Transformer FFNs are mixtures of experts and that MoEfication can convert models to MoE versions for efficient inference and provide insights into FFN mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
FFNs in pre-trained Transformers exhibit sparse activation, with most inputs activating only a tiny fraction of neurons.
MoEfication can maintain over 95% of original performance while using only 10-30% of FFN parameters.
MoEfication significantly reduces inference FLOPS, achieving up to 2x speedup with 25% of FFN parameters.
Routing patterns in MoEfied models reveal both general experts (used for most inputs) and input-specific experts (seldom used).
Larger models have sparser activations, making MoEfication more effective for them.
future_direction: Explaining the sparse activation phenomenon empirically or theoretically.
Inspiring future work on the design and training of MoE models.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that feed-forward networks (FFNs) in pre-trained Transformers are a key component, storing various linguistic and factual knowledge. However, the computational patterns of FFNs are still unclear. In this work, we study the computational patterns of FFNs and observe that most inputs only activate a tiny ratio of neurons of FFNs. This phenomenon is similar to the sparsity of the human brain, which drives research on functional partitions of the human brain. To verify whether functional partitions also emerge in FFNs, we propose to convert a model into its MoE version with the same parameters, namely MoEfication. Specifically, MoEfication consists of two phases: (1) splitting the parameters of FFNs into multiple functional partitions as experts, and (2) building expert routers to decide which experts will be used for each input. Experimental results show that MoEfication can conditionally use 10% to 30% of FFN parameters while maintaining over 95% original performance for different models on various downstream tasks. Besides, MoEfication brings two advantages: (1) it significantly reduces the FLOPS of inference, i.e., 2x speedup with 25% of FFN parameters, and (2) it provides a fine-grained perspective to study the inner mechanism of FFNs. The source code of this paper can be obtained from https://github.com/ thunlp/MoEfication.

papers.title: Language Models Represent Space and Time
papers.research_question: Do large language models learn coherent linear representations of space and time, i.e., do they form a world model?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models learn linear representations of space and time that are robust to prompting and unified across entity types, and individual 'space' and 'time' neurons exist that encode these coordinates.
papers.conclusion: Modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover spatial and temporal coordinates from internal activations, with performance increasing with model size and plateauing in middle layers.
Spatial and temporal features are linearly represented, as nonlinear probes do not improve performance.
Representations are robust to variations in prompting, though random tokens or capitalization degrade performance.
Probes generalize across entity types and to held-out geographic or temporal blocks, indicating unified representations.
Individual neurons exist that are highly predictive of space and time, and causal interventions confirm their importance.
papers.limitation:
Data comes only from English Wikipedia, skewing towards the Anglosphere, and entity type distribution is not uniform.
The true extent and structure of spatial and temporal representations remain unclear.
future_direction: Extracting representations in the model’s coordinate system rather than human coordinates, e.g., with sparse autoencoders.
Studying how these spatiotemporal representations are learned, recalled, and used internally across training checkpoints.
Investigating potential parallels with biological place and grid cells in the brain.
papers.abstract: The capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have sparked debate over whether such systems just learn an enormous collection of superficial statistics or a set of more coherent and grounded representations that reflect the real world. We find evidence for the latter by analyzing the learned representations of three spatial datasets (world, US, NYC places) and three temporal datasets (historical figures, artworks, news headlines) in the Llama-2 family of models. We discover that LLMs learn linear representations of space and time across multiple scales. These representations are robust to prompting variations and unified across different entity types (e.g. cities and landmarks). In addition, we identify individual "space neurons" and "time neurons" that reliably encode spatial and temporal coordinates. While further investigation is needed, our results suggest modern LLMs learn rich spatiotemporal representations of the real world and possess basic ingredients of a world model.

papers.title: An XAI-based Analysis of Shortcut Learning in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How and where do neural networks encode spurious correlations (shortcut learning), and to what extent are these features disentangled?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the neuron spurious score (s-score) to quantify a neuron's dependence on spurious features and shows that spurious features are partially disentangled in CNNs and ViTs, but the degree varies, and existing mitigation methods have incomplete assumptions.
papers.conclusion: Spurious features are partially disentangled in neural networks, but unlearning them is complex; the results lay groundwork for developing better mitigation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Both CNNs and ViTs learn spurious features, as shown by a significant gap between average and worst-group accuracy.
The neuron spurious score (s-score) can identify neurons focusing on spurious regions in CNNs, but in ViTs such neurons are harder to detect due to distributed attention.
In CNNs, some neurons exclusively encode spurious features, while others encode both spurious and core features.
Spurious features are encoded not only in the last layer but also in deeper components (subnetworks) of CNNs.
Existing mitigation methods like DFR improve worst-group accuracy by adjusting neuron interactions rather than completely eliminating spurious features.
papers.limitation: Explanation methods sometimes fail to capture fully what models are truly encoding. While heatmap attributions can visualize where the model is focusing within the input, they do not reveal what features the model is learning.
papers.abstract: Machine learning models tend to learn spurious features - features that strongly correlate with target labels but are not causal. Existing approaches to mitigate models' dependence on spurious features work in some cases, but fail in others. In this paper, we systematically analyze how and where neural networks encode spurious correlations. We introduce the neuron spurious score, an XAI-based diagnostic measure to quantify a neuron's dependence on spurious features. We analyze both convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision transformers (ViTs) using architecture-specific methods. Our results show that spurious features are partially disentangled, but the degree of disentanglement varies across model architectures. Furthermore, we find that the assumptions behind existing mitigation methods are incomplete. Our results lay the groundwork for the development of novel methods to mitigate spurious correlations and make AI models safer to use in practice.

papers.title: Representer Point Selection for Explaining Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we explain the predictions of a deep neural network by identifying influential training points (representer points) that have excitatory or inhibitory effects?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a representer theorem for deep neural networks that decomposes the pre-activation prediction into a linear combination of training point activations, enabling the selection of excitatory and inhibitory training points to explain model predictions.
papers.conclusion: The representer point selection method provides an efficient and insightful way to explain deep neural network predictions by identifying influential training points, with potential applications in model debugging and understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The method is more scalable and computationally efficient than influence functions, allowing for real-time explanations.
It provides both excitatory (positive) and inhibitory (negative) training points, offering richer insight into model behavior.
The method aids in dataset debugging by identifying mislabeled training points.
The sensitivity map (gradient-based attribution) can be decomposed into contributions from individual training points.
The method produces numerically stable representer values, unlike influence functions which can yield zeros or very small values.
papers.limitation:
The method requires the model to be at a stationary point and uses L2 regularization on the weight matrix.
The theoretical formulation applies to models with a linear layer before the activation function.
future_direction: Extend the method to NLP datasets with recurrent neural networks.
Use representer values for data poisoning attacks.
papers.abstract: We propose to explain the predictions of a deep neural network, by pointing to the set of what we call representer points in the training set, for a given test point prediction. Specifically, we show that we can decompose the pre-activation prediction of a neural network into a linear combination of activations of training points, with the weights corresponding to what we call representer values, which thus capture the importance of that training point on the learned parameters of the network. But it provides a deeper understanding of the network than simply training point influence: with positive representer values corresponding to excitatory training points, and negative values corresponding to inhibitory points, which as we show provides considerably more insight. Our method is also much more scalable, allowing for real-time feedback in a manner not feasible with influence functions.

papers.title: Latent State Models of Training Dynamics
papers.research_question: How do differences in data order and initialization manifest in model training, and how can we interpret training dynamics and phase transitions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes using Hidden Markov Models (HMM) to model training dynamics and identify detour states that slow down convergence.
papers.conclusion: Proposes directly modeling training dynamics as a new avenue for interpretability research and discovers detour states that are related to convergence time and sensitivity to random seed.
papers.key_findings:
Training dynamics can be represented by a low-dimensional discrete latent space using HMM.
In grokking tasks, different paths in the training map correspond to different convergence times, with detour states slowing convergence.
In image classification, training dynamics are stable and linear, but removing batch norm and residual connections induces detour states.
Adding layer normalization and decreasing batch size stabilizes grokking and removes detour states.
Linear regression on the latent state distribution can predict convergence time.
papers.limitation:
Assumes training dynamics can be represented by a linear, discrete, and Markovian model; a higher-powered model might capture more information.
Uses hand-picked metrics for dimensionality reduction; a fully unsupervised approach without explicit metrics deserves exploration.
For very large models, training an HMM across many random seeds may be infeasible.
future_direction: Relaxing the assumptions of the HMM.
Developing a fully unsupervised approach without explicit metrics.
Investigating whether models of training dynamics can generalize zero-shot across architectures and sizes.
Using early variation across seeds for hyperparameter search.
papers.abstract: The impact of randomness on model training is poorly understood. How do differences in data order and initialization actually manifest in the model, such that some training runs outperform others or converge faster? Furthermore, how can we interpret the resulting training dynamics and the phase transitions that characterize different trajectories? To understand the effect of randomness on the dynamics and outcomes of neural network training, we train models multiple times with different random seeds and compute a variety of metrics throughout training, such as the $L_2$ norm, mean, and variance of the neural network's weights. We then fit a hidden Markov model (HMM) over the resulting sequences of metrics. The HMM represents training as a stochastic process of transitions between latent states, providing an intuitive overview of significant changes during training. Using our method, we produce a low-dimensional, discrete representation of training dynamics on grokking tasks, image classification, and masked language modeling. We use the HMM representation to study phase transitions and identify latent "detour" states that slow down convergence.

papers.title: Interpreting Adversarial Examples by Activation Promotion and Suppression
papers.research_question: How to interpret the mechanism of adversarial perturbations at pixel, image, and network levels, and how does this interpretability help improve robustness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to interpret adversarial examples by revealing the promotion-suppression effect (PSE) on neurons' activations, linking pixel-level perturbations to discriminative image regions via CAM, and connecting unit sensitivity to concept interpretability via network dissection.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive interpretation of adversarial examples at pixel, image, and network levels, showing that adversarial attacks induce activation promotion and suppression effects linked to discriminative regions and unit interpretability, offering insights for improving robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial perturbations exhibit a promotion-suppression effect (PSE) and can be categorized into suppression-dominated, promotion-dominated, and balanced types.
Pixel-level adversarial perturbations are strongly associated with class-specific discriminative image regions localized by class activation mapping (CAM).
There is a tight connection between the sensitivity of hidden units to adversarial perturbations and their interpretability on semantic concepts, as revealed by network dissection.
The interpretability of adversarial patterns constrains the effectiveness of adversarial attacks; refining attacks by focusing on high-sensitivity pixels can maintain success with fewer perturbations.
Neuron masking based on sensitivity and interpretability can improve adversarial robustness at a slight cost to clean accuracy.
future_direction: Develop interpretability-driven defensive methods and consider attacks against interpretability, not just prediction.
papers.abstract: It is widely known that convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial examples: images with imperceptible perturbations crafted to fool classifiers. However, interpretability of these perturbations is less explored in the literature. This work aims to better understand the roles of adversarial perturbations and provide visual explanations from pixel, image and network perspectives. We show that adversaries have a promotion-suppression effect (PSE) on neurons' activations and can be primarily categorized into three types: i) suppression-dominated perturbations that mainly reduce the classification score of the true label, ii) promotion-dominated perturbations that focus on boosting the confidence of the target label, and iii) balanced perturbations that play a dual role in suppression and promotion. We also provide image-level interpretability of adversarial examples. This links PSE of pixel-level perturbations to class-specific discriminative image regions localized by class activation mapping (Zhou et al. 2016). Further, we examine the adversarial effect through network dissection (Bau et al. 2017), which offers concept-level interpretability of hidden units. We show that there exists a tight connection between the units' sensitivity to adversarial attacks and their interpretability on semantic concepts. Lastly, we provide some new insights from our interpretation to improve the adversarial robustness of networks.

papers.title: Beyond Signal Propagation: Is Feature Diversity Necessary in Deep Neural\n Network Initialization?
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether feature diversity in neural network initialization is necessary for successful training, by constructing networks with identical features at initialization.
papers.core_contribution: Random, diverse initializations are not necessary for training neural networks; networks with identical features at initialization can achieve high accuracy when trained with a symmetry-breaking mechanism, such as non-deterministic GPU operations.
papers.conclusion: Feature diversity is not necessary in neural network initialization, and symmetry breaking is a key factor for training networks with symmetric initializations.
papers.key_findings:
Networks with identical features at initialization (ConstNet) can achieve high accuracy on standard benchmarks when trained with symmetry breaking mechanisms.
Non-deterministic GPU operations can serve as a sufficient source of symmetry breaking to enable training.
Without symmetry breaking, training fails.
The forward and backward weight correlations in ConstNet converge to similar values as in randomly initialized networks.
In shallow networks, feature replication degrades performance, but adding small noise ameliorates this.
papers.limitation:
0-initialized networks are less robust to learning rate changes and may have slower convergence.
Reliance on hardware noise for symmetry breaking may lead to variability across different hardware and insufficient breaking in 16-bit training.
Dropout alone may not break symmetry in the first convolutional layer.
papers.abstract:
Deep neural networks are typically initialized with random weights, with
variances chosen to facilitate signal propagation and stable gradients. It is
also believed that diversity of features is an important property of these
initializations. We construct a deep convolutional network with identical
features by initializing almost all the weights to $0$. The architecture also
enables perfect signal propagation and stable gradients, and achieves high
accuracy on standard benchmarks. This indicates that random, diverse
initializations are \textit{not} necessary for training neural networks. An
essential element in training this network is a mechanism of symmetry breaking;
we study this phenomenon and find that standard GPU operations, which are
non-deterministic, can serve as a sufficient source of symmetry breaking to
enable training.

papers.title: Where You Place the Norm Matters: From Prejudiced to Neutral Initializations
papers.research_question: How do normalization layers influence the initial prediction bias in DNNs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that normalization placement (Pre-Norm vs Post-Norm) critically determines the initial prediction bias (Initial Guessing Bias), with post-activation normalization promoting neutral initializations and pre-activation normalization preserving or amplifying prejudice, thereby shaping subsequent learning dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Normalization placement is a critical architectural design choice that systematically shapes initial predictions and subsequent learning dynamics, offering principled guidelines for more controlled and interpretable network design.
papers.key_findings:
Placing normalization after activations (Post-Norm) promotes neutral initialization states, while placing it before activations (Pre-Norm) leads to prejudiced regimes.
BatchNorm after activation effectively suppresses initial prejudice, while LayerNorm after activation reduces but may not eliminate it on highly correlated data.
Initial Guessing Bias (IGB) affects training dynamics, including convergence speed and per-class fairness, with prejudiced initializations leading to asymmetric class performance.
