Theoretical analysis proves that for deep MLPs, BatchNorm before activation leads to weakly prejudiced initialization stable with depth, while BatchNorm after activation promotes neutrality.
Experiments on real datasets (CIFAR10, MNIST) confirm the theoretical predictions, though data structure can modulate the effects.
papers.limitation: The theoretical framework is developed for random, unstructured inputs, and deviations occur on highly correlated real data (e.g., MNIST), where LayerNorm after activation does not completely eliminate Initial Guessing Bias.
future_direction: Future study into the complex interplay between architecture-induced and data-induced biases.
papers.abstract: Normalization layers, such as Batch Normalization and Layer Normalization, are central components in modern neural networks, widely adopted to improve training stability and generalization. While their practical effectiveness is well documented, a detailed theoretical understanding of how normalization affects model behavior, starting from initialization, remains an important open question. In this work, we investigate how both the presence and placement of normalization within hidden layers influence the statistical properties of network predictions before training begins. In particular, we study how these choices shape the distribution of class predictions at initialization, which can range from unbiased (Neutral) to highly concentrated (Prejudiced) toward a subset of classes. Our analysis shows that normalization placement induces systematic differences in the initial prediction behavior of neural networks, which in turn shape the dynamics of learning. By linking architectural choices to prediction statistics at initialization, our work provides a principled understanding of how normalization can influence early training behavior and offers guidance for more controlled and interpretable network design.

papers.title: Feature Integration Spaces: Joint Training Reveals Dual Encoding in Neural Network Representations
papers.research_question: Does neural network encode information in two complementary spaces: feature identity and feature integration?
papers.core_contribution: This work provides systematic evidence for dual encoding in neural representations, meaningful nonlinearly encoded feature integrations, and introduces an architectural paradigm shift from post-hoc feature analysis to integrated computational design.
papers.conclusion: This work provides the first systematic evidence for dual-encoding spaces in neural network representations and introduces an architectural solution that achieves substantial improvements across multiple validation metrics, establishing foundations for next-generation SAEs.
papers.key_findings:
Joint training achieves 41.3% reconstruction improvement and 51.6% reduction in KL divergence errors over SAE-only baseline.
The architecture spontaneously develops bimodal feature organization with low squared norm features specializing in integration pathways.
Integration features exhibit selective sensitivity to experimental manipulations and produce statistically significant nonlinear interaction effects on model outputs.
Nonlinear integration components achieve 16.5% standalone improvement using only 3% of parameters, demonstrating parameter efficiency.
Sequential SAE+NFM approach shows 23.4% error reduction and 29.8% reduction in pathological KL divergence errors.
papers.limitation:
Scale constraints represent one primary limitation of this work. Our experiments on a 3B parameter model with 50k SAE features provide proof-of-concept evidence, but scaling to industrial-scale models with millions of features is likely challenging.
Integration interpretability presents ongoing challenges. While we demonstrated functional effects, these features remain largely opaque to direct inspection.
Limitations of traditional feature discovery approaches, as maximum activation analysis on secondary features failed to yield interpretable patterns.
future_direction: Dynamic analysis of how integration patterns evolve during training
Cross-model validation
Cross-layer analysis
papers.abstract: Current sparse autoencoder (SAE) approaches to neural network interpretability assume that activations can be decomposed through linear superposition into sparse, interpretable features. Despite high reconstruction fidelity, SAEs consistently fail to eliminate polysemanticity and exhibit pathological behavioral errors. We propose that neural networks encode information in two complementary spaces compressed into the same substrate: feature identity and feature integration. To test this dual encoding hypothesis, we develop sequential and joint-training architectures to capture identity and integration patterns simultaneously. Joint training achieves 41.3% reconstruction improvement and 51.6% reduction in KL divergence errors. This architecture spontaneously develops bimodal feature organization: low squared norm features contributing to integration pathways and the rest contributing directly to the residual. Small nonlinear components (3% of parameters) achieve 16.5% standalone improvements, demonstrating parameter-efficient capture of computational relationships crucial for behavior. Additionally, intervention experiments using 2x2 factorial stimulus designs demonstrated that integration features exhibit selective sensitivity to experimental manipulations and produce systematic behavioral effects on model outputs, including significant statistical interaction effects across semantic dimensions. This work provides systematic evidence for (1) dual encoding in neural representations, (2) meaningful nonlinearly encoded feature interactions, and (3) introduces an architectural paradigm shift from post-hoc feature analysis to integrated computational design, establishing foundations for next-generation SAEs.

papers.title: Learned feature representations are biased by complexity, learning order, position, and more
papers.research_question: How do extraneous properties like feature complexity, learning order, and distribution affect the learned feature representations in deep neural networks, even when features play equivalent computational roles?
papers.core_contribution: Learned feature representations in deep networks are systematically biased by extraneous properties like feature complexity and learning order, which poses significant challenges for interpretability and comparing representations across systems.
papers.conclusion: The systematic biases in learned feature representations highlight a key challenge for interpretability and for comparing representations between models and brains, as extraneous learning details can be conflated with computationally important aspects.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler features are represented more strongly and densely than complex features, even when both are learned equally well.
Features learned earlier dominate representations, making them path-dependent.
Feature prevalence in the training data and output position also bias representation strength.
These biases are general across architectures (MLPs, ResNets, Transformers) but can interact with hyperparameters like dropout and optimizer.
These representation biases impact downstream analyses like interpretability methods and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA).
papers.limitation:
Focus on simple, synthetic datasets.
Focus on classification tasks; continuous functions or richer contextual computation (e.g., language modeling) may differ.
Models are of toy scale; biases may differ in larger models.
Main analyses rely on linear regression, which may miss non-linear encodings.
future_direction: Study these biases on more realistic datasets with larger sets of entangled features.
Investigate how biases differ under other objectives (e.g., continuous functions) and in richly contextual computation.
Explore these effects at scale in larger models.
papers.abstract: Representation learning, and interpreting learned representations, are key areas of focus in machine learning and neuroscience. Both fields generally use representations as a means to understand or improve a system's computations. In this work, however, we explore surprising dissociations between representation and computation that may pose challenges for such efforts. We create datasets in which we attempt to match the computational role that different features play, while manipulating other properties of the features or the data. We train various deep learning architectures to compute these multiple abstract features about their inputs. We find that their learned feature representations are systematically biased towards representing some features more strongly than others, depending upon extraneous properties such as feature complexity, the order in which features are learned, and the distribution of features over the inputs. For example, features that are simpler to compute or learned first tend to be represented more strongly and densely than features that are more complex or learned later, even if all features are learned equally well. We also explore how these biases are affected by architectures, optimizers, and training regimes (e.g., in transformers, features decoded earlier in the output sequence also tend to be represented more strongly). Our results help to characterize the inductive biases of gradient-based representation learning. We then illustrate the downstream effects of these biases on various commonly-used methods for analyzing or intervening on representations. These results highlight a key challenge for interpretability $-$ or for comparing the representations of models and brains $-$ disentangling extraneous biases from the computationally important aspects of a system's internal representations.

papers.title: DORA: Exploring Outlier Representations in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we analyze the representational space of deep neural networks to identify outlier representations that may correspond to spurious correlations or undesired concepts in a data-agnostic manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DORA, a data-agnostic framework for analyzing neural representations using a novel Extreme-Activation distance metric, which can identify outlier representations that often correspond to spurious or undesired concepts.
papers.conclusion: DORA offers an effective data-agnostic approach to explore and interpret neural representations, enabling the identification of anomalous representations that often encode spurious or undesired concepts, thereby enhancing model transparency and safety.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Extreme-Activation distance metric aligns well with human judgment of concept similarity and outperforms traditional distance metrics in capturing semantic relationships.
DORA can effectively identify outlier representations that detect spurious correlations, such as watermarks or artifacts, in pre-trained models.
The framework is applicable across various architectures (CNNs, Transformers) and datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100).
Outlier representations corresponding to undesired concepts can persist even after fine-tuning on a different dataset.
DORA provides a practical tool for model interpretability and safety by revealing learned concepts that may lead to biased or harmful decisions.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at learning complex abstractions within their internal representations. However, the concepts they learn remain opaque, a problem that becomes particularly acute when models unintentionally learn spurious correlations. In this work, we present DORA (Data-agnOstic Representation Analysis), the first data-agnostic framework for analyzing the representational space of DNNs. Central to our framework is the proposed Extreme-Activation (EA) distance measure, which assesses similarities between representations by analyzing their activation patterns on data points that cause the highest level of activation. As spurious correlations often manifest in features of data that are anomalous to the desired task, such as watermarks or artifacts, we demonstrate that internal representations capable of detecting such artifactual concepts can be found by analyzing relationships within neural representations. We validate the EA metric quantitatively, demonstrating its effectiveness both in controlled scenarios and real-world applications. Finally, we provide practical examples from popular Computer Vision models to illustrate that representations identified as outliers using the EA metric often correspond to undesired and spurious concepts.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: When and where do feed-forward neural networks learn localist representations?
papers.research_question: Under what conditions do localist representations (local codes) emerge in feed-forward parallel distributed processing (PDP) neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Localist coding can emerge in feed-forward PDP networks, and the number of local codes is influenced by network architecture, data properties, and training noise, suggesting they may offer computational efficiency and noise resilience.
papers.conclusion: Localist representations can emerge in feed-forward PDP networks under conditions such as invariant features in the data and noisy training, and may be found in middle and higher layers of deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
The number of local codes follows a well-defined distribution across hidden layer neurons, with a peak determined by input data size, number of examples, and sparsity.
Fewer training examples per class leads to more local codes.
Sparse input data (low sparseness) increases the number of local codes.
Using a 1-hot output encoding drastically reduces the number of local codes in the hidden layer.
Dropout increases the number of local codes, suggesting local codes offer resilience to noisy networks.
papers.limitation:
The data used is a simple pattern classification task, which may not reflect more complex real-world data.
Local codes only emerge when there are invariant features shared within a category.
future_direction: Investigate the qualities of data passed within a neural network to see if local codes emerge in deeper layers.
Explore whether local codes have diagnostic use for generalization or overfitting.
Test the findings on standard datasets like the Iris dataset.
papers.abstract: According to parallel distributed processing (PDP) theory in psychology, neural networks (NN) learn distributed rather than interpretable localist representations. This view has been held so strongly that few researchers have analysed single units to determine if this assumption is correct. However, recent results from psychology, neuroscience and computer science have shown the occasional existence of local codes emerging in artificial and biological neural networks. In this paper, we undertake the first systematic survey of when local codes emerge in a feed-forward neural network, using generated input and output data with known qualities. We find that the number of local codes that emerge from a NN follows a well-defined distribution across the number of hidden layer neurons, with a peak determined by the size of input data, number of examples presented and the sparsity of input data. Using a 1-hot output code drastically decreases the number of local codes on the hidden layer. The number of emergent local codes increases with the percentage of dropout applied to the hidden layer, suggesting that the localist encoding may offer a resilience to noisy networks. This data suggests that localist coding can emerge from feed-forward PDP networks and suggests some of the conditions that may lead to interpretable localist representations in the cortex. The findings highlight how local codes should not be dismissed out of hand.

papers.title: Ablation of a Robot's Brain: Neural Networks Under a Knife
papers.research_question: How can ablation be used to determine the structure of information in neural networks, and what similarities exist between biological and artificial neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an ablation-based method to analyze neural networks, demonstrating that artificial neural networks exhibit robustness to damage and localization of function similar to biological neural networks.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates similarities in organization and information storage between biological and artificial neural networks through ablation, highlighting the need for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Ablation of neuron groups leads to consistent output shifts, showing localization of function.
Networks are robust to damage, with removal of single groups not eliminating task performance.
Clustering identifies 6 distinct functional roles for neuron groups.
Analogous functional regions exist across different training trials.
papers.limitation:
Granularity of ablations is coarse; future studies need finer-scale analysis.
Limited dataset due to reinforcement learning and real-time training constraints.
future_direction: Investigate similarities at different scales of ablation granularity.
Use larger datasets for more comprehensive analysis.
Further research to develop better theoretical understanding.
papers.abstract: It is still not fully understood exactly how neural networks are able to solve the complex tasks that have recently pushed AI research forward. We present a novel method for determining how information is structured inside a neural network. Using ablation (a neuroscience technique for cutting away parts of a brain to determine their function), we approach several neural network architectures from a biological perspective. Through an analysis of this method's results, we examine important similarities between biological and artificial neural networks to search for the implicit knowledge locked away in the network's weights.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: Develops unsupervised methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) for discovering important neurons in NMT models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates translation control by modifying individual neuron activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Modifying neuron activations allows for controlling translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Erasing top-ranked neurons (by the proposed methods) hurts translation quality more than erasing bottom-ranked neurons.
Individual neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Translation output can be controlled (e.g., tense, number, gender) by modifying the activations of specific neurons, though success varies by property.
Different ranking methods capture different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find token identity information.
The methods are task-independent and can be applied to other neural networks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is applied only to LSTM-based NMT models; application to other architectures like the Transformer is left for future work.
Controlling some properties (e.g., gender) is more difficult, possibly because they are more distributed than others (e.g., tense).
future_direction: Apply the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional sequence-to-sequence).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Analyze the spectrum of localized vs. distributed information in neural language representations more broadly.
papers.abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision. We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena. Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Understanding Neural Networks and Individual Neuron Importance via Information-Ordered Cumulative Ablation
papers.research_question: How do information-theoretic quantities (entropy, mutual information, and KL selectivity) relate to the classification performance and importance of individual neurons in trained neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that information-theoretic quantities (mutual information and KL selectivity) are positively correlated with neuron importance for classification when analyzed layer-wise, but not when compared across layers, and introduces information-ordered cumulative ablation as a method to study redundancy and synergy in neural network layers.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that it is ill-advised to compare information-theoretic quantities across layers due to their differing distributions, and that layer-wise analysis reveals a positive correlation between these quantities and neuron importance for classification, particularly in ReLU networks.
papers.key_findings:
Class selectivity is not a good indicator for classification performance when comparing neurons across different layers.
When analyzing neurons within a single layer, mutual information and class selectivity are positively correlated with classification performance, at least for networks with ReLU activation functions.
Information-ordered cumulative ablation can be used to formulate hypotheses about the redundancy and synergy of neurons within a layer.
The distribution of information-theoretic quantities (entropy, mutual information, KL selectivity) changes across layers, with deeper layers generally having higher values.
The correlation between these information-theoretic quantities and classification performance depends on the activation function and the regularization method used during training.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are restricted to fully-connected neural networks; results for convolutional, recurrent, or residual networks are not provided.
Results for networks with sigmoid activation functions or trained with batch normalization are inconclusive, showing at most weak correlation.
The quantization scheme used to estimate information-theoretic quantities is coarse, which may affect results.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other neural network classes such as convolutional, recurrent, or residual networks.
Investigate the use of finer quantization schemes to better estimate information-theoretic quantities.
Apply partial information decomposition (PID) to account for redundancy and synergy in neural network layers.
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate the use of three information-theoretic quantities-entropy, mutual information with the class variable, and a class selectivity measure based on Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence-to understand and study the behavior of already trained fully connected feedforward neural networks (NNs). We analyze the connection between these information-theoretic quantities and classification performance on the test set by cumulatively ablating neurons in networks trained on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10. Our results parallel those recently published by Morcos et al., indicating that class selectivity is not a good indicator for classification performance. However, looking at individual layers separately, both mutual information and class selectivity are positively correlated with classification performance, at least for networks with ReLU activation functions. We provide explanations for this phenomenon and conclude that it is ill-advised to compare the proposed information-theoretic quantities across layers. Furthermore, we show that cumulative ablation of neurons with ascending or descending information-theoretic quantities can be used to formulate hypotheses regarding the joint behavior of multiple neurons, such as redundancy and synergy, with comparably low computational cost. We also draw connections to the information bottleneck theory for NNs.

papers.title: Properties from Mechanisms: An Equivariance Perspective on Identifiable Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can we identify latent properties by leveraging knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that if the mechanisms governing latent evolution are known, then identification of latent representations is possible up to the equivariances shared by those mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: By exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of new identifiable representation learning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
With known deterministic mechanisms, latent representations are identified up to the equivariances of the mechanisms.
When only a hypothesis class of mechanisms is known, additional non-identifiability arises from imitation among mechanisms.
For affine mechanisms with distinct eigenvalues and sufficient offset diversity, identification up to an offset is achieved.
The mechanism-based perspective generalizes existing identifiable representation learning results, such as those in Klindt et al. (2020).
Stochastic mechanisms lead to similar identification results up to equivariances and imitators in distribution.
papers.limitation: The analysis assumes perfect reconstruction (bijective autoencoders), which is a strong and often impractical assumption.
future_direction: Developing practical algorithms that leverage mechanistic knowledge for representation learning.
Extending the theory to handle more complex and realistic mechanisms.
Addressing the open problems of scaling and applying the approach in practice.
papers.abstract: A key goal of unsupervised representation learning is "inverting" a data generating process to recover its latent properties. Existing work that provably achieves this goal relies on strong assumptions on relationships between the latent variables (e.g., independence conditional on auxiliary information). In this paper, we take a very different perspective on the problem and ask, "Can we instead identify latent properties by leveraging knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?" We provide a complete characterization of the sources of non-identifiability as we vary knowledge about a set of possible mechanisms. In particular, we prove that if we know the exact mechanisms under which the latent properties evolve, then identification can be achieved up to any equivariances that are shared by the underlying mechanisms. We generalize this characterization to settings where we only know some hypothesis class over possible mechanisms, as well as settings where the mechanisms are stochastic. We demonstrate the power of this mechanism-based perspective by showing that we can leverage our results to generalize existing identifiable representation learning results. These results suggest that by exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of new identifiable representation learning approaches.

papers.title: Emergence of functional and structural properties of the head direction system by optimization of recurrent neural networks
papers.research_question: Can a neural network recover both neural representations and the anatomical properties of neural circuits when trained on a goal-driven task?
papers.core_contribution: Training recurrent neural networks to perform head direction integration leads to the emergence of functional and structural properties that closely resemble biological head direction circuits.
papers.conclusion: Optimization of recurrent neural networks in a goal-driven task can recapitulate the structure and function of biological circuits, suggesting artificial neural networks can be used to study the brain at the level of both neural activity and anatomical organization.
papers.key_findings:
Two distinct classes of neurons (Compass units and Shifter units) emerged in the trained RNN, mirroring the functional organization observed in rodent and fruit fly head direction systems.
The connectivity patterns within the RNN showed local excitation and long-range inhibition among Compass units, and asymmetric connections from Shifter units to Compass units, aligning with known or hypothesized biological connectivity.
Perturbation experiments (lesioning) confirmed the functional roles of Compass units in maintaining a stable head direction representation and Shifter units in updating it based on angular velocity.
The network's functional organization adapted to input statistics: training with low angular velocities produced more Compass units, while high angular velocities produced more Shifter units.
The RNN could spontaneously generate and maintain a stable activity bump representing head direction through its recurrent connections, and this bump could be accurately shifted by the Shifter units.
future_direction: Future EM reconstructions together with functional imaging and optogenetics should allow direct tests of the model's predictions about connectivity.
The approach can be extended to study other neural systems beyond the head direction circuit.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests goal-driven training of neural networks can be used to model neural activity in the brain. While response properties of neurons in artificial neural networks bear similarities to those in the brain, the network architectures are often constrained to be different. Here we ask if a neural network can recover both neural representations and, if the architecture is unconstrained and optimized, the anatomical properties of neural circuits. We demonstrate this in a system where the connectivity and the functional organization have been characterized, namely, the head direction circuits of the rodent and fruit fly. We trained recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to estimate head direction through integration of angular velocity. We found that the two distinct classes of neurons observed in the head direction system, the Compass neurons and the Shifter neurons, emerged naturally in artificial neural networks as a result of training. Furthermore, connectivity analysis and in-silico neurophysiology revealed structural and mechanistic similarities between artificial networks and the head direction system. Overall, our results show that optimization of RNNs in a goal-driven task can recapitulate the structure and function of biological circuits, suggesting that artificial neural networks can be used to study the brain at the level of both neural activity and anatomical organization.

papers.title: Pruned Neural Networks are Surprisingly Modular
papers.research_question: What is the modular structure of multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) after training and weight pruning?
papers.core_contribution: Training and weight pruning produce MLPs that are more modular than randomly initialized networks, and dropout during training significantly increases modularity.
papers.conclusion: The process of learning via gradient descent and pruning selects for modularity, and modularity is closely associated with learning.
papers.key_findings:
Pruned neural networks are more modular than random networks with the same sparsity and weight distribution.
Networks trained with dropout are much more modular than those trained without dropout.
Modularity increases as a by-product of learning or memorization, not automatically from SGD or pruning alone.
Lesion experiments show that the identified modules have functional significance for network performance.
The modularity is not just due to topology; the specific weight values also contribute to clusterability.
papers.limitation: The paper provides almost no understanding of the specific function of 'modules', and we are as yet unable to infer any aspects of the behavior of the network from the techniques described.
future_direction: Extending results to larger networks trained on larger datasets.
Developing an appropriate notion of modularity for convolutional neural networks.
Understanding why networks are clusterable and why dropout has the effect it does.
papers.abstract: The learned weights of a neural network are often considered devoid of scrutable internal structure. To discern structure in these weights, we introduce a measurable notion of modularity for multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), and investigate the modular structure of MLPs trained on datasets of small images. Our notion of modularity comes from the graph clustering literature: a "module" is a set of neurons with strong internal connectivity but weak external connectivity. We find that training and weight pruning produces MLPs that are more modular than randomly initialized ones, and often significantly more modular than random MLPs with the same (sparse) distribution of weights. Interestingly, they are much more modular when trained with dropout. We also present exploratory analyses of the importance of different modules for performance and how modules depend on each other. Understanding the modular structure of neural networks, when such structure exists, will hopefully render their inner workings more interpretable to engineers. Note that this paper has been superceded by "Clusterability in Neural Networks", arxiv:2103.03386 and "Quantifying Local Specialization in Deep Neural Networks", arxiv:2110.08058!

papers.title: Natural language instructions induce compositional generalization in networks of neurons
papers.research_question: What neural computations allow networks to interpret linguistic instructions and perform novel tasks without explicit experience?
papers.core_contribution: Language instructions enable zero-shot generalization in neural networks by aligning sensorimotor representations with the semantic geometry of instructions, allowing composition of practiced skills for novel tasks.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how linguistic instructions induce compositional generalization in neural networks, offering testable predictions for neural representations underlying flexible cognition in the human brain.
papers.key_findings:
Models using sentence-level semantics (e.g., SBERT) achieve up to 83% correct zero-shot generalization on unseen tasks.
Language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that their geometry shares structure with instruction embeddings, facilitating compositionality.
Individual neurons in the sensorimotor network modulate their tuning based on the semantics of instructions.
The network can produce linguistic descriptions of novel tasks based solely on motor feedback, enabling knowledge transfer to partner models.
Generalization is supported by cross-condition generalization performance (CCGP) metrics that correlate with task performance.
future_direction: Guiding imaging studies to delineate brain areas involved in instruction following
Comparing compositional representations in nonlinguistic subjects like nonhuman primates
papers.abstract: A fundamental human cognitive feat is to interpret linguistic instructions in order to perform novel tasks without explicit task experience. Yet, the neural computations that might be used to accomplish this remain poorly understood. We use advances in natural language processing to create a neural model of generalization based on linguistic instructions. Models are trained on a set of common psychophysical tasks, and receive instructions embedded by a pretrained language model. Our best models can perform a previously unseen task with an average performance of 83% correct based solely on linguistic instructions (that is, zero-shot learning). We found that language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that activity for interrelated tasks shares a common geometry with the semantic representations of instructions, allowing language to cue the proper composition of practiced skills in unseen settings. We show how this model generates a linguistic description of a novel task it has identified using only motor feedback, which can subsequently guide a partner model to perform the task. Our models offer several experimentally testable predictions outlining how linguistic information must be represented to facilitate flexible and general cognition in the human brain.

papers.title: Engineering Monosemanticity in Toy Models
papers.research_question: How can we engineer monosemanticity in toy models? Specifically, can models be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by steering training to different minima, and how do bias and number of neurons affect monosemanticity?
papers.core_contribution: Models can be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by steering training to minima with moderate negative biases, and increasing the number of neurons per layer increases monosemanticity at the cost of compute.
papers.conclusion: Engineering monosemanticity in toy models is possible via negative biases and wider layers, pointing to future work on robust engineering and understanding polysemantic models.
papers.key_findings:
Models can be made more monosemantic without increasing loss by changing which local minimum training finds.
More monosemantic minima have moderate negative biases, enabling engineering of highly monosemantic models via negative bias initialization and weight decay.
Providing more neurons per layer makes models more monosemantic, albeit at increased computational cost.
In engineered monosemantic models, monosemantic neurons implement a simple algorithm balancing feature recovery against interference, and polysemantic neurons implement a low-rank linear map adjusting confidence.
The conclusions hold for various activation functions and feature frequency distributions.
papers.limitation:
The engineering approach is fragile because it depends on setting a bias weight decay rate that must be slow relative to the rate at which the model learns the task.
Naive introduction of sparsity in model weights results in significant reductions in task performance.
future_direction: Make the bias engineering more robust by tailoring bias decay per neuron or tying it to weight changes, or using regularizers.
Understand the algorithm implemented by highly polysemantic models.
Find ways to reduce compute cost of wider layers without excessive performance degradation.
papers.abstract: In some neural networks, individual neurons correspond to natural ``features'' in the input. Such \emph{monosemantic} neurons are of great help in interpretability studies, as they can be cleanly understood. In this work we report preliminary attempts to engineer monosemanticity in toy models. We find that models can be made more monosemantic without increasing the loss by just changing which local minimum the training process finds. More monosemantic loss minima have moderate negative biases, and we are able to use this fact to engineer highly monosemantic models. We are able to mechanistically interpret these models, including the residual polysemantic neurons, and uncover a simple yet surprising algorithm. Finally, we find that providing models with more neurons per layer makes the models more monosemantic, albeit at increased computational cost. These findings point to a number of new questions and avenues for engineering monosemanticity, which we intend to study these in future work.

papers.title: Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks
papers.research_question: How to attribute the prediction of a deep network to its input features in a way that satisfies fundamental axioms like Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Integrated Gradients, an attribution method for deep networks that satisfies Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance axioms, is simple to implement using gradients, and can be applied to various network architectures for debugging and rule extraction.
papers.conclusion: Integrated Gradients is a simple, axiomaticaly justified method for attributing predictions to input features, applicable to a variety of deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
Integrated Gradients satisfies Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance axioms, which are not satisfied by many prior attribution methods.
Integrated Gradients is the unique path method that is symmetry-preserving.
The method can be applied to image, text, and chemistry models for debugging and extracting rules.
Applied to a chemistry model, it helped identify degenerate features where atoms with the same type and bond counts were treated identically due to an architectural issue.
The method requires selecting a good baseline, and adversarial baselines can lead to attribution artifacts.
papers.limitation: The method does not address interactions between input features or the logic employed by the network.
papers.abstract: We study the problem of attributing the prediction of a deep network to its input features, a problem previously studied by several other works. We identify two fundamental axioms---Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance that attribution methods ought to satisfy. We show that they are not satisfied by most known attribution methods, which we consider to be a fundamental weakness of those methods. We use the axioms to guide the design of a new attribution method called Integrated Gradients. Our method requires no modification to the original network and is extremely simple to implement; it just needs a few calls to the standard gradient operator. We apply this method to a couple of image models, a couple of text models and a chemistry model, demonstrating its ability to debug networks, to extract rules from a network, and to enable users to engage with models better.

papers.title: Words in Motion: Extracting Interpretable Control Vectors for Motion Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we extract interpretable control vectors from hidden states of motion transformers to modify motion forecasts at inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that motion transformers exhibit neural collapse towards interpretable features, allowing extraction of control vectors that can modify predictions at inference. Using sparse autoencoders improves the linearity of control vectors and enables zero-shot generalization.
papers.conclusion: The work advances mechanistic interpretability and controllability of motion transformers by showing neural collapse and extracting interpretable control vectors. Sparse dictionary learning improves linearity and enables zero-shot generalization.
papers.key_findings:
High linear probing accuracy indicates neural collapse toward interpretable motion features in hidden states of motion transformers.
Control vectors extracted from hidden states can modify motion forecasts at inference while preserving feasibility.
Sparse autoencoders optimize control vectors, leading to more linear changes in predictions when scaling control vectors.
The method enables zero-shot generalization to unseen dataset characteristics, such as domain shifts in driving style.
The approach has negligible computational overhead at inference.
papers.limitation:
Assumed a flat latent space and relied on vector arithmetic, leaving investigation of latent space curvature for future work.
Analysis limited to probing accuracy and class-distance normalized variance for measuring neural collapse.
future_direction: Investigate how SAE parameterization might address potential latent space curvature.
Explore safety validation in latent space for end-to-end driving.
Use control vectors to modify internal representations via instruction-based inputs.
Incorporate features from other modalities (static and dynamic scene elements).
papers.abstract: Transformer-based models generate hidden states that are difficult to interpret. In this work, we analyze hidden states and modify them at inference, with a focus on motion forecasting. We use linear probing to analyze whether interpretable features are embedded in hidden states. Our experiments reveal high probing accuracy, indicating latent space regularities with functionally important directions. Building on this, we use the directions between hidden states with opposing features to fit control vectors. At inference, we add our control vectors to hidden states and evaluate their impact on predictions. Remarkably, such modifications preserve the feasibility of predictions. We further refine our control vectors using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). This leads to more linear changes in predictions when scaling control vectors. Our approach enables mechanistic interpretation as well as zero-shot generalization to unseen dataset characteristics with negligible computational overhead.

papers.title: Phase Diagram of Initial Condensation for Two-layer Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How does the scale of initialization affect the training dynamics and condensation phenomenon in two-layer neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes a phase diagram for initial condensation in two-layer neural networks, characterizing linear, condensed, and critical regimes based on initialization scales, and reveals the mechanism by which small initialization leads to condensation.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a phase diagram that comprehensively characterizes the dynamical regimes of two-layer neural networks based on initialization scales, providing insights into the condensation phenomenon and its dependence on hyperparameters.
papers.key_findings:
The training dynamics of two-layer neural networks exhibit three regimes—linear, condensed, and critical—depending on the initialization scales.
In the linear regime, weight vectors remain close to their initialization throughout training.
In the condensed regime, weight vectors condense toward the direction of z (the sum of y_i x_i) during initial training.
The condensation mechanism is explained by an effective linear dynamics approximation under small initialization.
The phase diagram is empirically validated through experiments with varying initialization scales.
future_direction: Extending the phase diagram to deeper neural networks.
Investigating other activation functions beyond smooth activations.
papers.abstract: The phenomenon of distinct behaviors exhibited by neural networks under varying scales of initialization remains an enigma in deep learning research. In this paper, based on the earlier work by Luo et al.~\cite{luo2021phase}, we present a phase diagram of initial condensation for two-layer neural networks. Condensation is a phenomenon wherein the weight vectors of neural networks concentrate on isolated orientations during the training process, and it is a feature in non-linear learning process that enables neural networks to possess better generalization abilities. Our phase diagram serves to provide a comprehensive understanding of the dynamical regimes of neural networks and their dependence on the choice of hyperparameters related to initialization. Furthermore, we demonstrate in detail the underlying mechanisms by which small initialization leads to condensation at the initial training stage.

papers.title: Language Through a Prism: A Spectral Approach for Multiscale Language\n Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent do deep models capture information at different scales (from subwords to documents), and can we force them to better capture structure across this hierarchy?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a spectral filtering framework to disentangle scale-specific information in language model representations and a prism layer that trains models to specialize neurons for different scales, improving performance on long-range tasks.
papers.conclusion: Spectral techniques are a powerful set of tools for uncovering and modeling multiscale phenomena in deep NLP models.
papers.key_findings:
Spectral filters can disentangle scale-specific information in BERT representations, with high-pass filters useful for word-level tasks and low-pass filters for document-level tasks.
The prism layer enables BERT to produce multiscale representations that improve performance on utterance- and document-level tasks while maintaining word-level performance.
Training with the prism layer increases the model's sensitivity to long-range context in masked language modeling.
The method is general and could be applied to other domains like images, audio, and video.
future_direction: Applying the spectral techniques to other domains such as computer vision, time series, and reinforcement learning models.
Using the tools for interpretability research to better understand knowledge and information processing at different scales.
Applying the method to track topics over time in linguistic change research.
papers.abstract:
Language exhibits structure at different scales, ranging from subwords to
words, sentences, paragraphs, and documents. To what extent do deep models
capture information at these scales, and can we force them to better capture
structure across this hierarchy? We approach this question by focusing on
individual neurons, analyzing the behavior of their activations at different
timescales. We show that signal processing provides a natural framework for
separating structure across scales, enabling us to 1) disentangle
scale-specific information in existing embeddings and 2) train models to learn
more about particular scales. Concretely, we apply spectral filters to the
activations of a neuron across an input, producing filtered embeddings that
perform well on part of speech tagging (word-level), dialog speech acts
classification (utterance-level), or topic classification (document-level),
while performing poorly on the other tasks. We also present a prism layer for
training models, which uses spectral filters to constrain different neurons to
model structure at different scales. Our proposed BERT + Prism model can better
predict masked tokens using long-range context and produces multiscale
representations that perform better at utterance- and document-level tasks. Our
methods are general and readily applicable to other domains besides language,
such as images, audio, and video.

papers.title: An Information Theoretic Approach to Reveal the Formation of Shared Representations
papers.research_question: How does network depth and input mixing affect the formation of shared representations (modality-invariant categorical representations) in a bimodal autoencoder?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an information theoretic approach to analyze the formation of shared representations in a bimodal autoencoder, demonstrating that deeper networks and a mixed-input framework enhance the development of modality-invariant categorical representations.
papers.conclusion: The information theoretic approach helps understand the formation of shared representations, and deeper networks with mixed-input frameworks facilitate better shared representations in bimodal autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
Shared representations (consistent visual and auditory cells) are formed in the autoencoder's hidden layers.
The number of cells forming shared representations increases with the depth of the network's encoding layers.
The mixed-input framework (concatenating modalities from the start) yields more shared representation cells than the two-stage framework (separate feature learning followed by correlation learning).
Classification performance in a shared-representation learning task is better with the mixed-input framework than the two-stage framework.
The information theoretic approach provides a quantitative measure of representation quality in hidden layers.
papers.abstract: Modality-invariant categorical representations, i.e., shared representation, is thought to play a key role in learning to categorize multi-modal information. We have investigated how a bimodal autoencoder can form a shared representation in an unsupervised manner with multi-modal data. We explored whether altering the depth of the network and mixing the multi-modal inputs at the input layer affect the development of the shared representations. Based on the activation of units in the hidden layers, we classified them into four different types: visual cells, auditory cells, inconsistent visual and auditory cells, and consistent visual and auditory cells. Our results show that the number and quality of the last type (i.e., shared representation) significantly differ depending on the depth of the network and are enhanced when the network receives mixed inputs as opposed to separate inputs for each modality, as occurs in typical two-stage frameworks. In the present work, we present a way to utilize information theory to understand the abstract representations formed in the hidden layers of the network. We believe that such an information theoretic approach could potentially provide insights into the development of more efficient and cost-effective ways to train neural networks using qualitative measures of the representations that cannot be captured by analyzing only the final outputs of the networks.

papers.title: Selectivity considered harmful: evaluating the causal impact of class selectivity in DNNs
papers.research_question: Is class selectivity in individual units necessary and/or sufficient for DNN function?
papers.core_contribution: Class selectivity in individual units is neither necessary nor sufficient for CNN performance, and can even impair it; reducing selectivity can improve accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Class selectivity in individual units is neither necessary nor sufficient for CNN performance, and can be detrimental. This encourages caution when focusing on single-unit properties and emphasizes distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
Reducing class selectivity can improve test accuracy, e.g., by over 2% for ResNet18 on Tiny ImageNet.
Class selectivity can be reduced by a factor of 2.5 in ResNet20 on CIFAR10 with no impact on test accuracy, and nearly to zero with only a small drop.
Increasing class selectivity significantly decreases test accuracy across all models and datasets.
The regularizer suppresses selectivity generally, not just by rotating it off-axis, indicating viability of low-selectivity distributed representations.
Networks are at a performance cliff with regard to class selectivity; naturally learned levels are at the limit of what impairs performance.
papers.abstract: The properties of individual neurons are often analyzed in order to understand the biological and artificial neural networks in which they're embedded. Class selectivity-typically defined as how different a neuron's responses are across different classes of stimuli or data samples-is commonly used for this purpose. However, it remains an open question whether it is necessary and/or sufficient for deep neural networks (DNNs) to learn class selectivity in individual units. We investigated the causal impact of class selectivity on network function by directly regularizing for or against class selectivity. Using this regularizer to reduce class selectivity across units in convolutional neural networks increased test accuracy by over 2% for ResNet18 trained on Tiny ImageNet. For ResNet20 trained on CIFAR10 we could reduce class selectivity by a factor of 2.5 with no impact on test accuracy, and reduce it nearly to zero with only a small ($\sim$2%) drop in test accuracy. In contrast, regularizing to increase class selectivity significantly decreased test accuracy across all models and datasets. These results indicate that class selectivity in individual units is neither sufficient nor strictly necessary, and can even impair DNN performance. They also encourage caution when focusing on the properties of single units as representative of the mechanisms by which DNNs function.

papers.title: Properties from Mechanisms: An Equivariance Perspective on Identifiable\n Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can we identify latent properties by leveraging knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?
papers.core_contribution: If we know the exact mechanisms under which latent properties evolve, then identification can be achieved up to any equivariances that are shared by the underlying mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: By exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of new identifiable representation learning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
When the true mechanism is known, the system is identified up to any equivariances of the mechanism.
With multiple known mechanisms, identification is up to equivariances shared by all mechanisms.
When only a hypothesis class of possible mechanisms is known, additional non-identifiability arises via imitation among mechanisms.
For affine mechanisms with distinct eigenvalues and certain conditions, identification is up to an offset.
The framework generalizes to stochastic mechanisms and can recover existing identifiability results, such as those in Klindt et al. (2020).
papers.limitation: The analysis assumes the encoder/decoder functions are bijective and that reconstruction is perfectly solved, which is a strong assumption and not easy in practice.
papers.abstract:
A key goal of unsupervised representation learning is "inverting" a data
generating process to recover its latent properties. Existing work that
provably achieves this goal relies on strong assumptions on relationships
between the latent variables (e.g., independence conditional on auxiliary
information). In this paper, we take a very different perspective on the
problem and ask, "Can we instead identify latent properties by leveraging
knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?" We provide a complete
characterization of the sources of non-identifiability as we vary knowledge
about a set of possible mechanisms. In particular, we prove that if we know the
exact mechanisms under which the latent properties evolve, then identification
can be achieved up to any equivariances that are shared by the underlying
mechanisms. We generalize this characterization to settings where we only know
some hypothesis class over possible mechanisms, as well as settings where the
mechanisms are stochastic. We demonstrate the power of this mechanism-based
perspective by showing that we can leverage our results to generalize existing
identifiable representation learning results. These results suggest that by
exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of
new identifiable representation learning approaches.

papers.title: Critical Learning Periods in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do deep artificial neural networks exhibit critical periods during training similar to biological systems, and how does the early training phase affect the final performance and network connectivity?
papers.core_contribution: Deep neural networks exhibit critical periods during training where early sensory deficits cause permanent performance impairment, and this phenomenon is linked to a loss of 'Information Plasticity' measurable via the Fisher Information of the weights.
papers.conclusion: Critical periods are not restricted to biological systems but emerge naturally in learning systems due to fundamental constraints arising from learning dynamics and information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks exhibit critical periods: early sensory deficits (e.g., image blur) can cause permanent impairment in final performance.
Sensitivity to deficits peaks during the early rapid learning phase and decreases afterward.
High-level deficits (e.g., vertical flip, label permutation) do not induce critical periods.
The Fisher Information of the weights shows two phases: an initial increase (memorization) followed by a decrease (consolidation), and deficit sensitivity correlates with Fisher Information.
The loss of 'Information Plasticity' (inability to redistribute information across layers) underlies the critical period phenomenon.
future_direction: Exploring whether biological networks prune connections as a consequence of a loss of Information Plasticity, rather than as a cause.
papers.abstract: Similar to humans and animals, deep artificial neural networks exhibit critical periods during which a temporary stimulus deficit can impair the development of a skill. The extent of the impairment depends on the onset and length of the deficit window, as in animal models, and on the size of the neural network. Deficits that do not affect low-level statistics, such as vertical flipping of the images, have no lasting effect on performance and can be overcome with further training. To better understand this phenomenon, we use the Fisher Information of the weights to measure the effective connectivity between layers of a network during training. Counterintuitively, information rises rapidly in the early phases of training, and then decreases, preventing redistribution of information resources in a phenomenon we refer to as a loss of "Information Plasticity". Our analysis suggests that the first few epochs are critical for the creation of strong connections that are optimal relative to the input data distribution. Once such strong connections are created, they do not appear to change during additional training. These findings suggest that the initial learning transient, under-scrutinized compared to asymptotic behavior, plays a key role in determining the outcome of the training process. Our findings, combined with recent theoretical results in the literature, also suggest that forgetting (decrease of information in the weights) is critical to achieving invariance and disentanglement in representation learning. Finally, critical periods are not restricted to biological systems, but can emerge naturally in learning systems, whether biological or artificial, due to fundamental constrains arising from learning dynamics and information processing.

papers.title: Interpretation of Deep CNN Based on Learning Feature Reconstruction With Feedback Weights
papers.research_question: How can we interpret a deep CNN by learning feature reconstruction with feedback weights to understand which features contribute to recognition and evaluate recognition success?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes attaching a feedback CNN to a pretrained feedforward CNN to interpret the deep CNN by reconstructing features and analyzing clusters in feature spaces, enabling accurate recovery of ground truth, generation of novel inputs, and identification of recognition errors.
papers.conclusion: The feedback weights provide a means to interpret the deep CNN, and the clustering-based interpretation and feature interpolation algorithm offer meaningful insights into neuron collaboration and recognition.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed approach accurately recovers ground truth input under data corruption.
It generates novel input data corresponding to an untrained feature vector without input data iterations.
It identifies incorrectly recognized input data by pinpointing the source of error in feature spaces.
The experiments on ModelNet datasets show higher accuracy than conventional approaches.
future_direction: Extend interpretation to connect semantic knowledge while extracting meaningful features using a deep neural network.
papers.abstract: Interpreting a deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) involves identifying the features in a hierarchy of layers that contribute to recognition. Although the current approaches serve as methods to interpret a deep CNN, further advancement is required for a more accurate and efficient way of understanding how a hierarchy of features formed by a deep CNN contributes to recognition. In this paper, we propose attaching a feedback CNN to a pretrained feedforward CNN as a means of learning how recognition is performed by the feedforward CNN. In other words, the features reconstructed in a hierarchy of the feedback CNN represent those learned by the feedforward CNN. By analyzing how clusters are formed in the layers of feature spaces in the feedback CNN, we can interpret which features critically contribute to recognition. It also helps to evaluate whether or not recognition is done successfully. In order to show this, we experimentally verify the capabilities of the proposed approach in terms of 1) accurately recovering the ground truth input under data corruption; 2) generating novel input data corresponding to an untrained feature vector without input data iterations; and 3) identifying incorrectly recognized input data by pinpointing the source of the error in feature spaces. The experiments conducted on the ModelNet datasets indicate that the proposed approach offers an extended capability of interpreting a deep CNN as described above with higher accuracy than the conventional approaches.

papers.title: Learning from Emergence: A Study on Proactively Inhibiting the Monosemantic Neurons of Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether reducing monosemantic neurons in neural networks can improve performance, and proposes a method to proactively inhibit them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes that reducing monosemantic neurons improves model performance and introduces a metric (Monosemantic Scale) and a method (Reverse Deactivation) to inhibit monosemantic neurons during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that proactively inhibiting monosemantic neurons via the proposed MEmeL method can improve model performance across various tasks and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
MEmeL improves performance on language (GLUE), image (ImageNet), and precipitation forecasting (HKO-7) tasks.
Monosemanticity decreases with model scale, and inhibiting it can lead to better performance.
Naive deactivation methods can intensify monosemanticity, while the proposed Reverse Deactivation method effectively reduces it.
The proposed Monosemantic Scale metric enables efficient online detection of monosemantic neurons.
Pretraining with MEmeL shows greater improvement than finetuning with it, supporting the hypothesis that reducing monosemanticity enhances general ability.
papers.limitation: Extending the research to very large models (e.g., large language models) is appealing yet impossible for research departments due to limited computational resources.
future_direction: Extending the method to extremely large models trained on large datasets.
Studying the dynamics of MEmeL in more depth.
papers.abstract: Recently, emergence has received widespread attention from the research community along with the success of large-scale models. Different from the literature, we hypothesize a key factor that promotes the performance during the increase of scale: the reduction of monosemantic neurons that can only form one-to-one correlations with specific features. Monosemantic neurons tend to be sparser and have negative impacts on the performance in large models. Inspired by this insight, we propose an intuitive idea to identify monosemantic neurons and inhibit them. However, achieving this goal is a non-trivial task as there is no unified quantitative evaluation metric and simply banning monosemantic neurons does not promote polysemanticity in neural networks. Therefore, we first propose a new metric to measure the monosemanticity of neurons with the guarantee of efficiency for online computation, then introduce a theoretically supported method to suppress monosemantic neurons and proactively promote the ratios of polysemantic neurons in training neural networks. We validate our conjecture that monosemanticity brings about performance change at different model scales on a variety of neural networks and benchmark datasets in different areas, including language, image, and physics simulation tasks. Further experiments validate our analysis and theory regarding the inhibition of monosemanticity.

papers.title: Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity
papers.research_question: Is there a general mechanism behind a broad suite of subliminal effects in language model training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Logit-Linear Selection (LLS), a method to select subsets of preference data that subliminally transfer behaviors, and provides a theoretical framework based on log-linearity to explain the phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: LLS provides a general mechanism for subliminal effects in language models, grounded in the log-linear structure of language models, with implications for data selection and safety.
papers.key_findings:
LLS can select subsets of real-world datasets to elicit hidden effects such as specific preferences, responding in a different language, and adopting a persona.
The subliminal effect persists across models with varying architectures, demonstrating universality.
The mechanism is explained by the log-linear abstraction and linear representations of language models.
Subliminal learning can occur even when the dataset contains no obvious instances of the target behavior.
The method works with preference data and can transfer behaviors across teacher-student model pairs, though more effectively when models are the same.
papers.limitation: The subliminal effect is weaker when the teacher and student models are different, and the reasons for this variation are not fully understood.
future_direction: Understanding the factors that account for variations in subliminal learning across different student models.
Developing defenses against subliminal learning in datasets.
Applying LLS for jailbreaking closed models and watermarking datasets.
papers.abstract: Training modern large language models (LLMs) has become a veritable smorgasbord of algorithms and datasets designed to elicit particular behaviors, making it critical to develop techniques to understand the effects of datasets on the model's properties. This is exacerbated by recent experiments that show datasets can transmit signals that are not directly observable from individual datapoints, posing a conceptual challenge for dataset-centric understandings of LLM training and suggesting a missing fundamental account of such phenomena. Towards understanding such effects, inspired by recent work on the linear structure of LLMs, we uncover a general mechanism through which hidden subtexts can arise in generic datasets. We introduce Logit-Linear-Selection (LLS), a method that prescribes how to select subsets of a generic preference dataset to elicit a wide range of hidden effects. We apply LLS to discover subsets of real-world datasets so that models trained on them exhibit behaviors ranging from having specific preferences, to responding to prompts in a different language not present in the dataset, to taking on a different persona. Crucially, the effect persists for the selected subset, across models with varying architectures, supporting its generality and universality.

papers.title: Complexity for deep neural networks and other characteristics of deep feature representations
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the nonlinearity and effective dimensionality of feature representations in deep neural networks, and how do these measures vary with depth, dataset, and during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces two observables—complexity and effective dimension—to quantify the nonlinearity and dimensionality of feature representations in deep neural networks, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing depth-wise hierarchy, dataset difficulty, and training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The introduced observables provide quantitative insight into the information processing and feature representations in neural networks, and can be applied to both artificial and biological neural systems, opening up new research directions.
papers.key_findings:
Complexity and effective dimension increase with the difficulty of the dataset.
During training, complexity increases first, followed by a rise in effective dimension.
Total correlation between neurons decreases during training, following a power law.
The observables can be applied to biological neural data (mouse visual cortex) and show similar trends.
The observables reveal a depth-wise hierarchy in feature representations, with higher layers having higher complexity and effective dimension for more difficult datasets.
papers.limitation: The method is defined for ReLU activations and may not generalize to other activation functions.
future_direction: Investigate interrelations with the Information Bottleneck principle.
Use methods from statistical physics (e.g., Ising models) for analysis.
Apply the observables to more complex networks and tasks.
papers.abstract: We define a notion of complexity, which quantifies the nonlinearity of the computation of a neural network, as well as a complementary measure of the effective dimension of feature representations. We investigate these observables both for trained networks for various datasets as well as explore their dynamics during training, uncovering in particular power law scaling. These observables can be understood in a dual way as uncovering hidden internal structure of the datasets themselves as a function of scale or depth. The entropic character of the proposed notion of complexity should allow to transfer modes of analysis from neuroscience and statistical physics to the domain of artificial neural networks. The introduced observables can be applied without any change to the analysis of biological neuronal systems.

papers.title: Learning-induced reorganization of number neurons and emergence of numerical representations in a biologically inspired neural network
papers.research_question: How does numerosity training reorganize neuronal tuning properties and population-level representations in a biologically inspired neural network?
papers.core_contribution: Numerosity training reorganizes neuronal tuning and population representations, leading to the emergence of sharp numerosity tuning and latent magnitude representations in a biologically inspired neural network.
papers.conclusion: Our findings elucidate mechanisms by which learning builds novel representations supporting number sense.
papers.key_findings:
Numerosity training reorganizes spontaneous number neurons (SPONs), with most SPONs dropping or switching their preferred numerosity.
Training increases tuning precision, stability, and selectivity of number-sensitive neurons, especially in the IPS layer.
Ablation shows that persistent SPONs are not critical for numerosity classification; newly trained and switched neurons are more important.
Representational similarity analysis reveals increased differentiation between numerosities after training.
Multidimensional scaling reveals latent representations of absolute magnitude and relative magnitude (midpoint anchoring) post-training.
papers.abstract: Number sense, the ability to decipher quantity, forms the foundation for mathematical cognition. How number sense emerges with learning is, however, not known. Here we use a biologically-inspired neural architecture comprising cortical layers V1, V2, V3, and intraparietal sulcus (IPS) to investigate how neural representations change with numerosity training. Learning dramatically reorganized neuronal tuning properties at both the single unit and population levels, resulting in the emergence of sharply-tuned representations of numerosity in the IPS layer. Ablation analysis revealed that spontaneous number neurons observed prior to learning were not critical to formation of number representations post-learning. Crucially, multidimensional scaling of population responses revealed the emergence of absolute and relative magnitude representations of quantity, including mid-point anchoring.
